News.title: Two teens arrested for murder 6 months after dad-of-three stabbed to death
News.content:
BLADE ARRESTS Two teens arrested for murder 6 months after dad-of-three stabbed to death







Next

TWO teens have been arrested after a dad-of-three was stabbed to death earlier this year.

Adrian Brown, 34, had been at the West Indian Sports and Social Club in Moss Side, Manchester, on May 8 when he was attacked at around 11pm.



The musician, known as Dre, suffered severe stab wounds to the chest and sadly died in hospital.

Addressing the incident, Detective Superintendent Toby Facey described it as a “shocking act of violence” as cops launched an investigation.



A 17-year-old boy and 18-year-old man were arrested on suspicion of murder today, cops said.

Police have also arrested a 27-year-old woman on suspicion of assisting an offender.



All three remain in custody for questioning.

In a heartbreaking tribute, his partner Tamia Zameer said at the time of his death: “R.I.P to my number one, Adrian.

“I love you always and forever. Me and your boys will cherish every moment that we had.

“We will miss you so much. Your legacy will forever live on and I will get the justice that you deserve.”



Adrian’s mum, Jennifer Meade, said: “My son, you did not deserve this. I can’t put into words how I feel. They took my boy.

“He was a loving son, brother, uncle, boyfriend, and he adored being a dad to my grandkids. I will miss you so much.

“Rest in peace, son. I love you more than you know.”

Detective Inspector Alex Wilkinson, of Greater Manchester Police (GMP), said the force had been working “tirelessly” to figure out what happened to Adrian that night.

“These arrests show the progress we are continuing to make and our commitment to bring offenders to justice,” he said.



“Our thoughts continue to be with Adrian’s family who have been updated on the investigation throughout and are being supported by specially trained officers.

“It has been almost six months since the fatal stabbing took place at the West Indian Sports and Social Club in Moss Side.

“We’d like to thank the people that have come forward since that night, however we believe that there may be more people out there who saw this tragic incident.

“All information is vital to our investigation to ensure we can support Adrian’s family and get justice for him.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Cops are urging anyone with information or footage to get in touch either online or over the phone.



Information can also be shared anonymously on the Greater Manchester Police website.

News.title: Labour’s immigration U-turn could leave taxpayers facing £5.2BILLION-a-year benefits bill, Tories warn
News.content:
Next

LABOUR’s immigration U-turn could leave taxpayers facing a £5.2billion-a-year benefits bill, the Tories warned last night.

Nearly half a million migrants granted permanent residency by 2030 could end up claiming Universal Credit, according to new Conservative analysis.



Their warning comes after Shabana Mahmood watered down her immigration crackdown after pressure from some Cabinet Ministers and more than a 100 Labour MPs.

Shadow Work and Pensions Secretary Helen Whately fumed: “Our country cannot afford the ballooning benefits bill. People who come to the UK should be contributing, not drawing benefits.



“We will prioritise Brits in the welfare system and stop giving benefits to immigrants. Indefinite Leave to Remain and Limited Leave to Remain will no longer give automatic access to Universal Credit and sickness benefits.

“This will save billions and there’s a principle at stake here too: British citizenship matters We are not a cash machine for the world.”

Home Office forecasts suggest 1.4million migrants will secure settlement by 2030, with the Tories estimating around 450,000 could claim Universal Credit if current claiming rates continue.

Their analysis found nearly one in three settled non-EU migrants already receive the benefit – with numbers soaring by almost 83,000 since June 2024.

The £5.2billion figure is a Conservative projection based on current claiming rates, rather than an official estimate of the cost of Labour’s concessions.

It comes after Ms Mahmood allowed nearly 300,000 foreign care workers and their families to retain a five-year route to settlement while also ditching proposals to make migrants wait until British citizenship before claiming benefits.

News.title: Fury as smoky-bacon flavoured crisps could be headed for the chop under Burnham’s Brexit reset
News.content:
Next

SMOKY bacon-flavoured crisps could be heading for the chop under Andy Burnham’s post-Brexit deal with Brussels.

They may breach EU regulations which ban “meaty” names on vegetarian food to supposedly stop shoppers from getting the wrong end of the stick.



That could spell trouble for veggie chicken and meat dishes for hard-working Brits if the PM agrees to follow the bloc’s new rules.

Britain and the EU agreed a food and drink deal before a summit taking place at the end of November.



Labour has agreed to align with EU plant and animal health rules including on labelling.

It comes as ketchup, mayonnaise and vinegar sachets could be banned from cafes and restaurants as the PM tries to align the UK with the EU.

The bloc has outlawed single-use plastic packaging for condiments in the catering sector on environmental grounds from January 1, 2030.

The regulations will forbid European restaurants and hotels from offering ketchup and mayonnaise sachets to dine-in customers from January 2030, to cut down on “unnecessary” waste.

The packets are also going to be banned in Northern Ireland under post-Brexit arrangements that require the country to follow some EU rules.

A No 10 spokesperson said: “A ban on single-serving sachets is not in the scope of any agreement with EU partners.



“It is not part of our EU reset.

“If any consultation on single-use sachets is taken forward, it will be solely as a result of the UK choosing to do so”

News.title: China bizarrely tries to claim bomb is a WINE bottle after its artillery shell was found in another country
News.content:
HINT OF GUNPOWDER China bizarrely tries to claim bomb is a WINE bottle after its artillery shell was found in another country







Next

CHINA has attempted to claim that a large military-grade explosive found in a shipping container in another country was simply a wine bottle.

The 32kg object, cylindrical with a pointed end, is just a “shell-shaped wine bottle”, Beijing insisted.



The explosive export was found in Papua New Guinea, where police identified it as a working artillery shell.

Four Chinese citizens were arrested after the alarming discovery at a shipping wharf in Port Moresby.



Papua New Guinea cops x-rayed the shell to verify its lethal contents after it was found on Friday.

A police report confirmed that the item was an undetonated 130mm Type 59 Artillery Projectile, packed with chemical explosives and a fuse, according to the Australian Broadcasting Corporation.



But China continued to claim that the 32kg object was simply a “shell-shaped wine bottle” that “poses no danger at all”.

The object sparked a diplomatic row between the two nations, as Beijing insisted that such a weapon could never have been exported from its shores.

The Chinese Embassy in Papua New Guinea wrote on Facebook: “China enforces some of the world’s strictest firearm control laws and regulations.

“Therefore, it is virtually impossible for an illegal military-grade artillery shell to be smuggled out of China to PNG.”



Some shared images online of an “artillery round replica militaria bottle holder” that is sold on Etsy.

But the replica was made of plastic, and significantly lighter than the object found in the shipping container.

One bemused commenter asked: “What sort of wine bottle weighs 32kg?”



Cops dismissed the idea that it could be a dummy.

Papua New Guinea’s military and police launched a joint investigation after finding the shell, said police commissioner David Manning.

He explained: “Police acted quickly upon receiving information that the artillery round had been discovered.

“The area was secured to prevent the risk of harm in the surrounding area.

“This enabled police and military explosive disposal experts to move in, examine the device and have it safely moved to be stored in a secure facility.”



It comes as island nations like Papua New Guinea have become caught up in power plays between China and the West, as powers compete for access to the Second Island Chain.

The strategic string of islands hosts naval bases which act as barriers to China’s sea operations.

Australia signed a defence deal with Papua New Guinea last October, the first of its kind.

Aussie PM Anthony Albanese and PNG’s foreign minister Justin Tkatchenko both slammed a Chinese nuclear-capable ballistic missile test in the Pacific that took place in July.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

And last week Australia’s defence minister Richard Marles warned China’s massive military build-up in the region was whipping up “conditions of pressure” in southeast Asia.



He said: “We’re obviously seeing the biggest conventional military build-up that the world has seen since the end of the Second World War from China.”

News.title: Britain is overspent, overborrowed and overtaxed yet Burnham STILL hands out cash
News.content:
Next

ANDY BURNHAM wants to please everyone, but if he keeps giving everything away we will have nothing left.

Four months into the job, and we still haven’t found anyone he is willing to say no to — apart from businesses begging him not to put up their taxes.



He forced Keir Starmer out of No10 with no plan other than to get his hands on the public credit card and embark on a spending spree for his backbenchers.

Look at the latest immigration chaos.



The Home Secretary, Shabana Mahmood, promised to be tough on indefinite leave to remain but all it took was a few grumpy Labour MPs to complain and Burnham caved.

On the face of it this is an immigration issue, but it is also another chance for Burnham to tap the public credit card.



Now low-paid foreign-born care workers will be able to get settlement after just five years, at a cost to the taxpayer of ­billions of pounds.

A price he seems to be willing to pay to buy off people in his own party.

Now add to that the already ballooning bill for working-age benefits, which will soon hit an eye-watering £183billion a year.

That’s more than we spend on defence, schools and policing put together.



It works out at about £10,000 for every working household in the country — ­especially hard to stomach at a time when families are feeling the pinch.

And now we hear this week from Burnham’s trip to the Commonwealth that he wants to apologise (again) for Britain’s part in the slave trade.

He said he wouldn’t put reparations on the table, but when asked whether his apology could end up costing taxpayers more, he couldn’t give a straight answer.



This is the trouble with a Prime Minister who simply cannot say no.

Once you open the door to more demands, where does it end? The bill could be enormous, and it won’t be Burnham picking up the tab.

The job of a Prime Minister is not to please everyone. It is to make difficult choices in our country’s best interests.

Britain is overspent, overborrowed, overtaxed and drowning in an out-of- control welfare system.

Every day that Andy Burnham ducks hard decisions and hands out more cash, Britain slides deeper into a mess of the Labour Party’s making.



At the Budget last month, he had a chance to do the right thing and cut wasteful spending.

Instead, he and his Chancellor spent yet more money we don’t have on things we can’t afford.

Labour’s welfare addiction has maxed out Britain’s credit cards, and the Government is taking out more credit cards to pay down that debt.



You’d have to be completely hard of thinking to believe that is a good idea.

Our children and grandchildren will one day be paying for their stupidity.

Hard-working taxpayers are already being crushed under the highest tax burden in our country’s history.

But worst of all, at a time when Russia might attack one of our Nato allies, Britain cannot fund our defence because the Prime Minister is giving all our money away.

We simply can’t afford Andy Burnham. If he is too weak to stand up to Labour backbenchers and French exchange students, what chance does he stand against Vladimir Putin?



This week he said he is going to release a ten-year plan. That’s very ambitious for a man without a ten-month plan.

But now we hear it will be a consultation instead! A plan to consult on a plan. And who knows how much cash he’ll have handed out by the time that’s finished.

Britain doesn’t need a Prime Minister working out what he thinks. We need a leader who already understands the difficult choices we must make and has the courage to make them. That is what my new Conservative Party have a plan to do.

We will cut spending by £70billion and get millions of people off welfare and back into work. The Labour Party think that is cruel, but any parent knows that sometimes the kindest thing is to say no.

We will cut the deficit by £35billion, and start living within our means. Borrowing so much is making our ­country poorer and weaker.



No other party in British politics seems to care about the mess we are leaving for our children.

We will fund Britain’s defence properly, because the world is a dangerous place and we are already under threat.

Cyber-attacks are happening every day on British businesses, and Russian warships are in the English ­Channel. There is no time to waste.

Then, we will cut your taxes. Because a strong economy will make life better for every single person in this country.

Under the Conservatives, there will be more opportunity, life will be more affordable and people will be rewarded for working hard and doing the right thing.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

That is what a real plan for this country looks like, and those are the decisions a serious leader would take. Britain cannot afford three more years of Andy Burnham spending like there’s no tomorrow because he wants to people please.

He should be taking the tough decisions, or he should get out of the way so ­someone else can.

News.title: FBI to search Thomas Markle’s rented US lock-ups for potential THIRD stash of child abuse images after tip-off from son
News.content:
Next

LOCK-UPS rented by Thomas ­Markle Snr in Hollywood are to be searched by the FBI as they investigate a potential third cache of child abuse images.

The probe will run alongside those into the Duchess of Sussex’s estranged father, 82, in the Philippines and Mexico.



The US agents were alerted to two units on the same site in Los Angeles following a tip-off from son Thomas Jnr, 60.

He told The Sun: “I dread to think what they might find.”



Thomas Markle’s son was interviewed for two hours by the FBI over the potential third cache of child sex images allegedly belonging to his father.

It meant the net is widening on the Duchess of Sussex’s estranged dad — following major investigations in the Philippines and Mexico.

Thomas Jnr told The Sun: “My father told me about the two units years ago. He’s had them for about 15 years.

“One is stuffed to the brim with Meghan’s old furniture. The other is packed with boxes, books, photos, mementoes for his career in Hollywood, stuff from Meghan’s college days and God knows what else.

“There’s something there, that’s my gut feeling, I dread to think what the FBI might find, especially given what has been found in the Philippines and Mexico.”

Thomas Jnr was interviewed at his home in Cordova, Philippines, as part of an international, multi-agency meeting over Microsoft Teams.



He gave his statement to an FBI agent based in Florida, where his dad is in a dementia home, plus a supervising agent who specialises in child sex abuse cases.

Also present on the call were an Assistant US Attorney, an FBI legal attache in the Philippines and numerous senior officers in its National Police (PNP).

Yesterday, officers from the PNP visited Thomas Jnr’s home in Cordova to log and clear the remaining tranche of his dad’s belongings.



The items, in several boxes, include family photos, some with Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, as a young girl.

Other items included a printer, frames, clothes and some Buddha statues, which the pensioner collected.

It is understood the officers were keen to have as much fingerprint evidence as possible.

Thomas Jnr said his dad, a former TV lighting director, had been paying £520 a month to rent the lock-ups in Los Angeles.

Receipts show Markle Snr paid a big brand storage firm as recently as October 21.



Thomas Jnr recalled his dad mentioning the units several times and his need to visit them.

He said: “I remember when we lived in Mexico he’d say he needed to travel to LA to his storage units.

“We tried to do this several times but he cancelled every time. At that point I never really thought anything of it. My dad lived in the city for many years so there could be stuff dating back years.



“Several family members offered to collect his stuff and pack it up, but he said, ‘No, no, no’.

“I did go there once with my dad but I didn’t go inside the unit.

“I stayed in the lobby because he told me to wait. What’s so secretive that he wouldn’t let anyone else access them? I know he gets billed around $700 (£520) for two units every month on autopay because I still get the receipts emailed to me.

“It’s been a tough few weeks so it never really entered my mind to tell anyone about the units until the haul was found in Mexico.

“I think it’s important the FBI searches the LA units as soon as possible. The more I’m learning about my dad, the more I am deeply shocked.”



Thomas Jnr has given the address for the facility to the FBI, but it was not clear when agents will raid it.

Last week we revealed in a world exclusive that Markle Snr was being probed by cops in the Philippines after his son handed over child sex abuse images he found in his dad’s things.

A second stash was then found in a lock-up in Mexico sparking a criminal probe there.



Thomas Jnr has submitted several legal affidavits to the Filipino authorities.

He said: “It’s been a long process but I’m determined to cooperate fully in the hope that justice will be done.”

Thomas Jnr became his father’s full-time carer after he suffered a stroke in 2022 and moved to Mexico to support him.

The pair moved to the Philippines in January 2025 before a blood clot led to the amputation of Markle Snr’s left leg.

He had treatment in Florida in May, leaving behind a collection of belongings in which his son claims to have found “hundreds, if not thousands” of child abuse images.



Markle Snr claims to have dementia and was transferred to a specialist care home last Friday.

Most pictures found in Mexico appeared to date from when he was in his 40s or 50s, following his 1987 divorce from Meghan’s mother, Doria Ragland.

Nearly half appeared to show the same young Asian female.

In one, Markle Snr is allegedly pictured sitting beside her on a hotel bed, with both fully clothed.

Other images reportedly show her naked in the same room.



Another 16 photos were said to show other naked girls.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Philippines, interior minister, Jonvic Remulla has said that all signs point to Markle Snr being a “possible sex offender of the grossest kind”.

Markle Snr has denied any wrongdoing, branding the claims made by his son “sick lies”.

News.title: Thomas Markle locked in ‘crisis talks’ with daughter at care home as he’s probed over ‘stash of child sex abuse images’
News.content:
Next

THOMAS Markle Snr was locked in “crisis talks” with daughter Samantha for over three hours at his care home in Florida.

The meeting came on Tuesday – the day it was announced police in the Philippines were “very close” to bringing formal charges against the 82-year-old over an alleged stash of child sex abuse images.



Markle Snr denies the allegations against him.

We revealed Samantha transferred the estranged father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex to a specialist memory care facility from a rehabilitation centre on Friday.



He claims to have developed dementia but only mentioned it after The Sun’s explosive allegations against him.

The day he moved to the new home was the same day it was reported a second alleged child abuse hoard was found.



Sources said Samantha spent hours with him on Tuesday to supposedly discuss an FBI investigation after her brother Thomas Jnr handed over the alleged stash to Filipino cops.

An insider said: “It was very odd.



“She was there for an unusually long time – they had a lot to discuss.

“Since the meeting she’s stopped speaking about the allegations on social media.

“Someone clearly has told her to stay quiet.”

Samantha, who was dropped off by her long-term partner Mark Phillips, hurried into the home clutching a Chik-Fil-A takeaway for Markle Snr.

Her boyfriend had earlier delivered a Big Gulp – a whopping 1litre cup of fizzy drink – for him to enjoy.



A source said: “His appetite for junk food has clearly not been affected.”

Samantha hid her face under a blanket in an attempt to go incognito.

But on the way out, Samantha was unable to hide a scowl and had two handbags with her.

Just minutes after, a small child was brought into the facility by their mum.

She looked to be visiting another patient with suspected paedo Markle Snr just yards from her.

News.title: PM is so desperate for EU ‘reset’ he appears willing to pay almost any price however extortionate, damaging or demeaning
News.content:
Surrender to EU







Next

IT hardly seemed possible but Andy Burnham is turning out to be an even worse negotiator for this country than Sir Keir Starmer.

So desperate is the Prime Minister for a “reset” with the EU that he appears willing to pay almost any price, however extortionate, damaging or demeaning.



Virtually every demand the Brussels bullies make, he is ready to capitulate.

And for what in return? The lifting of a few nitpicking checks on British food exports.



It leaves hard-pressed British taxpayers on the hook for costly new roads and green energy schemes in poorer EU nations, while Burnham signs us up to the bloc’s detrimental trade regulations and our own public services buckle.

He is also expected to fold in the face of pressure to shell out £450million to subsidise tuition fees at UK universities for European students.



Of course, it won’t end there. Like a blackmailer smelling weakness, the EU is already back for more.

It now wants the PM to rip up plans to deport foreign criminals back to Europe immediately.

So we will pay a king’s ransom to keep thousands of EU murderers, rapists and drug dealers in OUR jails.

And when they are eventually released, it will be to prowl OUR streets, endangering ordinary Brits.



How is that a good — or fair — deal?

Britain voted to leave the sclerotic, small-minded EU. Not to become its cash machine and a repository for its hardened criminals.

Got no Plandy

ON his first day as Prime Minister, Burnham confidently declared he had “a plan” to reinvigorate the nation.

Four long months on, it remains non-existent.

While we know our TikTok-obsessed PM’s stance on bar snacks and other banalities, we are clueless on what he will do about the biggest challenges facing Britain.



His long-promised “ten-year” blueprint for power was meant to shed some light.

Now left-wing bible New Statesman says even that has been downgraded to a humdrum pre-Christmas speech and ANOTHER interminable consultation.

Meanwhile, we are drowning in debt, the welfare bill is out of control and ferociously high taxes are crushing prosperity. Last week, the Chancellor had a perfect opportunity to jolt some life into the flatlining economy.

Exasperated M&S boss Stuart Machin hit the nail on the head yesterday when he dismissed the Budget as a “whole lot of nothing”.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Burnham is either unable or unwilling to take tough decisions. Insofar as he has a plan, it seems to be tax more, spend more and borrow more.



As Tory leader Kemi Badenoch argues, Britain cannot afford the cost of three more years of Andy Burnham.

News.title: Brit man infected with Ebola to be flown back to UK amid deadliest-ever outbreak
News.content:
Brit man infected with Ebola to be flown back to UK amid deadliest-ever outbreak

The British healthcare worker is expected to be flown back to the UK by medical evacuation

View 2 Images The Brit will be the fourth European to be medically evacuated after testing positive for the disease (Image: AP Photo/Sebastien Kitsa Musayi)

A British man in the Democratic Republic of Congo will be brought back to the UK for treatment after testing positive for Ebola, the Government has said.

‌



‌



The patient is understood to be a healthcare worker and is expected to be flown back to Britain by medical evacuation, though it is not clear when the flight will take place.

‌



A UK Government spokesperson said that the UK has 'well-established procedures' for cases like this, which have been activated.

‌



The FCDO spokesperson said: “A British citizen currently in the DRC has tested positive for Ebola. The UK has well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this, and those processes have been activated. Further information will be shared in due course as appropriate. The risk to the UK public from Ebola remains low.”

View 2 Images Health workers clean equipment inside a Ebola treatment camp in Butembo, DR Congo (Image: AP Photo/Sebastien Kitsa Musayi)

Dr Damien Tully, associate professor at the Medical Research Council/Uganda Virus Research Institute and London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine Uganda Research Unit, said news of the British man’s infection was “deeply concerning, but it is not entirely unexpected”.

‌



He added: “Healthcare workers are on the front line of these outbreaks, often treating severely ill patients under extremely challenging conditions. Even with rigorous protective measures, accidental exposures can occur.

“This case is a stark reminder of the risks faced by those responding to the outbreak of Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus in the DRC. However, it does not suggest that the virus has become more transmissible or that the threat to the UK has increased.”

‌



Dr Tully added that the risk to the British public “from this planned medical evacuation is extremely low” because Ebola is “transmitted primarily through direct contact with infected bodily fluids, and people are not generally infectious until they develop symptoms”.

More than 5,000 people have died in the DRC's deadliest-ever Ebola outbreak, which began in May and has seen more than 10,300 confirmed cases.

‌



A fatality rate of 48.6 per cent was reported at the end of last month for the illness. There are no approved treatments or vaccines to combat the disease, which is caused by the Bundibugyo virus.

The World Health Organisation has warned that the outbreak is on course to surpass West Africa's 2014-2016 epidemic, which killed more than 11,000 people.

Article continues below

Only four cases of Ebola have ever been confirmed in the UK, including three involving health workers who responded to the outbreak in West Africa between 2014 and 2015.

Last week, an Ebola patient was medically evacuated from Nigeria to Switzerland. Since May, two patients have been medically evacuated to Germany and one to the Netherlands. A fourth case was reported in France in July. All four people worked in healthcare or humanitarian roles in affected areas of the DRC, according to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control.

News.title: Is Prince Harry still taking petty swipes at his father? Why 'dig' at King Charles proves he hasn't moved on
News.content:
Is Prince Harry still taking petty swipes at his father? Why 'dig' at King Charles proves he hasn't moved on

The Duke of Sussex publicly announced he would not be taking on any engagements during his father’s Caribbean tour, with the Mirror’s Pod Save the King YouTube show delving into the ulterior motive for this

View 3 Images Prince Harry with his estranged father King Charles (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

Prince Harry was trying to "quell the fears" of the Palace when sources close to him assured he would not undertake any engagements during the King’s Caribbean tour, according to the Mirror ’s royal editor Russell Myers.

‌



‌



As the King’s tour has drawn to a close, Russell questioned on the Mirror's Pod Save The King YouTube show if the Duke was trying to placate the Palace with the statement, and pave the way to a reconciliation with his father. Russell said: “I do think it was rather interesting that we had to hear from Harry and make those comments about, ‘I'm not going to torpedo my father's tour.’ It would have been absolutely catastrophic, I suppose, if he had done that.

‌



"Very, very damaging for relations if they're trying to move that forward. But interesting that he felt that he needed to say that. Is he trying to make these public statements to quell the fears within the Palace and his own family?”

‌



Prince George leans on Prince William during secret trip abroad as they watch Aston Villa defeat READ MORE :

Content cannot be displayed without consent

The Mirror’s deputy royal editor Jennifer Newton countered that the statement may have been a subtle dig at the King and palace aides, as he complained previously about the Firm not sharing their calendar to avoid such clashes. Jennifer said: “I think it was quite interesting what a source close to Harry said, which was, ‘Well, I don't ever set out to overshadow my dad and brother, but they don't always share diaries with me, and that's fine.’ Which I thought that’s fair enough, but that was still a little bit of a dig, wasn't it?”

King Charles wrapped up his nine-day tour of the Caribbean today, which saw him visit the island nations of the Bahamas, Guyana, and Antigua and Barbuda, undertaking countless engagements before delivering an address at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting. As the monarch’s tour kicked off, a source close to the Sussexes told said Harry was mindful to not overshadow the nine-day trip by booking in his own appearances.

‌



View 3 Images Harry said he did not want to overshadow the King's Caribbean trip (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

The insider told the Times: “Harry doesn't set out with an intention to try to pull focus or draw attention away from what his father is doing or what his brother is doing. That's never his intention at all, but obviously for him to be able to mitigate against that he does need to have decent foresight of what's coming up."

‌



The source claimed that the Sussexes aren’t always informed in advance of events and are unable to withdraw from commitments so they do not disappoint charities. They added: “He can only mitigate against clashes if information is shared with him in advance. Some information is shared, but not all information is and that's fine."

View 3 Images Russell Myers and Jennifer Newton on Pod Save the King

‌



Just hours after the King jetted home from his Caribbean visit, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex announced that they would be heading to Belgium next week. In Brussels, Harry and Meghan will deliver a joint keynote address at the opening of the Lost Screen Memorial in the European Parliament.

The Lost Screen Memorial has been created by Harry and Meghan’s Archewell Foundation to commemorate the lives of children who have lost their lives as a result of the harm they suffered on social media. It was unveiled in New York last year and taken to Geneva earlier this year, where Meghan gave a keynote speech.

Article continues below

Afterwards, Harry will join a panel discussion in the European Parliament, which will consider how children can be protected online. The panel will cover topics including the responsibilities of tech companies and preventing online child sexual abuse and exploitation.

News.title: 'A little rich of him': Why the Tories have no right to lecture Labour on border control
News.content:
'A little rich of him': Why the Tories have no right to lecture Labour on border control

Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp laid into Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood earlier this week when she unveiled a massive overhaul of settlement rules for migrants

View 3 Images

Tory criticism of Labour's immigration reforms is a "little rich" after their record in power, the Mirror's Political Editor Lizzy Buchan has said.

‌



‌



Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp laid into Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood earlier this week when she unveiled a massive overhaul of settlement rules for migrants. Under the plans, half a million people face longer waits for indefinite leave to remain (ILR) as the standard wait to qualify will double from its current five years. High earners and NHS staff will be among those who can apply sooner.

‌



Ms Mahmood announced a carve out for care workers as she rowed back on controversial plans to make them wait up to 15 years to qualify. Mr Philp accused her of carrying out a humiliating U-turn - and claimed she'd bowed to pressure from within her party.

‌



Speaking to the Mirror's Nicola Thorp on the Sense Check show, Lizzy said it was difficult for the Tories to attack Labour after their record in Government on immigration. Net migration surged after Brexit, peaking at 944,000 in year ending March 2023. It was dubbed the "Boris wave" by critics.

Shabana Mahmood's huge changes to UK immigration rules explained in full READ MORE :

View 3 Images Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp tried to attack Shabana Mahmood over immigration reforms (Image: Jordan Pettitt/PA Wire)

Lizzy said: "The Conservatives were in charge when so many people came over. As was Chris Philp. I think it's quite hard for the Conservatives to really land blows with those kinds of attacks considering they not only allowed lots of people to come here legally during those years when Boris Johnson was PM and after, but also they allowed the asylum system to get out of control.

‌



"They started housing people in hotels. They're responsible for so much of that. So I think it's a little rich of him to say that. And actually... these reforms are really tough. [They are] far more hard line than anything the Conservatives did."

Mr Philp authorised use of asylum hotels as an immigration minister in the pandemic, which ramped up under the Tories. Labour has pledged to end use by the end of this Parliament.

‌



View 3 Images Lizzy Buchan Mirror Political Editor said 'The Government are trying to bring immigration under control and therefore starve Farage and his gang of that argument and that ability to kind of whip people up."

‌



Nigel Farage was nowhere to be seen in the Commons when Ms Mahmood delivered her statement on Monday - choosing instead to deliver an "emergency" press conference outside of Parliament.

Asked about Reform's response, Lizzy said: "It's a bit of a tricky one for Reform in a way because they want to get rid of ILR completely and replace it with, I think, rolling sort of five-year visas. But the plans are quite tough, and so it's not that easy for him to come at Shabana Mahmood... So I think it's quite tricky for them.

Article continues below

"Actually, that's part of why Labour's doing it, really. It takes some of the air out of what Reform are trying to argue about Britain's immigration system being totally out of control. The Government are trying to bring it under control and therefore starve Farage and his gang of that argument and that ability to kind of whip people up."

News.title: Helicopter crashes close to Florida beach days after jet disaster as one killed
News.content:
Helicopter crashes close to Florida beach days after jet disaster as one killed

One person has died and two others have been injured after a helicopter crashed in the waters off Key Biscayne in Florida

View Image The helicopter crashed in the waters off Key Biscayne in Miami-Dade County, Florida (Image: 7Skyforce)

One person has died and two others have been injured after a helicopter crashed into the water in Florida.

‌



‌



The helicopter went down near Key Biscayne, in Miami-Dade County, shortly before 11.30am local time (4.30pm GMT) on Wednesday.

‌



Miami-Dade Fire Rescue said crews were called at 11.26am to reports of a helicopter crash near Bill Baggs Cape Florida State Park. The US Coast Guard confirmed that one person died and that two people are receiving "a high level of care". In a statement, the Southeast Coast Guard said: "Three people were on the aircraft. One person is reported deceased and two people were transported by EMS to a higher level of care."

‌



Miami Fire Rescue said the two people taken to hospital were men. Their ages and relationship were not immediately known.

Authorities have not released further details about the person who died.

‌



Footage captured by a 7Skyforce helicopter showed what appears to be the wreckage of the aircraft submerged in the water, with its yellow skid floats visible above the surface.

Online flight trackers indicate that the helicopter had been flying over Biscayne Bay for around five minutes before its altitude suddenly dropped at around 11.17am.

‌



The aircraft had departed North Perry Airport at 10.48am and travelled towards Biscayne Bay, where it spent around 13 minutes before the crash.

The incident comes just days after a Learjet 60 travelling from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas, crashed on a street near Greenacres in Palm Beach County, Florida, around 75 miles north of Bill Baggs State Park.

Article continues below

Those killed in Sunday's crash included entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife Helen Sharp and their two young children, Emma and Charlie. Two friends of the couple, Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, and the children's nanny, Anita Maria Cetina, were also killed, alongside the pilot, Jeff Gregory, and his 20-year-old co-pilot, Nathalia Filgueiras.

The private jet nosedived before crashing in a fireball about nine miles from President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago resort.

News.title: Brits back Andy Burnham on slavery apology as Ed Miliband says taxpayers won't be hit
News.content:
Brits back Andy Burnham on slavery apology as Ed Miliband says taxpayers won't be hit

The legacy of the transatlantic slave trade has dominated Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s first trip to the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua

View 2 Images Andy Burnham and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband play steel pans during a visit to Hells Gate Orchestra Steel Pan Yard in St. John's, Antigua and Barbuda (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

British people have endorsed Andy Burnham’s stance to consider an apology for slavery but oppose reparations as the Prime Minister held crunch talks with Commonwealth leaders.

‌



‌



The legacy of the transatlantic slave trade has dominated the PM’s first trip to the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua. Ahead of the summit, Mr Burnham signalled he is open to a formal apology for Britain’s vile role in the trade of enslaved people but has been clear reparations are not on the table.

‌



A poll for YouGov found Brits support issuing an official apology for Britain’s role in the slave trade by 52% to 37%. But 65% are opposed to paying reparations to affected countries, with only 21% in favour.

‌



Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband reiterated that British taxpayers will not pay a penny more as a result of Mr Burnham’s “new approach” to the Commonwealth. Speaking to BBC Newscast, he accused previous governments of a “sweep under the carpet” approach to slavery but ruled out extra financial contributions.

John Healey rejects slavery reparations calls as Antigua PM wades into row moments after Charles meeting READ MORE :

View 2 Images Andy Burnham has opened the door to a formal apology on slavery (Image: Kin Cheung/Press Association)

Asked if taxpayers would contribute more, he said: "No. And that’s – for us, that’s never been what it’s about. And that’s why it’s been important that you know, and I did have this conversation with our partners in advance. I said, ‘look, we are going to say we are willing to say that we’re open to an apology, but we’re not going to shift our position on reparations.’

‌



“It’s not for us. It’s not the right answer. It’s not practical. It’s not feasible for us, but there are things we can work on co-operatively.”

He added: “And you know there’s been a lot of acceptance of that, and I mean people have been honestly a bit bruised by the past, what happened in the past, the sense that we just really just wanted to sweep this issue under the carpet and not confront it.

‌



“My sense is there’s a bit of a sigh of relief that OK well at least you know at least there’s a sense of we’ve got a shared interest now in moving the Commonwealth on.”

He also criticised what he described as a “sorry, not sorry” from Sir Tony Blair, who in 2006 expressed “deep sorrow and regret” for Britain’s involvement in the slave trade but stopped short of an official apology.

‌



Commonwealth members have welcomed the shift in position on an apology from the British state. A communique to be signed at the end of the summit is expected to welcome the UK’s promise of structured dialogue over the issue.

Music-mad Mr Burnham tried his hand at playing the steel drum on Wednesday, performing a rendition of Mary Had a Little Lamb alongside the Hell's Gate steel orchestra.

‌



Director Khan Cordice told him “you’re a musician”, to which Mr Burnham replied: “I play a little music.” He was later joined by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband for a duet.

The PM previously showed off his skills when he was handed a guitar by a Ukrainian soldier on a visit to Kyiv, playing “Rusholme Ruffians” by The Smiths.

Article continues below

:: YouGov surveyed 2,258 adults living in Great Britain between November 2 and 3 ::

News.title: Dustin Hoffman on affair with married woman: 'her husband walked in with a gun'
News.content:
The Graduate made Dustin Hoffman a global filmstar and yet he hated it for one main reason… he has acne. Of his role as graduate Benjamin Braddock, who is seduced by Mrs Robinson (Anne Bancroft) the bored wife of his father’s business partner, he says: "After The Graduate, I went back to the theatre in New York, because it was a horrible experience. I was fighting acne.”

Dustin hated the close-ups of his face, adding: "I've had lifelong acne, literally. I mean, I take Accutane [acne treatment] three times a week, or else I'd look like a 15-year-old. I'm 89 and I still have, you know, lifelong acne." Now, with more than 70 movies under his belt, in a career spanning 60 years, Dustin has won two best actor Oscars - for Kramer vs Kramer (1979) and Rain Man (1988) and was nominated for The Graduate (1967), Midnight Cowboy (1969) Lenny (1974, Tootsie (1982) and Wag the Dog (1997).

He adds: "I was paid $3,000 for The Graduate [worth $30,000 today]. I remember I went back to the unemployment office in New York and, at that time, Life Magazine had taken a photo of me. I was the most famous face in America waiting in the unemployment line to get a $50 cheque, which you could live on. I became this cultural icon, but I just wanted to go back to the theatre.

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

‌



“I remember my father saying to me ‘do you know how lucky you are?’ He was right. I mean, what are the odds of someone being in their first film with the best director of all time, at that moment, who was Mike Nichols? To be cast in that, not only is it a hit, but it becomes this phenomenon. What's the odds? A million to one? Two million?"

View 6 Images 1989: Dustin Hoffman poses with the Oscar he won for best actor for his role in the film Rain Man (Image: Bettmann Archive)

Looking back, he jokes that playing a 21-year-old seduced by an older woman, was ‘triggering.’ He says: "In my youth, I was having an affair with a married woman. She thought that once her husband went to sleep, he stayed asleep.

‌



"So there we were, having a festival of sorts, and he walked in with a gun. He pointed it at me and said ‘get out, get out’. When you have a gun pointed at you, you realise, ‘This is it. I'm gonna die, I'm gonna die’. And you will do anything, you know, to avoid getting killed!"

Speaking on the US podcast, Conan O'Brien Needs A Friend, ahead of the release of his new memoir, Look At Me, on Tuesday, produced with the help of The New Yorker magazine writer, Ariel Levy, Dustin says working at Macy’s kickstarted his acting career.

He worked in the New York department store alongside his former room-mates, then young aspiring stars - Gene Hackman and Robert Duvall. He remembers: "I sold hockey games. Someone would come by shopping and they would start playing with me. I started to get good at it, and because I'm an actor, I tried to be a retired, hurt, French hockey player. Gene was right there working at adult games also."

View 6 Images Dustin Hoffman as Benjamin Braddock and Anne Bancroft as Mrs Robinson in The Graduate

‌



Dustin and Hackman moved to New York seeking fame, after performing at the Pasadena Playhouse in California during the 1950s. Hackman was 27 and Dustin was19. He says: "I did not think I would ever get into acting. I was supposed to be the failure in the family. My brother was a triple-A student, he was an athlete.

"He was asked to be on a major baseball team when he graduated, but chose college because he thought he'd have a longer career. I was the designated failure. I was very comfortable with that. Nobody expected anything from me. I was a very bad student. The worst. Nobody fails acting."

He certainly hasn’t - although he says he almost walked out of Rain Man, which he starred in alongside Tom Cruise, as he didn’t know how to portray his character, autistic savant Raymond Babbitt. He says: "The first day of shooting we're looking at a car in a scene. I looked at the daily rushes and said to my wife, ‘I'm quitting. I don't know what I'm doing’.

"Tom is a really decent human...despite his good looks. But I could not do the scene. We were about to run out of film and the director said ‘just improvise’. So it's just Tom and I on the hidden camera, and we're acting away. Then we run out of film. I said, ‘I'm out of here, I cannot play this guy’.”

‌



View 6 Images Dustin Hoffman and Gene Hackman at the 1968 Academy Awards, where Hoffman was nominated for Best Actor in The Graduate and Hackman was nominated for Best Supporting Actor in Bonnie and Clyde (Image: Bettmann Archive)

But, accidentally, Dustin had nailed it. He continues: “Suddenly, the director goes, ‘that's it. We have it. That's the guy you were looking for’".

Disguising himself as a woman for the comedy Tootsie was another massive challenge. He recalls: "I said to Columbia Pictures ‘I do not want to do this unless I can be believable in makeup, hair, as a woman. I don't want to walk down the street and have people turning in real life and saying, ‘Who's that guy in drag?’ Finally we found a way.”

While movie bosses were convinced by his performance, his daughter, Jenna - then a teenager - was horrified. Dustin says: “She was in eighth grade at school at the time. I said to myself, ‘I'm going to go there and test it out’. So I went there in costume. I went up to one of her teachers and started talking and I got away with it.

‌



View 6 Images Dustin Hoffman and Jon Voight on Willis Avenue Bridge from 'Midnight Cowboy' 1969 (Image: Getty Images)

"But Jenna was furious. She came up to me and said, ‘get out of here, Dad, how can you do this to me?’ She recognised me!"

Turning back to earlier days, he remembers taking the part of Ratso Rizzo, an impoverished small-time conman, in Midnight Cowboy (1969) - a small part, considering his massive profile after The Graduate. He says: “Mike Nichols who produced The Graduate calls me up. He says, ‘what are you doing? It's not even the lead, it's a supporting part. Why are you trying to destroy? I made you a star.’ I didn't want to be a star. I only wanted to do good work.”

Meanwhile, Dustin, at least partly, credits an allergy for his longevity. Recalling the making of Marathon Man (1976) Dustin says: “That was a time when you went to a party and there were lines of coke, you know, on a table. Everybody snorted. I did. Thank God I'm allergic, because I couldn't breathe after that. I was allergic to it or I wouldn't be here now.”

‌



View 6 Images Lisa Hoffman and Dustin Hoffman (Image: Getty Images for AFI)

Married to businesswoman Lisa Hoffman - having divorced from his first wife, actress and ballerina Anne Byrne, in 1980 - apart from suffering with sniffles and needing to leave himself reminder notes around the house, the father of six is showing few signs of his advancing years.

Sticking to his early philosophy, after The Graduate brought him instant fame, he says: “Even if you become a star you are still you.”

But, despite his own attempts at self-sabotage, when he tried to turn his back on his early fame, Dustin remains a worldwide star. In fact, the only thing he has ever really failed at is being the family failure.

‌



*Dustin Hoffman's new memoir, Look At Me, published by Simon & Schuster, is out next Tuesday, priced £25.

News.title: Screens and homework harming children's creativity, parents say
News.content:
Screens and homework harming children's creativity, parents say

Parents believe digital devices are impacting their child's creativity - along with homework and busy routines.

View 3 Images Parents say screen time is affecting their child's creativity (Image: PinPep)

Three quarters of parents believe their children's creativity is being stifled by screen time, homework and over-scheduled lives. A survey of 2,000 parents revealed that youngsters spending excessive time on digital devices (49%) was the single biggest obstacle to them developing their creativity.

‌



‌



This was followed by homework (47%), hectic morning and evening routines (29%) and insufficient free time after school (20%). However, parents also confessed their own commitments are not helping. As well as feeling tired, 62% say work obligations frequently prevent them from supporting their child with creative pursuits. This was along with having to manage household and family duties.

‌



View 3 Images Ashley Banjo joined members of Devas Youth Club to help unleash their creativity (Image: PinPep)

‌



Parenting expert Sue Atkins has joined forces with Ben's Original, which commissioned the study, to assist parents in reducing mealtime stress and enabling families to discover more time for creativity together.

Sue Atkins said: “Creativity doesn’t have to mean expensive toys, elaborate activities or hours spent making things.

“Some of the loveliest opportunities for children to use their imaginations happen in everyday moments - helping prepare dinner, inventing stories or simply chatting around the table.

‌



“When children are invited to join in, experiment and have fun without worrying about getting things right, they’re building confidence, curiosity and connection.”

The research emerges as Ben's Original has partnered with BBC Children in Need, launching limited-edition Pudsey microwaveable rice packs and unveiling its "Do Something Great with Every Plate" campaign, pledging £200,000 to support children and young people facing challenges across the UK.

‌



The research revealed that 84% of parents believe children are under more pressure than ever before, while 56% admitted their little ones avoid creative activities for fear of 'getting it wrong'.

View 3 Images More than half of parents say their child worry about getting things wrong (Image: PinPep)

‌



School tests and grades (57%), expectations from adults (49%) and fear of being laughed at (48%) were amongst the key contributing factors. Despite this, 41% of parents are keen to enjoy more imaginative activities with their children.

Those looking to nurture creativity do so to boost their child's confidence and self-expression (75%), happiness and mood (68%) and mental health and emotional wellbeing (64%). With parents noticing their children are happier (31%), calmer (23%), and more confident (20%).

‌



Celebrity Ashley Banjo joined members of Devas Youth Club to help unleash their creativity by painting custom designs onto plates, followed by a DIY dinner.

Ashley Banjo said: “As a dancer, you quickly learn that you’re not going to get every move right the first time. You have to give it a go, get things wrong and keep going; that’s all part of the fun.

‌



“I loved seeing the kids at the youth club this week, seeing them lose themselves in creativity, then sit down for a meal together.

“It was a reminder of why spaces and wider initiatives like this are so important in local communities."

News.title: Vance sensationally turns on Trump's war as VP fights for his political future
News.content:
Vance sensationally turns on Trump's war as VP fights for his political future

JD Vance has turned on Donald Trump's Iran war, saying it is the reason for the Republican disaster in the midterm elections, as he weighs his own political future and a possible run for president

View 2 Images JD Vance said the Iran war was the reason for the disaster in the midterm elections (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

United States Vice President JD Vance has turned on Donald Trump's Iran war, blaming it for the disaster in the midterm elections.

‌



‌



In a nationwide romp, Democrats ousted Republicans from coast to coast, with many surprising places in between, as voters rejected the president’s party for the promise of something different for the country.

‌



And Vance has been quick to blame the war in Iran as he weighs his political future and a possible run for president in 2028.

‌



Vance listed all the other reasons the party lost in an X post - and appealed to Republican voters to give the party another chance.

"The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night," Vance said.

‌



View 2 Images JD Vance appears to be positioning himself for a run for president (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

Donald Trump faces two-year nightmare after Republican wipeout in midterms READ MORE :

US steps up Iran war fears and moves military assets into Middle East as UK becomes more of a terror target READ MORE :

His message was that backers of the Iran war should take responsibility for the defeat, with Trump having championed the conflict.

‌



"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest," he said.

The results have set up a divided government, with Congress poised to reassert itself as a coequal branch ready to challenge Trump and reverse course after two years of unified Republican control.

‌



And Trump has been consulting with advisers on whether Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth should be sacked, stated CBS News sources. While it has also been reported that blame is expected to land on Adm Brad Cooper, head of US Central Command, and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen Dan Caine, who both played big roles in guidance on the Iran war.

The Iran war has led to an increase in inflation globally and it appears that rising prices as well as the state of the democracy were the main reasons for the poor showing by the Republicans.

‌



Democrats are promising a 100-day agenda starting with efforts to lower the costs of gas, groceries and other goods, as well as bills to reverse cuts to the Affordable Care Act and Medicaid healthcare programmes. They’re also ready to launch a robust oversight agenda to, as House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries says, “hold the crooks accountable.”

Impeachment — of the president or his Cabinet members — is also an option. The top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, Rep Robert Garcia of California, issued a one-sentence warning: “Lawyer up.”

‌



Sen Ron Wyden, the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, issued his own one-word missive: “Subpoenas.” Democrats will be under pressure to quickly show that they have solutions for the high gas and grocery prices, the war in Iran and concerns about the direction of the country.

For Jeffries and his leadership team, it will be their first time in the majority, managing a class of newcomers including a handful of far-left democratic socialists.

Article continues below

With the majority in the 435-member House well past the 218 needed and the Senate Democrats holding at least 54 of 100 seats in that chamber, Jeffries and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer will have room to manoeuvre.

News.title: Bowen: Trump's loss limits powers at home, but it will likely be different abroad
News.content:
In the weeks leading up to the midterms the deployment of US forces and Trump's own, often belligerent, statements ramped up talk that the US was getting ready to go back to war with Iran.

On the eve of the elections, the US carried out a limited bombing raid on an Iranian island in the Gulf.

Before he was hospitalised with a stroke, the US Senator Chris Murphy, a Democrat, went to a classified briefing about potential military options for renewed war with Iran.

Without going into detail, he condemned the plans as "insane", warning that they would trigger a "devastating escalation".

There has been speculation that the Americans have plans to bomb civilian infrastructure.

Not only would that be likely to constitute a war crime, it might also be answered by devastating Iranian strikes on equivalent targets on US allies in the Gulf. Its list of potential targets could start with the United Arab Emirates, which is as close to Israel as it is to the US.

The regime in Tehran watches political developments in the US closely. It has not concealed its satisfaction that the consequences of its blockade of the Strait of Hormuz have become a domestic political issue in the US.

Tehran is aware of the damage caused to Trump and the Republicans by the sustained rise in the prices of everything (from petrol and diesel to agricultural fertilisers) caused by the war and its attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

The Speaker of Iran's parliament, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, posted a warning on social media.

He said: "Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message. If the US govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare."

Benjamin Netanyahu, now acting prime minister of Israel after its election last week, and manoeuvring hard to form a new government, has repeated that he wants to bring down the Islamic regime in Tehran.

Reports in Israel and the US say that he is pushing Trump to go back to war.

Netanyahu does not have the seats to form a new government with his outgoing coalition.

But if a major war restarted and was sustained, and if Israelis came under direct fire, he could have new options of forming a unity government that he would use his considerable political skills to dominate.

News.title: What Democrats can and can't do with their new power after taking Congress
News.content:
Election night was a fever dream for Democrats. In January, reality will set in.

They had a reason to be giddy on Tuesday night: Next year, Democrats will take control of both chambers of Congress after a blowout victory.

"Today begins the great American comeback," an ecstatic Hakeem Jeffries, House Democratic leader, declared.

After months of promises on the campaign trail â to investigate corruption; lower the costs of healthcare, groceries and petrol; and curtail the Iran war â they will now begin the much tougher process of putting plans into action.

A shift in the balance of power in Washington doesn't necessarily mean Democrats will immediately get to start checking items off their legislative wish list. Democrats have Congress, but Republican President Donald Trump still has the power to reject legislation.

The Democrats should not consider what just happened "a mandate," US Senator Chris Coons told the BBC, warning that the party was still "deeply unpopular".

"We need to prove we can get stuff done, actually deliver answers to their concerns and questions about low wages and rising costs in particular."

News.title: Everything you need to know from the US midterm elections
News.content:
Talarico's supporters went beserk as the projected results arrived at an election-night party, wrote the BBC's Gary O'Donoghue. Attendees hugged, kissed and drank to a reality they dared not believe would come true.

Hinojosa became the first Latina to be elected governor of the state.

Among the other states where history was made by the Democrats were Kansas, where Adam Hamilton took a closely-fought Senate seat - giving the state its first Democratic senator for nearly a century.

Senior party figures who cheered the results included Hakeem Jeffries, the top Democrat in the House of Representatives, who is now poised to take over as the Speaker of the lower chamber of Congress.

"Today begins the great American comeback," he told a crowd of supporters.

If Jeffries' colleagues choose to keep him as the leader of their party's delegation in House, he will be the next Speaker, taking over from Republican Mike Johnson and becoming the first black person to fill that role.

News.title: How voter shifts in Texas helped elect a Democratic senator and governor
News.content:
History was made in Texas on Tuesday with two stunning victories for the Democrats. For the first time in history, Texas elected its first Latina governor, and the first Democrat governor since 1995. It also elected its first Democratic senator since 1988.

These results follow a widespread public pushback against President Donald Trump's handling of his first two years back in office.

The BBC's Ros Atkins breaks down the dramatic shift in the state between the 2024 election and the 2026 midterms.
