World.title: Liberia: From Extraction to Eco-Prosperity, What Liberia Can Learn from Anji, China’s Bamboo Revolution
World.content:
Monrovia–Liberia’s environmental future will depend on choices that go beyond one focused. The country must determine how to manage its forests, wetlands, rivers, and agricultural landscapes while expanding employment, improving public health, and creating opportunities for rural communities.

By Willie N. Tokpah

Anji County China is one area that offers evidence that ecological protection and economic development can reinforce one another when conservation is supported by investment, effective institutions, market access, and locally relevant industries.



This President Xi Xiapin’s concept in his speech at 2020 at the 75th UN General Assembly at the United Nations on Carbon Nutrality, where following that, he launch3d an initiatie of using bamboo as a substitute for plastic.

A policy was also issued on Octover 15, 2026, by the Chinese Government, which prevented the production of plastic takeaway containers for food or shopping bags in China. This is intended to address some global problems such as Climate Change, plastic polution and other environmental problems.

With approximately 10 billion tons of plastics being produced by the world and only 10 percent being used properly and efficiently and recycling plastic remains costly. China believed that using bamboo as a substitute for plastic is an answer for the world since bamboo is totally biodegradable.

What if Liberia’s forests, rivers, wetlands ,and other natural resources could become a stronger source of jobs, healthier communities, and sustainable income for the people who depend on them? That concern is gaining relevance following a visit by Liberian media representatives to Anji County in eastern China, during a two-week media seminar, where bamboo processing, ecological conservation, sustainable agriculture, and rural tourism have helped reshape the local economy.

For Liberia, a country endowed with extensive tropical forests, freshwater systems, mangroves, and other valuable ecosystems, Anji offers a development lesson, protecting nature need not come at the expense of economic growth. Under the right conditions, conservation can become a foundation for prosperity. But translating that experience into reality will require more than admiration for China’s achievements.

Financing, infrastructure, technical capacity, environmental, enforcement, and community ownership will determine whether Liberia can turn its natural resources into sustainable livelihoods.

Liberian Health and environmental science researcher and former Chairman of the Public Health Department at the University of Liberia, Forkpah Pewee and Dr. Anthony Saah Tengbh, Environmental Scientist and Academic Chairman, Department of Environmental Studies and Climate Change at the University of Liberia say elements of the Anji model could work in Liberia if they are adapted to local conditions and supported by practical investments.

However, the Environmental Protection Agency’s position remains unclear. FrontPage Africa sought comments from EPA Executive Director Dr. Emmanuel King Urey Yarkpawolo on the lessons Liberia could draw from Anji and the role environmental regulation could play in developing sustainable enterprises.

He had not responded by the time of publication. His nonresponse does not establish opposition to the approach but leaves unanswered questions about how the country’s environmental regulator would support, oversee, and measure such initiatives.

Anji’s transformation, when conservation becomes an economic strategy. Located in Zhejiang Province, Anji County covers approximately 1,886 square kilometers and has a population of roughly 470,000. It is known for its bamboo forests, white tea, and rural landscapes.

The county was not always the green destination it is today. During the 1980s and 1990s, industrial activities, including quarrying, paper production, and other pollution-intensive operations, contributed to environmental degradation. In Yucun Village, authorities subsequently moved away from environmentally damaging activities and pursued alternative livelihoods, including tourism and other businesses linked to the natural environment.

The transition required difficult economic adjustments, as closing polluting industries initially affected some incomes. Over time, Anji increasingly linked ecological conservation with bamboo processing, agriculture, and tourism.

A 2022 peer-reviewed study of the county’s ecological conservation policies found that protected areas experienced less expansion of construction and agricultural land than the study’s modeled alternative scenario.

The areas accounted for approximately 39 percent of the county’s land but more than 80 percent of its estimated ecosystem-service value in 2015. The findings support the importance of protecting ecologically valuable landscapes, although they do not establish that conservation alone caused all of Anji’s subsequent economic growth. For Liberia, the lesson is that a forest can provide more than raw materials. Properly managed, it can also protect water sources, sustain biodiversity, support livelihoods, and attract visitors. Beyond bamboo poles, Building an industry

One of Anji’s most important achievements is its ability to turn bamboo from raw material into a broad range of finished products. The resource supports manufacturing activities involving furniture, flooring, household utensils, kitchenware, packaging, building materials, and other goods.

Bamboo shoots are also used as food, while processing innovations create additional uses for plant residues. According to figures reported by China’s State Council Information Office in June 2025, Anji’s bamboo industry recorded an output value of 19.2 billion yuan in 2024, an increase of 7 percent over the previous year.

The report also said bamboo-related income benefited more than 51,000 farming households, with average additional household earnings of 6,500 yuan that year. These figures illustrate the scale of an established Chinese industry, not an earnings forecast for Liberia.

Anji’s advantage lies in the connections between growers, processors, manufacturers, traders and customers. Each stage creates opportunities for employment and income. Liberia could adapt that principle by processing suitable natural resources locally instead of relying predominantly on raw-material sales.

Liberia’s untapped bamboo wealth, an industry waiting to grow

Liberia is not starting from zero. The country possesses bamboo and rattan resources that could support furniture-making, household products, handicrafts, selected construction materials, and other manufactured goods.

Previous technical-assistance programs have also sought to develop local skills in bamboo processing. A World Bank report on Liberia’s forest sector identified bamboo and rattan as resources with considerable commercialization potential. It highlighted limited access to processing equipment and technical skills, including the ability to split, slive, and weave bamboo as an obstacle to developing the industry.

These constraints help explain why the existence of a resource does not automatically translate into jobs and business growth. With appropriate training, equipment, and market access,

Liberian entrepreneurs could explore making chairs, tables, beds, shelves, mats, window blinds, household utensils, decorative products, and selected packaging materials. Some bamboo species also produce edible shoots, while processing residues may have other uses where technical and environmental assessments establish their viability.

These are potential opportunities, not guaranteed profitable ventures. Each product would require an assessment of raw-material supply, production costs, quality standards, customer demand, and competition from imports.

Liberia has already received bamboo-related technical assistance from China. According to a Chinese government account, a bamboo and rattan weaving program began in 2007, alongside training in vegetable production and biogas technology.

AidData’s project record reports that 55 trainees had learned to make basic household products by 2008 and that approximately 900 people had received training through the program by 2022.

Those figures document training activities but do not establish how many participants subsequently operated successful businesses. In August 2025, Liberia’s Ministry of Youth and Sports also announced the groundbreaking for a China-supported technical-assistance training facility at the Samuel Kanyon Doe Sports Complex.

World.title: Liberia: EPA Puts Gender at the Center of Climate Action, Orders Every Department to Deliver
World.content:
Opening his address, Dr. Yarkpawolo argued that environmental work cannot be separated from the people it is meant to serve. The theme of the launch, he said, reflects the kind of institution and country Liberia is trying to build

MONROVIA — The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has turned the lens on itself, unveiling its first Gender Policy and a refreshed national Climate Change Gender Action Plan, and warning its own managers that the commitments must show up in everyday decisions rather than gather dust on shelves.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

Executive Director Dr. Emmanuel K. Urey Yarkpawolo made the declaration on Tuesday at the Corina Hotel in Sinkor, where the two documents were launched under the theme “Advancing Gender Equality for Inclusive Climate Resilience in Liberia.”



Gender, Children and Social Protection Minister Gbeme Horace-Kollie joined government officials, development partners, and representatives of civil society, women’s and youth groups, and persons with disabilities at the event.

“A matter of people’s lives”

Opening his address, Dr. Yarkpawolo argued that environmental work cannot be separated from the people it is meant to serve. The theme of the launch, he said, reflects the kind of institution and country Liberia is trying to build.

He painted a picture of those at the heart of the agenda: a woman farming to feed her family, a young person looking for work, and a person with a disability who deserves an equal chance to contribute. Policies, he said, must recognize their circumstances and open doors for them to take part.

Findings that shaped the policy

The EPA’s first Gender Policy did not emerge in a vacuum. According to the Executive Director, it was shaped by an institutional gender assessment, consultations with staff and stakeholders, and a review of existing policies.

The assessment credited the Agency with progress but also exposed a gap: gender considerations had not yet been woven fully into the Agency’s work.

To address that, the policy sets out practical guidance on hiring and promotion, training, leadership, workplace culture and accountability. It also tackles discrimination and sexual harassment head-on. Dr. Yarkpawolo said every employee should be able to grow professionally in a workplace that protects dignity and safety.

Linking gender to national climate goals

The second document, the updated Climate Change Gender Action Plan, takes forward an earlier plan. It was developed through research, stakeholder consultations and training, with support from UN Women, and it ties gender equality to Liberia’s national climate pledges under NDC 3.0.

The EPA’s first Gender Policy did not emerge in a vacuum. According to the Executive Director, it was shaped by an institutional gender assessment, consultations with staff and stakeholders, and a review of existing policies

The plan focuses on eight sectors: agriculture and food security, coasts and fisheries, forestry, health, water and sanitation, waste, energy, and transportation.

Its core argument, the EPA chief explained, is that climate change does not hit everyone equally. Differences in access to land, finance, information and decision-making mean some people are far more exposed than others. He pointed to a woman farmer who may read shifting rainfall patterns better than most, yet lacks the means to adapt. Climate programmes, he said, should tap such knowledge while removing the obstacles she faces.

Early steps already taken

Dr. Yarkpawolo told the audience the Agency is not starting from zero. Among the steps already taken, he said, is the elevation of the gender function to senior management, ensuring it has a stronger voice where institutional decisions are made.

The Agency has also invested in women’s skills, including international training for its women environmental inspectors. Stronger skills, he said, improve the Agency’s ability to monitor environmental conditions and protect communities.

He singled out Madam Madrid Chuka Piah, head of the EPA’s radiation laboratory, as proof of what women are contributing in specialized scientific roles.

The Agency has likewise hired persons with disabilities, whom he said strengthen the institution. Even so, he acknowledged the work is unfinished, saying the EPA must keep adapting its workplace so they can participate fully.

Tough questions ahead

With the documents now launched, the Executive Director shifted from planning to performance. The Gender and Climate Change Baseline Assessment process, he said, helped pinpoint gaps; implementation must now close them, measure progress and flag where more action is needed.

He listed the questions that will guide that scrutiny. Are women benefiting from training and promotion? Can persons with disabilities participate in a meaningful way? Are climate projects reaching those facing the steepest barriers? Do budgets actually back the promises made?

No department left out

Dr. Yarkpawolo was unambiguous about who carries the load. He expects every department to take responsibility for implementation. The Gender Unit will guide and coordinate, but managers across the Agency must bring these commitments into their daily decision-making.

Beyond the EPA’s walls, he called for cooperation across government and sustained partnership with civil society, communities and development partners. Clear responsibilities, sufficient resources and regular monitoring, he said, will determine whether the policies succeed.

The Executive Director thanked Gender Coordinator Madam Grace Biah and her team, the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, technical experts, and all others who contributed. He reserved special appreciation for UN Women for backing the update of the Climate Change Gender Action Plan.

World.title: ICT sector key to grow Zambia agenda-Mutati
World.content:
Government says the Information and Communication Technology (ICT) sector will play a critical role in supporting the Grow Zambia Agenda and driving the country’s digital transformation.

Speaking at the Zambia Development Agency (ZDA) Zambia-Germany ICT Business Forum in Lusaka, Minister of Technology and Science, Felix Mutati, said Government is prioritising digital infrastructure to expand and improve connectivity across all economic and social sectors.

Mr Mutati explained that ICT is a critical sector that cuts across and supports other economic pillars by providing the infrastructure and digital solutions needed to enhance productivity, efficiency and service delivery.

He outlined five key pillars that would support the Grow Zambia Agenda as trusted digital identity, interoperability, intelligence, digital infrastructure and inclusivity.

Mr Mutati explained that trusted digital identity would help eliminate duplication in public service delivery, while interoperability would enable government systems to communicate and share information, reducing the need for citizens and businesses to move from one office to another to access services.

“Government systems must be able to shake hands so that citizens do not have to move from one office to another to access services,” he stated.

Mr Mutati further explained that the intelligence pillar would promote the use of science, research, data and Artificial Intelligence (AI) to improve efficiency, reduce operational costs and increase productivity.

He cited the discovery of a significant copper ore deposit through the use of AI as an example of the technology’s potential.

He added that digital infrastructure was being brought into the country duty-free to support investment and expansion.

He pointed out that inclusivity would require collaboration between government and private sectors.

“I am because we are, because no matter how clever, intelligent and capable you are, you cannot achieve much on your own without partnerships and collaboration,” Mr Mutati further added.

Speaking at the same event, German Ambassador to Zambia, Soenke Siemon, reaffirmed Germany’s commitment to supporting the country’s digital transformation through partnerships and investments in the ICT sector.

Mr Siemon said Germany has supported several digital reforms, including the integration of public data at the Zambia Revenue Authority (ZRA), the digital revenue management system and beneficial ownership reforms at the Patents and Companies Registration Agency.

He said the ICT sector was becoming an important driver of Zambia’s economic growth.

“The ICT sector is becoming an important driver of Zambia’s economic growth, having recorded the highest positive contribution to growth in 2025, with the trend continuing into the second quarter of 2026,” he further explained.

Meanwhile, Zambia Development Agency (ZDA) Director General, Albert Halwampa, said Zambia is committed to creating a conducive business environment to attract investment in the ICT sector.

Mr Halwampa said the agency had digitised all its services, allowing investors to apply for investment licences online without physically visiting its offices.

He urged German companies to take advantage of the opportunities available in Zambia, saying the agency was ready to facilitate partnerships and investments.

World.title: Zambia accelerates Energy diversification
World.content:
Ministry of Electricity, Principal Public Relations Officer, Bob Sianjalika says Zambia has embarked on an energy diversification programme aimed at reducing the country’s dependence on hydroelectricity and increasing power generation capacity to 10,000 megawatts by 2031.

Speaking in an interview with the media today, Mr Sianjalika says the move follows the lessons learnt from the 2023 and 2024 droughts, which exposed the risks of relying heavily on hydroelectric power.

He said during the drought period, about 75 to 85 percent of the country’s electricity came from hydropower, making electricity generation vulnerable to reduced rainfall.

Mr Sianjalika added that the government is therefore promoting an energy mix that includes solar, wind and thermal power to strengthen the country’s energy security and reduce the impact of future droughts.

“More than 30 energy projects are currently at different stages of implementation across the country, all aimed at increasing electricity supply to the national grid” he added.

Mr Sianjalika said three additional solar power plants, each with a generation capacity of 100 megawatts, are expected to be commissioned before the end of 2026.

He says the Rural Electrification Authority (REA) is also implementing solar mini-grid and mini-hydropower projects to extend electricity access to communities that are not connected to the national grid.

Mr Sianjalika says the Presidential Constituency Energy Initiative, which targets the development of two megawatts of power in each of the country’s 226 constituencies, is expected to contribute 312 megawatts to national generation capacity.

Mr Sianjalika says ZESCO is also investing in solar energy as an alternative source of electricity, while private sector participation in power generation has increased following reforms introduced by the government in 2024.

He says the reforms have opened up the electricity sector to private investment, including opportunities for electricity trading.

Mr Sianjalika says the investments from both government and private players are expected to contribute towards achieving the national target of 10,000 megawatts.

He says Zambia’s current installed electricity generation capacity stands at approximately 4,377 megawatts, with the country working towards reaching 5,000 megawatts in the near future.

Mr Sianjalika says the government is confident that the various projects being implemented will help the country achieve its 10,000-megawatt target within the next four years.

World.title: Muchinga Province Minister pledges accelerated development
World.content:
Newly appointed Muchinga Province Minister Jairo Simbeye has pledged to accelerate development in the province through hard work, collaboration and inclusive leadership.

‎

‎Mr Simbeye says sustainable development can only be achieved through strong partnerships among Government institutions, stakeholders and the citizens.

‎

‎Speaking during a welcoming ceremony held at the Provincial Administration in Chinsali, Mr Simbeye stated that he would promote teamwork and ensure that all stakeholders are involved in the implementation of Government programmes under the Grow Zambia Agenda.

‎

‎He stressed the need for unity and mutual respect regardless of political affiliation, noting that meaningful development can only be realised through collective effort.

‎

‎”I wish to thank President Hakainde Hichilema for according me this opportunity to serve the people of Muchinga Province at this level, and I will not take this opportunity for granted,” he added.

‎

‎Mr Simbeye, who is also a Nkombwa Constituency Member of Parliament in Isoka District, further assured the people of Muchinga Province that he would serve with dignity, impartiality and diligence.

‎

‎He also thanked residents of the province for the warm welcome and emphasised the need for enhanced service delivery from civil servants across the province.

‎

‎And Muchinga Province Permanent Secretary Tuesday Bwalya, described Mr Simbeye’s appointment as a commendable decision by the Head of State, noting that the Minister is familiar with the challenges affecting the province’s development.

‎

‎Dr Bwalya said the Minister’s understanding of the region would place him in a better position to address developmental concerns.

‎

‎He noted that Muchinga Province has lagged behind in certain areas of development and expressed confidence that the Minister’s political leadership would help unlock support for both stalled and new projects.

‎

‎”As Provincial Administration, we are delighted to welcome you and assure you of our full support as we work together to improve the livelihoods of our people through the Grow Zambia Agenda,” he said.

‎

‎Dr Bwalya further stated that the Minister’s support would be instrumental in enhancing the province’s contribution to the country’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP), particularly through the commercialisation and expansion of the gold mining sector.

World.title: Lusaka youths rally behind the Grow Zambia agenda
World.content:
A group of young people from Lusaka has joined in championing the Grow Zambia Agenda.

The five youths comprising three males and two females have embarked on a 480 km journey dubbed “Youth Walk,” aimed at raising awareness on the importance of everyone to get involved in the development of the country.

A 12 days journey which started on Wednesday October 28 from Lusaka to Livingstone is scheduled to end on Sunday November 08, 2026.

So far, the young people have spent seven days walking while raising awareness of the Grow Zambia Agenda to the people they meet along the way.

In Choma the youths paid a courtesy call on the District Commissioner Funds Mubele who was joined by Choma Mayor Honest Mweemba to support the initiative.

Group lead Israel Mwambazi said the initiative to raise awareness on Grow Zambia Agenda is a resolve by the group to support President Hakainde Hichilema and the development of the country.

“As youths, we have embarked on this journey as a demonstration of commitment to support President Hakainde Hichilema in his agenda to develop the country,” he said.

Choma District Commissioner Funds Mubele commended the young people for championing the grow Zambia agenda target set by President Hakainde Hichilema

“It’s encouraging to see that young people like you, have taken this positive step to support the Grow Zambia Agenda through raising awareness among the citizens especially those along the great north road,” he said.

Mr Mubele said the initiative shows the need for everyone to be involved in the Grow Zambia Agenda target set by president Hakainde Hichilema.

And Choma Mayor Honest Mweemba stated that the grow Zambia agenda must be supported by every well-meaning Zambians.

Mr Mweemba encouraged the group of young people to continue championing the Grow Zambia agenda.

World.title: Mporokoso roundabout construction completed
World.content:
Mporokoso Town Council has completed the construction of a roundabout in the District at a cost of over K98,000 using the 2026 Constituency Development Fund (CDF).

The roundabout was among several projects approved for implementation under the 2026 CDF.

Speaking during an inspection of the completed works, Mporokoso Town Council Assistant Director of Engineering Patson Chisanga commended the contractor for the quality of workmanship exhibited on the project.

Mr Chisanga said the local authority was satisfied with the finished works, adding that the project had been successfully completed.

“We are very happy with the finished works on the Mporokoso Roundabout. The contractor has done a good job on this project,” he said.

Meanwhile, Mporokoso Town Council Public Relations Officer Martha Nakamba says the local authority plans to install road signage along the four routes connecting to the roundabout to guide motorists.

Ms Nakamba explained that the road signage was not included in the initial project cost of K98,714 but would be installed as part of efforts to improve traffic direction and safety.

She has since appealed to members of the public to protect the infrastructure from vandalism and avoid littering the surrounding area.

Ms Nakamba said the roundabout has enhanced the appearance of Mporokoso town, and urged residents to take collective responsibility for maintaining its cleanliness and beauty.

World.title: Rains blow off Mungwi classroom roof
World.content:
A 1×2 classroom block has been blown off by torrential rains coupled with strong winds at Chisali Primary School in Mungwi District in Northern Province.

Kampamba Village Headman Peter Chileshe confirmed the sad development in a telephone interview with the media in Mungwi shortly after inspecting the area today.

Headman Chileshe said two other infrastructures, a house and a shop have also been affected by the hailstorm.

The Traditional leader disclosed that on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, the area experienced a hailstorm around 16:30 hours that left part of the roof for the 1×2 Classroom block blown off at the learning institution.

He added that no casualty was recorded as only bags of maize for the feeding program were soaked and some books.

Headman Chileshe has since appealed to relevant authorities to come to the aid of the school which runs from ECE to grade 7 with a total enrolment of over 1200 pupils.

“We appeal for quick interventions from the government and well-wishers to come on board to repair the blown off roof, especially that lessons are likely to be adjusted to accommodate all classes,” he explained.

The Traditional leader said a quick response to have the classroom repaired will enable the school revert back to the normal schedule.

He also appealed to well-wishers to help the family of 5 to restart their life after their house was also damaged by strong winds experienced in the area.

World.title: Lwandamina names 30 for Burundi  AFCON qualifier
World.content:
Chipolopolo interim coach George ‘Chicken’ Lwandamina has named a 30-member provisional squad for Zambia’s back-to-back Group I qualifiers for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations against Burundi.

The squad, announced by the Football Association of Zambia (FAZ), is a blend of foreign-based players and top-performing local stars.

In-form Zesco United striker Kennedy Musonda, fit-again Red Arrows defender Zephaniah Phiri and red-hot Red Arrows airman Ackim Mumba headline the local call-ups.

Portugal-based midfielder Chanka Zimba returns to the national fold after finding a new base, while Gift Mphande has also earned a look-in from the technical bench.

The team will set up camp in Ndola on Thursday, with foreign-based players expected to join when the FIFA international window opens on 9 November.

Lwandamina is expected to trim the provisional squad to 26 for the final stages of preparation.

Zambia will host Burundi on Friday, 13 November at the Levy Mwanawasa Stadium in Ndola, before travelling to Bujumbura for the return fixture four days later on 17 November.

The double-header is crucial for Zambia’s qualification hopes. Algeria lead Group I with four points, with Zambia second on three points. Togo are third, also on three points, while Burundi are bottom with one point after two rounds of matches.

Victory in both legs would put Chipolopolo in a commanding position to qualify for the AFCON PAMOJA 2027, which will be jointly hosted by Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania from 19 June to 17 July 2027.

Lwandamina, who took over on an interim basis, will be looking to build momentum and stability in the squad as Zambia push for a return to Africa’s biggest stage.

Some players have been excluded from this assignment as they are part of U23 squad playing Burkina Faso on 11 November in Ouagadougou and Heroes four days later.

World.title: Mambwe Maternity Annex renovated
World.content:
The Maternity Annex at Nsefu Clinic in Mambwe District in Eastern Province that was recently renovated by Painted Dogs Lagoons, at a cost of about K350, 000

has officially been handed over to the community.

The maternity annex, which was in a deplorable state, has now been given a new face-lift to provide a safe and dignified environment for mothers in the chiefdom to access maternal health services.

Speaking during the handover ceremony, Director of Health Services, Luwi Kawanda thanked His Royal Highness Senior Chief Nsefu for engaging Painted Dogs Lagoons to undertake the renovations.

Dr Kawanda also expressed gratitude to the Director of Painted Dogs Lagoons for renovating the facility.

“The improvements made to the infrastructure will ensure that mothers in the chiefdom access maternal health services in a safe environment,” she noted.

She revealed that Nsefu Clinic serves a catchment population of more than 10,000 people, hence the need for quality infrastructure.

Meanwhile, Nsefu Ward Councillor, Kalima Chibwana said he was pleased with the works done by cooperating partners and commended the community for participating in ensuring that the works were completed on time.

Mr Chibwana said the facility will serve the people in the ward and urged mothers to preserve the facility so that it continues to benefit them.

Meanwhile, Painted Dogs Lagoons Director, Peter Woeste thanked Senior Chief Nsefu for creating an enabling environment for them to do business in the chiefdom.

Mr Woeste said he was very happy to help in renovating the annex for the benefit of the community where they are doing business.

He revealed that the renovations cost about 350 thousand Kwacha.

“Our Organization also supports schools in the area by providing textbooks and other learning materials,” he said.

And Senior Chief Nsefu who was represented by his Personal Secretary, John Mbewe commended Painted Dogs Lagoons for the intervention, while calling for more support.

He requested that the main clinic building also be worked on and that staff houses are needed to enhance service delivery to the community.

He called on the Clinic Administration to ensure the facility is well taken care of so that community members receive the intended services in a timely manner.

Senior Chief Nsefu also urged people in his chiefdom to normalise taking expectant mothers to the clinic for safe deliveries.

“For the Community Resource Board (CRB), I urge you to identify areas that need support so that in future, cooperating partners doing business in the Chiefdom can help,” he said.

World.title: Africa: Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games - Kenya on Top, Madagascar on Podium, Senegal Looks to Future
World.content:
Dakar — African women's rugby made its mark at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games. At the Iba Mar Diop complex, Kenya secured gold after a spectacular final against Australia, while Madagascar took bronze. For Senegal, the host country, this first international experience opens new avenues for the development of the sport among young girls.

African women's rugby has reason to be ambitious. In Dakar, the young Kenyan women delivered one of the standout performances of the Youth Olympic Games' rugby sevens tournament, defeating Australia 17-12 in a final that went to extra time. This victory highlights the growing strength of women's rugby on the continent.

Trailing on the scoreboard, the Kenyan women found the strength to level the score (12-12) at the end of regulation time, before securing the victory with a decisive try in extra time. A hard-fought win, achieved through courage and determination, that rewards the journey of an ambitious team.

"We came here with one goal: to win gold. We came to represent Kenya," said captain Zain Hido, emotional after her team's victory.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Beyond the medal, this victory confirms the ability of young African players to compete with top-level opponents. It also sends an encouraging signal for a sport that seeks to expand its reach and increase its visibility across the continent.

Madagascar confirms its potential

Kenya was not the only African team to distinguish itself. Madagascar also achieved a remarkable performance by winning the bronze medal, confirming the potential of its new generation of players.

The Ladies Makis demonstrated consistency throughout the tournament, conceding only one defeat, against Kenya in the semi-final. This performance rewards their commitment and the efforts they made to reach this level of competition.

"This medal is for us, for our country! It's the first time for us, it's incredible," said Princia Ranaivoson, bursting with joy after this third place.

Behind this result lie weeks of preparation and the sacrifices of young female athletes forced to juggle training, studies and international ambitions.

Their coach, Dina Razafindratsara, praised the commitment of her players, whose journey testifies to the training work undertaken in Madagascar.

This bronze medal represents encouragement for Malagasy women's rugby and underlines the importance of continuing efforts in coaching, training and access to international competitions.

Senegal, a first to prepare the next generation

For Senegal, the tournament ended without a victory, but with important lessons learned. Finishing last in the standings, the Lionesses suffered a defeat against Spain (0-27), highlighting the experience gap that still separates them from some international teams.

But for this young team, the stakes went beyond sporting results. It was primarily about discovering the demands of international competition and gauging the road ahead.

"I'm proud of the girls. Today, the team represented our country well. They fought hard, even though they lacked experience," declared the national coach, Oumar Diop.

This participation is part of a dynamic of development of women's rugby in Senegal, in particular through the Rugby Rising Play program, supported by World Rugby to encourage the practice of this sport among young girls.

According to the coach, several players joined this initiative less than two years ago. Their participation in the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games therefore represented their first experience at the highest international level.

"After the Youth Olympic Games, we will continue the work, keep this team, train it and always try to compete against the best. We still have a lot of work to do," he added.

For Senegalese rugby, the challenge now is to transform this first participation into a real dynamic of development, by multiplying opportunities for competition and consolidating training systems.

An African podium that brings hope for women's rugby

With two African nations on the podium, the Dakar 2026 women's rugby sevens tournament offers an encouraging illustration of the continent's sporting potential.

Close 

Kenya's victory and Madagascar's bronze medal demonstrate the progress made by some federations, while Senegal's participation highlights the challenges still faced by countries where the sport is still developing.

Beyond individual and collective performances, these results highlight the importance of investing in training, technical coaching, and access for young girls to sports infrastructure.

For African federations, the challenge now will be to capitalize on the visibility offered by these Games to strengthen talent identification, support, and competition programs.

In Dakar, young African rugby players will not only have played matches and won medals. They will also have helped to raise the profile of their sport and pave the way for a generation of athletes determined to advance women's rugby on the continent.

World.title: Africa: How Many More COPs Before Climate Promises Become Action?
World.content:
A woman wades through floodwaters in Bor, Jonglei State, South Sudan, where communities continue to live with the effects of flooding from previous years as the country prepares for further climate-related shocks.

Every year before COP, the same question surfaces: what is the one thing Africa needs from this summit?

Ahead of COP31, the answer emerging from a World Resources Institute Africa webinar was clear: Africa must move beyond asking what it can receive from global climate negotiations and focus on what it can bring. With geopolitical tensions, energy disruptions and climate shocks exposing vulnerabilities across African economies, speakers argued that the continent must use the summit to advance practical solutions that strengthen energy security, protect food systems and mobilise climate finance.

A reinvented agency



Olufunso Somorin, Regional Principal Officer for Climate Change and Green Growth at the African Development Bank, said these challenges were interconnected, warning that simultaneous disruptions to energy, food and economic systems could undermine the continent's development gains. He described them as a triangle of reality - when one is hit, the others strain, and when all three are hit, the development gains of recent years are at risk.

"COP of today, it is now a trade forum. It is now a marketplace."

He said that Africa needed to rethink its approach to global climate negotiations and strengthen its position as a partner in shaping climate solutions rather than simply seeking assistance. His answer was what he called a "reinvented agency". Africa, he said, must move "away from this idea of Africa that needs to be helped, to an Africa that needs to be partnered with."

He also questioned the pace of the process itself, asking that after 30 COPs, how many more does it take to get things done?

That means understanding what COP has become. "COP of today, it is now a trade forum. It is now a marketplace. And what you get out of a marketplace is largely based on who you are and what you bring to the marketplace," he said.

Strengthening energy security

Energy security was one of the key issues at COP31, with the prevailing situation of geopolitical tensions and disruptions to the global energy supply underpinning the risks of being dependent on external energy sources. Africa has significant renewable energy potential. However, the challenge remains translating these resources into reliable and affordable electricity that can support economic growth, businesses, and industrial development.

Yasmin Abdulwassie, Senior Manager for Climate in Africa at the Children's Investment Fund Foundation, said high financing costs and limited public budgets remained major obstacles to scaling up renewable energy investments. "The challenge is really translating that potential into affordable, reliable energy that can be replicated and scaled," she said.

She said philanthropy can help by funding project preparation, policy reform and investment pipelines, so that transition pathways are country-led. She pointed to South Africa's Just Energy Transition Partnership. The initiative, she said, initially announced with $8.5 billion, had grown to more than $14 billion, proof that investors back credible country platforms.

She also highlighted Senegal's Renewable Energy Investment Facility as another emerging example of efforts to attract investment and support the country's energy transition. "So that type of catalytic role that philanthropy plays is not just about unlocking finance, but helping countries turn lasting financing possibilities for economic reform," said Abdulwassie.

Somorin said that achieving universal energy access would require stronger partnerships that connect national ambitions with clear financing strategies. He cited Mission 300, which aims to connect 300 million people in sub-Saharan Africa to electricity by 2030, as an example of how shared targets and country-specific strategies can accelerate progress.

He said 37 African countries had developed national energy compacts outlining their strategies for expanding electricity access, helping attract investment from development finance institutions, the World Bank, the African Development Bank and philanthropic organisations. He said the initiative demonstrated the importance of having a collective goal while agreeing on practical steps to achieve it.

"It is a new way of defining partnership where you have a collective goal, but you also have a shared discussion on the how. How do we get there? What do we need to do differently?" he said.

Beyond energy security, COP31 is urged to give greater attention to adaptation, particularly ensuring that climate finance reaches countries and communities most vulnerable to climate change.

Abdulwassie said that the climate summit should move adaptation commitments toward "real, measurable outcomes," particularly in food systems, water and livelihood infrastructure. She set out three priorities. The first is a credible financing pathway. Countries have committed to tripling adaptation finance by 2035, but Abdulwassie said the detail is missing. "How are we going to do it? How will progress be measured?" she asked, adding that these questions need answers at COP31 and at every milestone after it.

The second is better indicators, and here she pointed to the Belém-Addis vision, a two-year process that runs toward COP32 in Ethiopia. Current metrics, she said, tend to count activities, such as how many farmers completed climate-smart agriculture training. She argued the measure should be whether a farmer's livelihood "stays intact or improves despite climate shocks," and that credible results of that kind are what attract further financing.

The third is matching national adaptation plans with investment plans. She cited a Malawi initiative, backed by philanthropy and led by the African Climate Foundation, in which more than 20 of the country's priority adaptation proposals have been matched with potential investors. The aim, she said, is to give adaptation the same investable pipelines that mitigation projects increasingly have.

Closing the adaptation finance gap

The challenge of mobilising climate finance for adaptation was also highlighted by Somorin, who said African countries needed to rethink how adaptation projects are financed and how their economic value is presented to investors.

"Adaptation is very complex," Somorin said, and the sector has made it harder by lumping everything together as "climate action." He said that adaptation remains more difficult to finance than mitigation because projects often lack the clear financial returns that attract private investors.

Put all climate projects in one finance basket, he said, and about nine in ten that emerge would be mitigation projects. They are simply easier to finance and attract capital more readily. Africa also faces a structural handicap. In every other region, he said, private capital drives climate action. Africa is the only place where public money leads.

His first proposed fix is to stop treating the two as separate. "You use mitigation finance to drive adaptation goals," he said. He gave an example of a solar-powered irrigation scheme in a semi-arid region that cuts emissions through clean energy, but it also lets farmers grow and earn all year round, which is an adaptation result. The more deliberately adaptation is built into mitigation projects, he said, the more capital will reach it.

"I argue that you use mitigation finance to drive adaptation goals," he said.

Somorin also called for a change in how investors assess adaptation projects, arguing that their wider economic benefits should be recognised alongside their immediate financial returns.

He said financiers needed to understand the distinction between financial viability and economic viability, particularly where investments generate long-term benefits that may not immediately translate into revenue. Somorin said the task is to help financiers see that the economic value is real and can be monetized, either now or later, as new markets emerge to turn it into financial returns.

Africa has documented 11 financial instruments for mitigation projects but, at best, three for adaptation. Expanding these financing options, he said, would let more resources flow and would bring non-traditional investors into the adaptation space.

Philanthropy can help unlock larger investments

While development finance institutions have a role in mobilising investment for climate action, Abdulwassie said philanthropic capital could help address some of the structural barriers preventing African countries from accessing climate finance. "Philanthropy alone, we know, cannot close that gap," she said. However, she identified three areas where it could have a catalytic impact: strengthening national institutions, developing country-led investment platforms, and building stronger partnerships across the climate finance ecosystem.

The first is institutional capacity. Where African institutions don't exist, or need strengthening, she said, philanthropic money is best spent building them. That leads to country ownership and brings "the local voice, the local agenda" to the table, alongside partners such as the African Development Bank. She pointed again to South Africa's Just Energy Transition Partnership, where philanthropic partners and multilaterals helped the government negotiate what international financing would look like. She also made a pointed aside: more grants should go directly to countries to help scale such efforts.

The second is building investment platforms with countries rather than for them. Philanthropy can provide technical expertise, convene partners and help design financing mechanisms and instruments. The models must be contextual, she said, because every country's energy pathway, food system and growth path is different.

The third is strengthening the wider ecosystem of African climate leadership. She cited philanthropic support for the first two Africa Climate Summits, the resulting Nairobi and Addis Ababa declarations, and efforts to give African countries a collective voice through the African Union during South Africa's G20 presidency.

The stakes, she said, are high: climate finance flowing into Africa is less than 2% of what is needed, nowhere near the continent's needs. Without African leadership in these rooms, she argued, the finance ambitions cannot be met.

"Bringing in that collective voice because I believe that ensures that African leadership is there to shape African priorities," she said.

Turning country platforms into action

Somorin said his experience working with country platforms at the African Development Bank had shown that strong national leadership was essential to their success.

He outlined three factors that can help these platforms move beyond coordination. First, governments need clearly defined climate goals and realistic objectives that reflect their national capabilities, political circumstances, and development priorities.

"Nothing substitutes for strong leadership," he said. He named the difference it makes by comparing Rwanda with Niger. Clear, well-structured country goals matter, he said, but so does honesty about capability. Countries that are still asking partners to help train their people, when they should be implementing, are not ready to move. Goals also have to fit a country's political and socioeconomic realities. He said, "You cannot ignore" even when they seem unrelated to climate.

Second, countries must understand the strengths of their development partners, including multilateral institutions, philanthropic organisations and NGOs, and bring them together around clearly allocated responsibilities.

Third, governments must demonstrate their own commitment by contributing resources to the initiatives they want partners to support. Somorin said that countries which tell partners they need support for 80% of a project because they will supply 20% make faster progress than those that put in nothing and ask for everything. A government that commits a set share of its budget over five years, and assigns people to learn and deliver, finds it much easier to leverage what others bring.

Building towards an African COP32

Ethiopia is set to host COP32 in 2027. Abdulwassie said African countries should begin preparing now to ensure the summit delivers beyond political commitments. She said that COP32 should not be viewed as an Ethiopian event alone, but as an opportunity for African countries to unite around shared development priorities and strengthen the continent's influence in global climate discussions.

"COP32 is not just an Ethiopian COP, but an African COP," she said.

Abdulwassie outlined three priorities for the road to COP32. First, African leaders must work together to agree on key priorities. She pointed to the African Union summit in February and the pre-COP period as chances to agree on priorities that can outlast political cycles, including the action agenda and the initiatives each presidency will announce.

Second, Africa should use the run-up to COP32 to showcase successful climate initiatives already underway, demonstrate their results and identify which approaches can be adapted or scaled up in other countries.

Third, she called for greater recognition of local voices, particularly those of young people and communities already driving climate action. She said communities' ambitions and practices need to reach leaders and be translated into action. "How do we make sure the voice of youth in particular ... is translated into action?" she asked. She warned that decisions made today would shape the world inherited by future generations.

Close 

Development partners, she said, should engage Africa not in terms of handouts but as true partners, in a relationship where Africans have resources to trade and engage with, at COP32 and beyond.

To make COP31 a success for Africa, Abdulwassie pointed to stronger continental unity, partnerships and visibility in global climate discussions.

She said African countries needed to speak with a stronger collective voice while building momentum around energy, food security and water resilience. She also stressed the importance of having more Africans present at the summit to share their ambitions, experiences and progress.

Somorin said Africa's voice and leadership must be central to global climate discussions, particularly given the continent's limited contribution to climate change and its disproportionate exposure to its impacts. The voice, agency and significance of that continent, he argued, can never be ignored, but the starting point is Africa asserting its own agency, because the global climate equation is incomplete without Africa's development and resilience.

He urged African countries to move away from the perception of a continent waiting to be helped.

"Africa should be recognised not only for its vulnerability but also for its potential to contribute to global solutions," said Somorin. "If there's any region that could play a significant role in the global solution, it is Africa."

Protecting Africa's industrialisation ambitions

Soha Benchekroun, a climate resilience and industrial development policy researcher and adviser, argued that climate negotiations must give greater consideration to Africa's right to industrialise and move up global value chains.

The aim for COP31, and for the "African COP" in Ethiopia a year later, said Benchekroun, is to make sure climate action "does not undermine our industrialization trajectories." Most African countries are only starting to climb global value chains and build manufacturing and processing capacity at home. Many have moved to restrict raw material exports and promote local processing, a trend she called positive.

The threat, she said, comes from unilateral trade measures adopted in the name of climate policy by industrialized countries: carbon border adjustments, carbon pricing and related regulations. She said the negotiated rules should seek to limit the harm of these measures to African and other developing economies. The timing is pressing, she noted, with more carbon border mechanisms on the way, including the UK's, due to start in January 2027.

"Justice and a good outcome is first about doing no harm to our African development and industrial development pathways," she said.

Benchekroun also said that the just transition debate has focused on wider energy access while giving the right to development, and industrial development in particular, only marginal attention. "We do not expect COPs to sort out our energy infrastructure challenges, nor to promote our own industrialization," she said, "but at least a good start would be to not hinder them." What lifts a continent out of poverty, she said, is infrastructure, industrial development, and local value addition, paired with ways to turn them into benefits for society.

World.title: South Africa: Voters Demand Water, Electricity and Dignity As Ramaphosa Heads to Polls
World.content:
South Africans in queuing to vote in the 2026 Local Government Elections.

Voters at Hyde Park High School in Johannesburg want the local government elections to bring better services, safer communities and leaders who listen.

Gloria Chabalala brought her daughter to the voting station to teach her about a democratic right her grandparents only enjoyed later in life.

Johannesburg voters want more than election promises. They want water, electricity, housing and safer communities.

As South Africans cast their ballots in the 2026 local government elections, voters at Hyde Park High School say they are hoping for leaders who will put their needs first.

The voting station is also where President Cyril Ramaphosa and First Lady Dr Tshepo Motsepe are expected to cast their ballots.



For residents, however, the election is about choosing leaders who can improve their daily lives.

Among those who arrived to vote was Johannesburg resident Melisa Mandy, who praised the smooth voting process and the help she received from election officials.

"The IEC is very helpful, telling us exactly where to go. It's quite an efficient and fast process," she said.

Mandy, who was born and raised in Johannesburg, said she had watched the city change over the years.

She hopes the election results will bring positive changes to the city she calls home.

"It's a special occasion today. I think it's a turning point in the country. Everyone needs to participate," she said.

For another voter, Gloria Chabalala, election day was also a chance to teach her young daughter about South Africa's democracy.

She brought her daughter to the voting station so she could see what it means to take part in an election.

Her daughter still has about 10 years to go before she is old enough to vote, but Gloria wants her to understand the importance of having a say in who leads the country.

She remembered her late father, who died in 2005.

Although he lived into his 70s, he only had the opportunity to vote a few times during his lifetime.

His experience is a reminder to Gloria that the right to vote was not always available to all South Africans.

"I was telling my daughter how important it is for her to vote because her grandparents only got to vote much later in life. It's important that they understand the importance of us being here and this right that we have," she said.

Gloria said her daughter already knows about some of South Africa's political parties and is beginning to understand the choices voters make.

But beyond teaching her daughter about democracy, Gloria wants the elections to bring real change.

Close 

She believes South Africans deserve leaders who will tackle the problems affecting their communities.

"We all deserve dignity. We all deserve water, we all deserve electricity. We all deserve housing. We don't need crime," she said.

For Gloria, these are basic needs that every community should have.

She hopes those elected will serve all residents and make decisions that put people's needs ahead of their own interests.

While Mandy hopes to see Johannesburg change for the better, Gloria wants her daughter to grow up understanding the value of voting and the responsibility that comes with choosing leaders.

Both voters see the elections as an opportunity for change, but their hopes go beyond what happens at the ballot box.

As Ramaphosa and Motsepe prepare to vote at Hyde Park High School, residents are making their own choices about who should lead their communities.

For Gloria, the real test will come after the votes have been counted.

She wants leaders who will turn election promises into working services and make sure communities have the water, electricity, housing and safety they deserve.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - November 4, 2026
World.content:
UN to Withdraw Peacekeeping Mission from Western Sahara

The United Nations has started preparations to withdraw its peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara. This follows Russia and the United States vetoing each other's proposals to extend the 35-year deployment. The UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) was established in 1991 to monitor a ceasefire and support a settlement between Morocco and the pro-independence Polisario Front. The latest disagreement in the Security Council followed a US proposal to renew the mission's mandate while placing Morocco's autonomy plan at the centre of efforts to resolve the dispute. Russia rejected the proposal, arguing that it favoured Morocco's position and could prejudge questions of sovereignty. The US subsequently vetoed Russia's alternative proposal. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has expressed concern about the possibility of renewed fighting and urged both parties to exercise restraint. He also reiterated the need to respect the Sahrawi people's right to self-determination. Morocco controls most of the territory, while the Polisario Front continues to push for an independent state.

HRW Urges Ethiopia to Lift Suspension of Independent Newspaper



Human Rights Watch has called on the Ethiopian government to immediately reverse its decision to suspend the licences of The Reporter, one of the country's oldest independent media outlets and its last privately owned Amharic newspaper. The Ethiopian Media Authority announced that the publication's print and online operations would be suspended indefinitely, accusing it of repeatedly violating media laws and publishing content that undermines national interests, including foreign investment, tourism and diplomacy. Human Rights Watch said that the decision reflects an escalating crackdown on independent journalism and civic freedoms in the country. Since 2025, authorities have reportedly shut down several media outlets, deported foreign correspondents and targeted local journalists through arrests, office raids and other forms of intimidation. The organisation said the government has also increased pressure on The Reporter, including the arrest of some of its journalists. Its director for the Horn of Africa, Laetitia Bader, said that the government should lift the suspension, while Ethiopia's international partners should pressure authorities to end attacks on independent media.

Service Failures, Water Crisis, and Coalitions Set to Shape South African Municipal Elections

Service delivery failures, water shortages, electricity disruptions and rising living costs are among the key issues influencing South African voters as the country heads to municipal elections. Residents in communities like Tembisa have vented their anger at sewage in the streets, inconsistent electricity and poor local infrastructure, with some wondering if voting will make any real change. Water supply and quality have become particularly important issues with a number of areas facing prolonged shortages and aging infrastructure unable to meet demand. Water rights organisation WaterCAN said that almost 70% of the country's wastewater treatment works are in a critical state, contributing to pollution in rivers and streams. The elections are also expected to test the African National Congress's declining support, with polling suggesting the party could lose further ground and more municipalities could be governed through coalitions. Immigration has been a major theme in the campaign messages as parties look to capitalize on public concerns about illegal immigration and border management. Meanwhile, the Independent Electoral Commission is investigating more than 700 complaints relating to election misinformation, including false claims about asylum seekers being mobilised to vote. Analysts said that turnout will be crucial in determining the outcome, particularly as municipal elections have historically recorded lower participation than national polls.

Libyan Religious Body Issues Ruling Prohibiting Sale and Use of Nike Products

Libya's highest religious authority, Dar al-Ifta, has issued a religious ruling prohibiting Muslims from buying, selling, or wearing clothing bearing the Nike logo. The Tripoli-based institution argues that the American sportswear company's name is derived from the Greek goddess of victory and that its famous swoosh logo is inspired by her wings. It says wearing clothing displaying the logo amounts to promoting symbols associated with the worship of multiple gods, which it considers contrary to Islamic teachings. The religious committee has also accused Nike of supporting Israel and reiterated calls for a boycott of companies it considers supportive of the country during the war in Gaza. The ruling was approved by Libya's Grand Mufti, Sadiq al-Gharyani, but does not amount to an official government ban and carries no specified legal penalties. The institution has previously issued similar rulings against jewellery and watches bearing the logo of French luxury brand Van Cleef & Arpels. The latest decision has sparked mixed reactions on social media, with some welcoming it while others have questioned its relevance amid Libya's wider political and economic challenges.

At Least 27 Civilians Killed in Burkina Faso Attacks

Human Rights Watch said that at least 27 civilians were killed in two attacks by Al-Qaeda-linked armed group Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM) in Burkina Faso's northern Yatenga province in September. The first attack took place on September 1, when more than 60 fighters stormed an artisanal gold mining site near Soubo village, killing 24 civilians, injuring at least 20 others and destroying hundreds of shelters, motorcycles and mining equipment. Witnesses said the attackers opened fire on people who were sleeping or working at the site, while some victims were shot as they attempted to escape. Four days later, an explosive device detonated on a road near Mera village, killing three people travelling on a motorcycle, including a five-year-old child and a 65-year-old woman. Human Rights Watch said that the attacks appear to constitute war crimes and has called on Burkina Faso's authorities to strengthen protection for vulnerable communities, investigate the killings and prosecute those responsible. The organisation also raised concerns about the use of improvised explosive devices, which pose a serious threat to civilians. It says the attacks come amid a wider pattern of violence by Islamist armed groups and serious abuses against civilians by government forces and allied militias.

Close 

Kenya Registers Thousands of Ethiopian Refugees Fleeing Clashes

Kenyan authorities, working with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) and the Kenya Red Cross Society, have begun registering Ethiopian refugees fleeing renewed clashes in the border town of Moyale. More than 50,000 people have reportedly crossed into Kenya since fighting intensified in late October, prompting growing concern over the humanitarian situation along the border. The registration exercise began around October 31 at temporary reception centres in Marsabit County, including Harhosa and OMC camps. Officials are issuing identification wristbands to newly arrived refugees before conducting household profiling to establish their needs and coordinate humanitarian assistance. Many displaced people are currently sheltering in temporary camps, schools and churches, while others are staying with relatives and host communities. Humanitarian agencies say urgent assistance is needed, particularly food, clean water, emergency shelter, sanitation, healthcare and protection for women and children. The UNHCR, International Organization for Migration, UNICEF and other partners are working with Kenyan authorities to coordinate the response. They have appealed for approximately 8.9 million dollars to provide assistance over three months. The latest influx follows renewed clashes in Moyale, where longstanding territorial and administrative disputes between Ethiopia's Oromia and Somali regional states have escalated into violence, resulting in civilian casualties, injuries and the destruction of homes and businesses. Kenyan authorities have also increased security along the border following reports of stray bullets landing in areas on the Kenyan side.

World.title: Ethiopia: Ethiopian-American Pleads Guilty to Spying for Ethiopia, Faces Up to 22 Years in U.S. Prison
World.content:
Addis Abeba — Abraham Teklu Lemma, a naturalized U.S. citizen of Ethiopian descent and former U.S. government IT contractor, pleaded guilty on November 3 to conspiring to transmit highly classified national defense information to Ethiopian government officials, potentially exposing him to nearly 22 years in prison.

Abraham, 53 or 54, of Silver Spring, Maryland, admitted conspiring from 2021 until his arrest in August 2023 to collect and transmit classified U.S. government materials to Ethiopian officials in political, military and intelligence roles, according to the U.S. Department of Justice.

The information, which included documents, handwritten notes, photographs, maps and satellite imagery, was primarily related to the armed conflict in Ethiopia and classified up to Top Secret/Sensitive Compartmented Information (TS/SCI).

"[He] exploited a position of trust to provide highly classified U.S. government information to a foreign government," U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro said, describing the conduct as a betrayal of his oath and a threat to national security.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg said Lemma "betrayed the United States to an extraordinary degree," using his IT access to remove classified national defense information from secure facilities and transmit it to Ethiopian officials.

Prosecutors said Abraham hoped the information would help Ethiopian officials "to target and kill paramilitary fighters in a regional conflict."

According to the Justice Department, Abraham worked as an IT administrator and contractor at the U.S. Department of State, Department of Justice and National Reconnaissance Office, holding Top Secret/SCI security clearance.

He allegedly concealed his activities by hand-copying classified information into notes that he carried out of secure facilities, while also removing electronic materials from classified systems. He used encrypted messaging applications to transmit the information.

In one exchange on December 18, 2021, Abraham told a conspirator, "We have to finish these people once and for all, otherwise there will never be peace in Ethiopia." Later that day, after sharing additional information, he wrote, "Please send Dro[nes]."

The materials were linked to the armed conflict and paramilitary groups opposing the Ethiopian government, prosecutors said.

Abraham was arrested in August 2023 after a criminal complaint unsealed the following month accused him of gathering and delivering national defense information to aid a foreign government, conspiracy and willful retention of classified information.

Court documents from the case described his access to and copying of dozens of intelligence reports, including at least 85 during one period, many concerning Ethiopia. Investigators alleged he removed classification markings, copied materials onto CDs and DVDs, and transmitted them through encrypted applications to an individual connected to Ethiopia's intelligence service.

He initially pleaded not guilty.

Under the plea agreement, which remains subject to court acceptance, he faces a recommended sentencing range of 120 to 262 months in prison. Sentencing is scheduled for April 14, 2027, before Senior Judge John D. Bates.

The case was investigated by the FBI's Washington Field Office, with prosecutors from the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia and the Justice Department's National Security Division.

Close 

Abraham's activities overlapped with the devastating war in the Tigray region, which erupted in November 2020, six years ago this month. The two-year war brought together Ethiopian federal forces, Eritrean troops and Amhara forces against the Tigray forces.

The war later spread to the Amhara and Afar regions, resulting in widespread casualties and displacement. It was marked by crimes against humanity, war crimes and forced deportations in Tigray, as well as war crimes in Amhara and Afar, before formally ending with the November 2022 Pretoria Cessation of Hostilities Agreement. However, implementation challenges and residual tensions persisted after the deal.

U.S. prosecutors said Lemma's alleged efforts were intended to support Ethiopian officials in targeting opposing paramilitary fighters during and after the conflict.
