World.title: Burkina Faso: Islamist Armed Group Targets Civilians
World.content:
Deadly Attack on Mining Site; Apparent Use of Banned Explosive Devices in Northern Province

An Al-Qaeda-linked armed group killed at least 27 civilians in two attacks in Burkina Faso's northern Yatenga province in September 2026.

The group's relentless, unlawful attacks put civilians across Burkina Faso at grave risk. The laws of war prohibit attacking civilians, and those who order, commit, or assist serious violations of the laws of war with criminal intent may be prosecuted for war crimes.

Burkina Faso authorities should urgently strengthen protection for threatened communities, investigate abuses, and fairly prosecute those responsible.

(Nairobi) - An Al-Qaeda-linked armed group killed at least 27 civilians in two attacks in Burkina Faso's northern Yatenga province in September 2026, Human Rights Watch said today. These attacks violated international humanitarian law and are apparent war crimes.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

On September 1, the Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin, or JNIM) attacked a gold mining site in Soubo, Ouahigouya district, killing 24 civilians, injuring at least 20 others, and burning property. On September 5, three civilians on a motorcycle, including a child, were killed by an explosive weapon on a dirt track near Mera village, also in Ouahigouya district. Local residents believe JNIM forces had planted an improvised explosive device (IED).

"The JNIM armed group's relentless, unlawful attacks put civilians across Burkina Faso at grave risk," said Ilaria Allegrozzi, senior Sahel researcher at Human Rights Watch. "The authorities should urgently strengthen protection for threatened communities, investigate abuses, and fairly prosecute those responsible."

In September and October, Human Rights Watch remotely interviewed 15 people, including 4 witnesses to the Soubo attack and 3 to the Mera attack, as well as human rights defenders and journalists. Human Rights Watch verified and geolocated four videos posted online showing the aftermath of the Soubo attack and analyzed satellite imagery and fire detection data to corroborate witness accounts.

On September 1 at about 1 a.m., over 60 JNIM fighters riding motorbikes stormed an artisanal gold mining site about 1.5 kilometers northwest of Soubo village. They fired on civilians sleeping and working there, and at those trying to flee.

"I've seen dozens of injured people, many by bullets, others because they fell while fleeing and fractured their legs or arms," a 45-year-old man said. He said that those with gunshot wounds were treated at the regional university hospital in Ouahigouya. Witnesses said the attack lasted about two hours. Fearing further attacks, residents stayed away from the site for two to three days.

During the attack, JNIM fighters destroyed hundreds of temporary structures such as sheds and huts, as well as motorcycles and mining tools.

JNIM's Sharia Committee, in a September 30 response (English, Arabic) to Human Rights Watch, acknowledged that JNIM forces attacked Soubo, but stated that the victims were members of the government-allied militias, known as Volunteers for the Defense of the Homeland (Volontaires pour la défense de la patrie, or VDP) and "not civilians." However, witnesses told Human Rights Watch that soldiers and VDPs were neither present during the attack nor stationed at the site, although they occasionally patrolled the surrounding area.

Mining sites are lucrative revenue sources for JNIM in Burkina Faso. The armed group leverages mining economies to generate revenue through "taxation" and extortion, recruit new fighters, secure essential supplies, and expand territorial control.

Witnesses said that they believed JNIM, whose fighters include many ethnic Fulani, attacked the site in retaliation for the military's targeting of Fulani people since 2022. Fulani communities, they said, had also worked at the gold mining site but had been killed and otherwise abused by the military and VDPs who viewed them as JNIM collaborators. A 45-year-old man said that while hiding in a pit to avoid getting shot, he heard a fighter say: "You chased us away, but you won't exploit this place."

At about 9:30 a.m. on September 5, an explosive weapon detonated as people rode a motorcycle along a dirt track about three kilometers from Mera village on the route to Soubo and Sissamba. It killed the 40-year-old driver and his two passengers, a 65-year-old woman and a 5-year-old boy. Mera is near the Soubo mining site, in an area where JNIM fighters frequently carry out attacks.

Witnesses said they saw no JNIM fighters nearby at the time of the explosion but had seen at least four fighters traveling along the track on two motorbikes the previous evening.

A motorbike rider, 40, said, "I saw a motorcycle in front of me with three people on it, and suddenly there was an explosion.... Dust flew around like a whirlwind. I heard a loud bang that threw me off [the bike]. The explosion shook the ground."

Human Rights Watch could not independently verify the type of explosive weapon used or how it was detonated. However, JNIM has repeatedly carried out attacks in Burkina Faso using IEDs. A 2025 report by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines, a global coalition of nongovernmental organizations including Human Rights Watch dedicated to eradicating landmines and cluster munitions, noted JNIM's use of IEDs in Burkina Faso. In 2024, Burkina Faso was among the countries with the highest rate of casualties--more than 200--due to landmines and explosive remnants of war globally.

All parties to Burkina Faso's armed conflict are bound by Common Article 3 to the 1949 Geneva Conventions and customary international humanitarian law. The laws of war prohibit attacking civilians, looting, and destroying civilian property. Individuals who order, commit, or assist serious violations of the laws of war with criminal intent may be prosecuted for war crimes. The Burkinabè government has an obligation to investigate and appropriately prosecute alleged war crimes committed within its territory.

"JNIM forces should immediately cease unlawful attacks against civilians and appropriately punish responsible commanders," Allegrozzi said. "Burkina Faso's authorities should urgently improve demining efforts and increase assistance to victims of IED attacks."

Since the start of its insurgency in Burkina Faso in 2017, JNIM has repeatedly attacked civilians and forcibly displaced tens of thousands of people. Burkina Faso's armed forces and VDPs have also committed serious abuses against civilians, especially Fulani, during operations against Islamist armed groups. In a report released in April 2026, Human Rights Watch documented that the Burkinabè and allied militia have targeted Fulani communities because of their alleged support for Islamist armed groups, resulting in the ethnic cleansing of entire communities.

The nongovernmental group Armed Conflict Location and Event Data reported that JNIM carried out 125 attacks across Burkina Faso from January to August, resulting in the killing of 188 civilians, at least 16 of them in IED attacks.

Explosive devices can be designed or fabricated to be detonated by a person's presence, proximity, or contact. Such victim-activated devices function as antipersonnel mines and are prohibited internationally, regardless of whether assembled in a factory or improvised from locally available materials. They can also be made to detonate on command by various simple means or by a simple timer. Victim-activated IEDs are inherently indiscriminate weapons and are banned under the Mine Ban Treaty, which Burkina Faso ratified in 1998.

Soubo, Yatenga Province, September 1

Witnesses said they identified the attackers by their clothes, including headscarves and a white flag with black writing, characteristic of JNIM.

"They carried weapons and wore turbans," said a 40-year-old artisanal miner and farmer. "They shouted Allah Akbar and shot at people at random." JNIM is known to operate in the area and carry out attacks against government security forces and civilians.

"The assailants began shooting everywhere and then went shed-by-shed," a 37-year-old restaurant owner said. "I lay down in my restaurant and they found me.... They shot point-blank at two of my customers who fell in front of me." She said that when JNIM fighters set her restaurant on fire, she had to get up to avoid being burned. One fighter wanted to kill her, but another told him to let her go because she was a woman. "They told me: 'Tell your husbands not to come here anymore. These places belong to us."'

When residents who had fled the site of the attack returned, they found the victims' bodies still on the ground or inside the mining pits. "I went back to the site three days later and saw the huge damage, a site covered in ashes," said a 40-year-old artisanal miner. "I saw at least 20 bodies. The bodies were swollen and gave off a foul smell. I helped pick up the bodies and carry them for burial." Residents said the bodies were buried in the cemeteries of the nearby villages of Soubo, Pirgo, and Sissamba.

In June, Burkina Faso's territorial administration minister had issued a decree suspending artisanal mining activities in Ouahigouya district from July 1 to September 30, to protect miners "from the high risk of landslides during the rainy season." However, residents said, about a thousand people--mostly artisanal miners, but also shopkeepers, owners of small restaurants, and children--were at the site at the time of the attack. They said people had continued working despite the authorities' suspension order, since officials never visited the site to enforce the suspension or check whether activities had ceased.

Close 

"The terrorists burned a lot of property, huts under which there were small restaurants, motorcycles, small straw houses, mills, water pumps, and other equipment," the 40-year-old artisanal miner said. "The fire spread from one hut to another. My barrel and my shed were also burned."

Human Rights Watch analyzed NASA satellite data and found evidence of numerous fires at the Soubo mining site on September 1 at 1:11 a.m. local time, corroborating witnesses' accounts.

Human Rights Watch also verified and geolocated four videos posted to TikTok on September 2 and 4, showing the destruction at the mining site. However, the videos only show a small part of the destruction visible in the satellite imagery. In imagery recorded on October 10, hundreds of structures are destroyed or no longer visible with burn scars on and around partially damaged structures, while others are completely destroyed. Satellite imagery recorded prior to the attack, on August 26, shows that the site contained at least 800 structures, consistent with witness accounts that at least 1,000 people were at the site.

Human Rights Watch reviewed a list provided by residents with the names of 24 victims, all civilians, including three women, ages 31, 36, and 37, and 21 men, ages 27 to 45.

Mera, September 5, Yatenga province

A farmer, 43, working in a field with other men near the road said he rushed to the scene after hearing the explosion. "When we arrived, we found a large hole at least one meter deep," he said. "A few pieces of the woman's remains were not far from the hole - the woman had no body left. The man had been propelled far from the hole, near the bushes, as well as the child who had lost his lower limbs."

"The blast knocked the wind out of me, dust filled my throat, and I couldn't see anything," a 37-year-old man said. "The debris went very high before falling everywhere. I smelled a sharp, irritating odor, like sulfur." He said that he and other people "took plastic tarps, collected the bodies and body parts, and carried out the burial the same day just after 2 p.m. in Yaoua village."

Witnesses said that after the explosion, soldiers arrived at the scene. The farmer said, "The military stepped in after the explosion to secure the area, searched for other IEDs and defused three of them, so we could safely take the bodies and bury them."

World.title: Kenya: Govt Eyes HPV Vaccination for Boys Amid Low Second-Dose Uptake Among Girls
World.content:
Nairobi — The government is considering extending the Human Papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination programme to boys as Kenya steps up efforts to prevent cervical cancer and other HPV-related diseases.

Medical Services Principal Secretary Ouma Oluga said vaccinating boys could become an important part of the country's long-term disease prevention strategy, although the current programme remains focused on girls.

His remarks come amid concerns over low completion rates for the HPV vaccine among girls, with the latest Kenya Mini Demographic and Health Survey showing that only 20 per cent have received the recommended second dose.

The survey found that 59 per cent of girls had received at least one dose of the HPV vaccine, an increase from 30 per cent recorded in the 2022 survey.



However, the significant drop between first-dose and second-dose coverage raises concerns about Kenya's ability to ensure that more girls complete the recommended vaccination schedule.

Oluga acknowledged that more efforts are needed to strengthen HPV vaccination and expand protection against the virus among young people.

He said the government could consider extending the programme to boys in the future, describing it as an important area for further attention.

"Maybe in the future, we will also consider vaccinating boys," Oluga said.

The PS also highlighted the burden of cervical cancer in Kenya, saying the disease affects approximately 7,000 women every year.

Cervical cancer is largely caused by persistent infection with high-risk types of HPV, a common virus primarily transmitted through sexual contact.

HPV vaccination before exposure to the virus offers the strongest protection against infection and related diseases.

While HPV vaccination programmes have traditionally prioritised girls because of the vaccine's role in preventing cervical cancer, vaccinating boys can also help reduce transmission and protect them against other HPV-related conditions, including certain cancers.

The latest survey figures suggest that Kenya has made progress in increasing access to the first HPV vaccine dose, with coverage rising from 30 per cent in 2022 to 59 per cent.

However, the fact that only 20 per cent of girls have received the second dose points to persistent challenges in follow-up, public awareness and access to vaccination services.

Close 

Expanding the programme to boys would require additional planning and resources, with the government yet to announce a timeline for the proposed intervention.

Oluga's remarks therefore signal a possible future policy direction rather than an immediate change to the national HPV vaccination programme.

DEMOCRATS' LATEST GUN-CONTROL PUSH RUNS INTO INCONVENIENT FACT ABOUT HOW SCHOOL KILLER WAS STOPPED

World.title: Philadelphia 'boycott ride' targeting Jewish businesses draws condemnation from city, state leadership

Jewish organizations called on Philadelphia and Pennsylvania leaders to condemn an upcoming "boycott ride" targeting pro-Israel and "Zionist establishments" in a statement Monday.

The organizations Philly Bike On Your Left, Philly Writers Against the War on Gaza, Boycott CookNSolo and Philly Solidarity Calendar shared a flier promoting the bicycle boycott event at Rittenhouse Square on Nov. 8.

"Ride around Rittenhouse with us as we show these zio business owners that we see them for the disgusting humans they are," Philly Bike On Your Left wrote on Instagram.

ISRAEL, JEWS TARGETED WORLDWIDE AS WELL-FUNDED LEFTIST, ISLAMIST GROUPS JOIN FOR ‘NAKBA 78’ PROTESTS

The flier included the names of Philadelphia businesses, including Dizengoff, Huda, Schlesinger’s and Mac Mart, all of which are owned by either Israeli or Jewish Americans.

The Anti-Defamation League (ADL) Philadelphia, American Jewish Committee Philadelphia/Southern NJ, Jewish Federation of Greater Philadelphia and StandWithUs released a joint statement condemning the event as "Jew-Hatred, plain and simple" and called on city and state leadership to do the same.

"Free speech protects political expression and criticism of Israeli government policies. It does not provide a license for threats, harassment, intimidation, or discrimination. There is a profound difference between criticizing a government and targeting businesses because their owners are Jewish or perceived to be connected to Israel," the statement read.

The organizations also remarked that the boycott's scheduled date would occur on the eve of the 88th anniversary of Kristallnacht, a Nazi-organized attack on Jewish homes, synagogues and businesses in Germany and Austria.

WEAPONIZING THE CHARGE OF GENOCIDE FUELS AN INCREASINGLY DANGEROUS ANTISEMITISM

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Philadelphia Mayor Cherelle Parker's office pointed to remarks shared Tuesday by Philadelphia Commission on Human Relations (PCHR) Executive Director Renee Chenault-Fattah.

"The Philadelphia Commission on Human Relations reaffirms its 75-year commitment to fighting racism, antisemitism and, in recent years, Islamophobia. Acts of bigotry, violence and hate cannot be tolerated, and we will never stand by and allow businesses, individuals or jobs to be run out of our city, full stop," the statement read.

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro also issued a statement to Fox News Digital condemning the event and assuring Jewish communities that his administration was working with authorities ahead of Sunday.

"The Shapiro Administration is aware of this planned protest and the Pennsylvania State Police is engaged with our local partners to ensure the safety and wellbeing of our neighbors in Philadelphia. This bike ride, masquerading as a protest to advance the cause of justice, is nothing more than blatant antisemitism designed to intimidate and drive Jewish businesses out of our communities, and there is no place for that in our Commonwealth," Shapiro spokesperson Rosie Lapowsky said.

Ahead of the planned boycott, some of the targeted businesses reported receiving broad support from the public.

Mac Mart owner Marti Lieberman told Fox News Digital that while it is "heartbreaking" to have to defend her business, she hoped the attention would shed light on what other small-business owners were facing.

OAKLAND COFFEE SHOP ACCUSED OF KICKING OUT JEWISH DAD, 5-YEAR-OLD SON AND SHUTTERS AMID ANTISEMITISM LAWSUITS

"We are absolutely feeling the love from this community, and we don’t take a single order, kind message, or person showing up for us for granted," Lieberman said. "Our hope is that this attention also sheds some light on what small business owners are dealing with, often quietly, and brings accountability to those choosing to target and tear down businesses without considering the real people behind them."

"At the end of the day, we want to keep doing what we built Mac Mart to do: feed people, make them feel welcome, and send them off a little happier than when they arrived. Everyone is still welcome at our window," she added.

Huda owner Yehuda Sichel defended his Jewish heritage and pledged to stand against the boycott.

"I’m proud to be Jewish and supportive of Israel. Neither should make my business a target," Sichel told Fox News Digital. "As the grandchild of Holocaust survivors, seeing Jewish businesses targeted on the eve of the Kristallnacht anniversary is deeply personal."

"Since this was announced, we've received nothing but positive support, with people coming in to patronize our business in response to this boycott," he added. "Our doors are open to everyone, and we’re not going anywhere."

World.title: Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz called 'cheaters' as gambling case opening statements begin in court
World.content:
Cleveland Guardians pitchers Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz were in a Brooklyn court on Wednesday during opening statements in their gambling case.

The relievers are accused of rigging their own pitches during games to benefit bettors. Both have pleaded not guilty to conspiracy charges and are on non-disciplinary leave from the club without pay while facing prosecution. They were arrested in November 2025 and have been free on bail since.

The pitchers were described by Assistant U.S. Attorney Rebecca Urquiola Wednesday as "cheaters" during opening statements , and she said they "sold their pitches."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Urquiola said Clase befriended a sports betting gambler in the Dominican Republic in early 2023 who shared his interest in dominoes and cockfighting, which is legal in his home country.

She said Clase saw gamblers profiting from his pitches and "decided it wasn't enough to help his friends make money," so he asked for kickbacks.

Clase eventually agreed to tell "his new friend" what kinds of pitches he would throw in certain games, enabling gamblers to reap at least $460,000 on platforms that allow customers to bet on whether a pitch would be a ball or a strike, she said.

Defense lawyers, however, said their clients were innocent and that a gambler who befriended Clase falsely claimed to other gamblers that the pitcher was providing inside information on his pitches and tried to sell them the information.

He said Clase was 25 in the spring of 2023 when he met a 41-year-old gambler, Enoc Pena, who made over 7,000 bets from 2023 to 2025 and had a history of lying to get what he wanted.

Pena "didn't see a peer, a friend. He saw a mark," Bronson said.

WORLD SERIES CHAMPION MARK TEIXEIRA WINS US HOUSE SEAT IN TEXAS: 'I'M EXCITED'

Soon Pena was bringing Clase food and picking him up at the airport in the Dominican Republic, the lawyer said. The pitcher, in turn, gave him tickets to Guardians games and loaned him money.

As Pena bragged to fellow gamblers that he was close to Clase and tried to sell them information, he was actually guessing which pitches Clase would throw in games and managed with fellow gamblers to lose over 200 bets on Clase's pitches, the lawyer said. Pena was "selling lies," Bronson said, urging jurors to ask themselves if his client would risk "a fortune and his lifelong dream over a few thousand dollars."

Bettors allegedly won $400,000 from betting platforms on pitches thrown by Clase between 2023 and 2025. Ortiz allegedly joined the scheme in June 2025.

In one instance, the indictment alleges, Clase used his phone in the middle of a game to coordinate with a bettor on a pitch he would throw.

Clase turned himself into arguably the game's best closer, pitching to a 1.21 ERA in his last full season in 2024, which was good for a third-place finish in the American League Cy Young Award vote. His 2025 ERA was 3.80 by the time he was investigated. Ortiz boasts a lifetime 4.36 ERA, with his best season also coming in 2024 with a 3.32 ERA.

Clase inked a five-year, $20 million deal just before opening day in 2022, a few months after finishing fifth in the AL Rookie of the Year voting. Ortiz was making the veteran minimum of $782,600 last season because he was not yet arbitration eligible.

OutKick’s Ryan Gaydos, Jackson Thompson and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

World.title: Florida congressman diagnoses GOP's blue tsunami losses: 'We failed to make them think we cared about them'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

As Republicans sift through the wreckage of a devastating election night that handed Democrats control of both chambers of Congress by large margins, one Florida Republican who bucked the national trend says the GOP fundamentally misread the electorate.

In an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital, Congressman Randy Fine — who expanded his own winning margin by five points despite the national backlash — offered a candid assessment of his party's shortcomings and warned that Republicans must now prepare for an "ugly two years" battling Democrats over immigration and other contentious issues.

While Republicans held their ground in Florida, winning the governor's mansion, the Senate race, and maintaining their 20-8 edge in the US House, nationally the GOP got crushed under the weight of a blue tsunami.

ILHAN OMAR HIT WITH EXPULSION THREAT AS GOP LAWMAKER VOWS TO BOOT HER FROM CONGRESS OVER DOJ PROBE

Congressman Fine presents no easy answer to the GOP's divergence in fortunes between Florida and the rest of the country:

"You know, I think that's a hard question to answer. What I would say, I can speak to my race, and I'm actually one of the few Republicans in the country whose margin increased from my last election. I won my special election after having $14 million spent against me. I won it by 14 points. I won last night by 19 points. And so what I can tell you is what worked for me.

"My constituents want a fighter, someone who says what they believe. They know it's not driven by polls or anything else and fights for them, whether it's fighting for their constituent service issue or fighting on illegal immigration or fighting to bring money to the district. And that's why I went up so much. I took my race seriously because I knew the winds were against us.

"And so, Florida, I think just people know how good we have it and they don't want to screw up the state. I think that's why we won all 20 of these races."

Fine refuses to single out anyone in GOP leadership for the electoral outcome, and believes the Republicans must approach each election cycle as a unified team:

"Well, look, I'm not a finger pointer, but what I would say is this. We're a team and the team lost. And so then the whole team bears responsibility and that includes me. I mean, while I did well, my team lost, and I'm not going to be here pointing the fingers at anybody.

FROM CAMPUS RADICALS TO BEIJING'S AI SABOTAGE: REP RANDY FINE SAYS 'US FIGHTING TO SAVE WESTERN CIVILIZATION'

"I think that what we did is we failed to understand what the American people wanted. I think we failed to make them think we cared about them. Now, I didn't fail in my district, but I think nationally people came to believe that we weren't interested in them and that's wrong.

"We were, but we failed to communicate it, and maybe that's part of my special sauce is I know how to communicate better than many of these people."

With Democrats firmly in control of both chambers of Congress, Fine anticipates two years of playing defense, and a continuous fight to explain why Democrats' policies will be harmful to the country:

"I don't know that we're going to push the agenda. I think what we're going to be is we're going to be on defense. We're going to have to fight back. And you know, as my father told me this morning, he goes, 'Randy, you've been a fighter your whole life. You were built for the fight.'

"So we're going to be having to fight against stupid policies that they will be pushing. And it's going to be an ugly two years, but we're gonna have to explain why all of the things that they said they would do during the campaign are so bad. We obviously didn't succeed in doing that. But as they put those policies forward, we're going to have to make the argument for why they would damage America."

Immigration is the single issue that Fine identifies as having the greatest potential to harm the country:

"I think they will seek to reopen the border and allow illegals to flood in. I think they will seek mass amnesty, rewarding all of the illegals that are here. And I think they will stop any requirement for people who come to this country to assimilate. They believe in the ‘third worldification’ of America. And that's going to be the number one thing we have to fight back against."

Florida and Texas painted a particularly stark contrast in electoral outcomes. Fine suggests the Sunshine state GOP was better prepared to face headwinds:

"Well, I think maybe our candidates at the top of the ticket were better. You know, Byron Donalds is an incredible spokesman for the conservative movement. Ashley Moody is a multiple-time winner statewide. And I think Texas allowed itself to slide on a lot of these things.

"They had a big influx of illegal immigrants. And they also really didn't fight back against the Islamification of their state in a way that we have in Florida. Demographics are destiny. And I think, to some degree, Texas was overtaken by that yesterday."

Fine has long been an outspoken critic of Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, and believes he represents a danger to the country:

"Of all the races last night, that one breaks my heart the most. I mean, someone who literally supports Muslim terror, someone whose family is embedded in so many aspects of Muslim terror. Someone who's really a danger to this country being elected to the United States Senate. It's an unspeakably horrible thing, a historically bad thing. Someone who doesn't support the United States. Someone who supports the Muslim Brotherhood.

"It breaks my heart. I'm not from Michigan, I don't know what they were thinking, but it's a terrible, terrible, terrible day. Look today for me has been a hard day. You know I won my election last night, I was super excited. My margin went up. It's unheard of in this cycle and so I'm super excited, then I watched the bottom fall out of the election results and realized so many good people lost today.

"So it's a challenging day for me, the high of winning so decisively with the low of realizing the battle that we have ahead of us, but God puts us where he wants us to be and I'm a fighter and I am ready for the fight."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Finally, as it appears that either Jim Jordan or Steve Scalise is likely to be the next House Minority Leader, Fine declined to weigh in:

"No, I mean, these are discussions. I've not spoken with either Scalise or Jordan at this point. They've got a lot of phone calls to make, and we'll get to that when we get to that. But it won't be Mike Johnson. He's taken himself out of consideration."

World.title: Trump answers questions from reporters after Republican midterm losses
World.content: President Trump took questions from reporters on the midterm results, the future of Republican leadership, the war with Iran and the possibility of impeachment in his first appearance since election night.Nov. 4, 2026

World.title: House Speaker Mike Johnson will not stay on as Republican leader after GOP losses
World.content:
WASHINGTON — A day after Democrats captured the House majority, Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., told his staff Wednesday morning he will not stay on as Republican leader in the new Congress, according to four sources on the phone call.

His announcement follows massive losses for his party in House races Tuesday.

Johnson’s departure will leave open the position of House minority leader. Republicans are scheduled to hold an internal election to select their candidate for the position Nov. 10.

Majority Leader Steve Scalise, who is the No. 2 GOP leader, a close Johnson ally and a fellow Louisiana Republican, announced his bid for minority leader in a letter to GOP colleagues on Wednesday. He became a national figure after he survived an assassination attempt during the 2017 congressional baseball shooting.

“Last night’s election was far worse than any of us expected. We fought hard and left it all on the field, but clearly, we were unable to defy history,” Scalise wrote to his colleagues.

“This is no doubt a challenging time for our conference, but overcoming adversity is nothing new to me,” he said. “We will need to be honest with ourselves about what happened, but it is more important now than ever for us to emerge from this stronger and united because the stakes couldn’t be higher.”

Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, a conservative leader in the House and staunch defender of President Donald Trump, is also running for GOP leader, he told colleagues in a letter Wednesday.

Earlier in his career, Jordan, a former collegiate wrestler and coach, was the founding chairman of the hard-right House Freedom Caucus and a frequent thorn in the side of GOP leadership. He unsuccessfully ran for minority leader and speaker before working with leadership as a committee chairman.

A former Oversight Committee chairman as well, Jordan made the case that he is “battle-tested on the oversight front” and prepared to combat Democrats’ myriad investigations of Trump.

“I know the Democrats’ playbook. I know what it will take to lead our Conference in the minority, to stay unified, and to coordinate and calibrate our response to the Democrats’ tactics,” Jordan said in his letter. “We need a Leadership team that is active and engaged, forward-thinking and straight-shooting.”

And in a surprise, Rep. August Pfluger, R-Texas, the chairman of the Republican Study Committee, the largest caucus of conservatives on Capitol Hill, said he would challenge Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., for the GOP whip spot, the No. 2 leadership job in the minority.

In the wake of Tuesday night’s drubbing, some Republicans are calling for wholesale change in the leadership team.

“We need a complete reset of all leadership,” said one senior GOP lawmaker.

Rep. Greg Steube, R-Fla., made similar remarks, saying House GOP leadership alienated conservatives.

“You have been embarrassingly weak and more afraid of governing conservatively than of disappointing the voters who put us in office,” Steube said in a post on X.

“Instead of standing firm on our principles, you have governed out of fear, continually knelt to the moderates in our conference (who all got crushed last night anyway), and discarded conservatives like me who warned of last night’s results,” he added. “Please do us all a favor and step aside so new leadership can take a truly conservative direction, with the courage to do the things we were elected to do.”

Johnson has served two terms as speaker, having risen from obscurity to the top job after Republicans ousted then-Speaker Kevin McCarthy, R-Calif., in October 2023.

The Louisiana Republican, who won re-election to his House seat Tuesday night, is expected to remain in the House next year, though it’s unclear if he will serve out his full two-year term or leave early as other former speakers have done.

Punchbowl News first reported Johnson’s decision.

World.title: Stocks surge as ‘blue tsunami’ puts political uncertainty to rest
World.content:
Stocks surged on Wednesday after Democrats won commanding victories in key races across the country, making it immediately clear to investors which party would control the House and Senate.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite closed higher by 1.4%. The broader S&P 500 surged 1.58%, its best day since August. The Russell 2000, which tracks small and medium sized companies, soared 1.5%. The Dow rocketed higher by 1,569 points, its best day since April 2025.

A few stocks missed out on the rally, though, most glaringly those of SpaceX and Tesla, which are run by Elon Musk, who spent hundreds of millions of dollars backing Republicans in the midterms.

Wall Street welcomed the clarity of the election results, which marked a departure from previous years in which it took several days for decisive projections.

“The combination of a large Democratic majority in Congress and President Trump’s statement that he is willing to work with the opposition should act as a break on extreme policy outcomes and bring down risk premia,” said Deutsche Bank’s George Saravelos in a note Wednesday morning.

“The market is increasingly likely to interpret surprising policy shifts from the Executive as time-bound by the next Presidential election or the new domestic political configuration,” he added.

Since 1946, stocks have been higher a year after every midterm election, noted Truist chief investment officer Keith Lerner. “Simply moving past the uncertainty of the midterms has also often led to a relief rally,” he said.

As the earliest results began to roll in on Tuesday night, Nasdaq 100 futures plunged as much as 2.5%. But by Wednesday, the picture had changed dramatically.

Economists at Goldman Sachs wrote that Democrats might now move to limit some of President Donald Trump’s most economically disruptive actions.

“We expect Democrats to use fiscal deadlines to seek to limit the war with Iran, roll back selected tariffs, and reverse spending cuts enacted last year,” they said in a note.

The price of oil, which has been pushed sharply higher this year due to the Iran war, declined by more than 9%.

But, experts said that results poised a major risk to the AI boom from politicians who will now take office.

“Key market implications include incrementally negative AI sentiment on greater expectations for data center restrictions,” said strategists at Morgan Stanley.

“At the federal level, the outcome is less likely to change the outlook for data center and AI regulation, which would still need bipartisan support,” said Goldman’s economists. “However, Democratic wins at the state and local level are likely to lead to short-term data center moratoria, potentially affecting about 45% of planned US data center capacity expansion.”

Several Democrats who won key governor’s races Tuesday have called for a pause in data center construction in their states, including Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia and Amy Acton in Ohio. In Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott.

Possibly more than any other state, Texas has been a major focus for AI investors and a critical market for data centers.

Texas “is the one state with enough scale” where a slowdown could make a difference, Wolfe Research’s head of U.S. policy and politics, Tobin Marcus, wrote in a recent note.

SpaceX and Tesla, both engaged in the AI and data center businesses, fell more than 3%. Musk would have been positioned to be one of the biggest beneficiaries of Republican victories.

On the other hand, shares of Amazon, Microsoft and Google parent company Alphabet, jumped 6%, because investors believe that in the case of a major data center construction slowdown, those cloud providers are best positioned with enough capacity in place already.

Apple also jumped 6%, to a record high, along with the its other trillion-dollar peers.

Analysts at JPMorgan Chase also pointed to a potential “investigation risk” facing CEOs who have close ties to Trump.

Major companies ranging from Nvidia to Apple to NBC News’ parent company, Comcast, have donated millions of dollars to Trump’s pet projects, most notably his ballroom, and some of their leaders have regularly appeared alongside him at events.

Top Democrats have already signaled their interest in launching investigations of some of Trump’s projects in January, when their new congressional majority will give them subpoena power.

Shares of Trump Media & Technology Group, which owns the president’s Truth Social site, plummeted 25% to an all-time low. In August, the company launched a high-speed data feed, allowing trading firms to pay for early access to the president’s announcements before the general public.

Democrats vs. data centers

Tech stocks have played more of a role than any other sector to the surge in the value of U.S. equity markets over the last two years.

Trillion-dollar companies such as Amazon, Nvidia, Microsoft and Google parent Alphabet, as well as a handful of smaller data center startups, have poured hundreds of billions of dollars into developing AI models, building data centers and buying the equipment needed to operate them.

The AI boom has been a primary driver behind the Nasdaq 100’s gain of 40% since Election Day 2024, more than the S&P 500’s roughly 30% jump.

Any widespread slowing or halting of data center construction could put those unprecedented and sweeping investments, which many of the country’s top companies have stakes in, at risk.

“Democrats winning gubernatorial races in Texas, Ohio, and Georgia — which have a significant share of the U.S. project pipeline — means new pauses and restrictions on data center development,” Evercore’s Sarah Bianchi wrote late Tuesday.

She added that “2027 is shaping up to be a turbulent year as developers will be forced to adapt to a shifting policy landscape,” but cautioned traders not to get ahead of themselves.

Bianchi wrote that “the impact of any pause or moratorium will hinge on the details, such as any grandfathering, and whether projects facing prolonged disruption can relocate to other states.”

Democrats were also projected to win Senate races in a number of battleground states where data centers were a major issue during the campaign, including Georgia, North Carolina, Michigan, Ohio, Iowa and Kansas.

“Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Musk wrote on X the midterm results became clear. He has also proposed putting servers for AI systems in orbit above Earth. Most experts say the idea faces significant hurdles.

Even before Tuesday’s projected results, markets had been on edge for months about whether, and how, the AI boom and the massive investments tied to it would deliver returns.

On Friday, the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq both posted their worst days since mid-June after Intel and Amazon, two key suppliers to AI companies, reported mixed earnings results.

World.title: 5 key insights from the NBC News Exit Poll about the blue tsunami
World.content:
It was a historic blue tsunami: The Democratic Party captured both chambers of Congress, flipping as many as seven seats in the Senate and at least 29 in the House of Representatives.

Just two years ago, the nation had been hit by a red wave. How did things turn around so dramatically?

A cocktail of crucial factors: Voters feeling fed up with the economy, Democratic candidates emerging as more well-liked, important voting blocs — including Latinos and Black men — shifting blue, opinions about the Republican Party dropping and a resounding rejection of President Donald Trump himself, according to the NBC News Exit Poll.

Here are five key insights we have gleaned about Tuesday’s stunning midterms analyzing data from the poll, which surveyed more than 79,000 voters nationwide.

Follow live updates on the midterm elections

1) Americans were deeply negative on the state of the economy and gloomy about the future of the country.

An overwhelming majority of voters (75%) rated the nation’s economy as “not so good” or “poor,” the poll showed. And they soured on their trust in Republicans to handle it.

Sixty-nine percent said the U.S. economic system favors the wealthy, and only 31% said it favors most Americans. This perception came at a time when the vast majority of voters expressed concerns about the cost of living. More than 80% of voters said they were worried about the price of necessities: gas and diesel fuel, food and groceries, utilities and healthcare.

Thirty-seven percent of voters said they favored Republican control of the economy, while 43% favored Democrats — a flip in perspective from the 2024 election. Voters also blamed Trump: 65% said the president’s policies had made the economy worse. Just 27% said they had made the economy better.

A David Crowley supporter at an election night event in Milwaukee on Tuesday. Nam Y. Huh / AP

Sixty-two percent said higher-than-usual prices are more because of Trump’s policies than factors outside his control, and 65% said his tariff policies hurt the national economy.

Their frustration extended beyond the economy — and into a pessimistic view of the U.S. overall. Three in four voters said they were unhappy with how things are going in the U.S., and more than a third (38%) said they were angry about the state of the country.

More than half of voters (57%) said that life for the next generation of Americans will be worse than today; just 22% said they believed it would be better.

2) Democratic candidates enjoyed advantages on favorability, character and experience.

In an overwhelmingly negative political environment, Democratic Senate candidates emerged as well-liked in races that looked tough for them at the beginning of the election cycle, according to the poll.

Democrats above water on favorability included Jon Ossoff in Georgia, where a remarkable 59% of state voters said they viewed him favorably; James Talarico in Texas, where 52% of voters said they viewed him positively; and Josh Turek in Iowa, where 49% of voters said they viewed him favorably. All three candidates won their races.

Republicans, meanwhile, struggled to win over voters.

In two key Senate races, voters expressed negative opinions about Republican candidates’ personal character.

A watch party for the Democratic candidate for Senate, Adam Hamilton, in Overland Park, Kansas, on Tuesday. Evert Nelson / USA TODAY via Reuters

In Kansas, 43% of voters said Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, an OB-GYN who faced scrutiny after The New York Times reported that he sued hundreds of patients over unpaid bills, had the right character for the job. Marshall has described the story as a “hit job.”

Voter opinions were worse about Ken Paxton’s personal character. Only 34% of Texas voters thought positively of the attorney general, who has battled scandals for years and was impeached in 2023 by the Republican controlled state House before the state Senate acquitted him.

Both Paxton and Marshall lost their Senate bids.

Candidates aligned with Trump also struggled. In North Carolina, Michael Whatley was seen as too supportive of Trump (60%), and in South Carolina, where the president endorsed Darline Graham, only 35% of voters said she had the right experience.

3) After flirting with the GOP in 2024, big Democratic voting blocs swung back with a vengeance.

By ignoring or denigrating many of the new voters who were key to Trump’s victory two years ago, Republicans squandered the opportunity to cement a new coalition of voters.

Latinos, who notably gave Trump almost half (46%) of their votes in 2024, bounced back to the Democrats, who garnered 62% of Latino support in races for the House, the poll showed.

Among Black male voters, 1 in 5 went for Trump in 2024. That share shrunk to 13% for Republican House candidates this year.

Trump narrowly won men under age 25 in 2024, getting 49% of their votes compared to 48% for Democrat Kamala Harris. But young men swung dramatically away from the GOP in House races this year: Democrats swept them by a 68% to 28% margin.

On the whole, more Trump voters had buyer’s remorse (6% supported Democratic House candidates) than Harris voters (3% defected to the GOP).

4) And Trump himself was soundly rejected by voters.

Trump tried to energize his base by encouraging his supporters to vote like, “I’m on the ballot.” But the nation had largely soured on his presidency, according to the poll.

Trump’s approval rating among voters, just 38%, was the lowest Election Day rating for any president since 2008.

Forty-three percent of voters said they cast their House ballot to express opposition to Trump. Just 16% said they voted to express support for him.

Voters gave Trump overwhelmingly negative marks on key aspects of his presidency, saying that he prioritizes “his own personal interests” over the country’s (62%), that his war against Iran was the “wrong decision” (63%) and that his immigration actions had “gone too far” (57%).

5) A key distinction: It’s a blue tsunami, not a progressive earthquake.

Politicians and pundits alike mistook Trump’s 2024 victory as an endorsement of his deeply conservative plans. But the 2024 NBC Exit Poll found little evidence of an ideological shift to the right.

The story is the same this year: On key issues, voters are no more progressive than they were two years ago.

Among voters this year, 64% said abortion should be legal in most or all cases. That’s just a notch below the share of 65% in 2024.

Twenty-three percent of the electorate considered themselves liberal in 2024, while 35% called themselves conservative. Those numbers hardly budged among voters in 2026, standing at 25% liberal, 34% conservative.

Voters’ opinions of socialism remained largely negative, at 54% unfavorable and 33% favorable. Just 1 in 5 voters this year considered themselves democratic socialists. By contrast, capitalism remains relatively well-regarded in the minds of voters (57% favorable, 32% unfavorable).

World.title: Progressive William Lawrence defeats GOP Rep. Tom Barrett in swing Michigan district
World.content:
Progressive activist William Lawrence has defeated Rep. Tom Barrett, R-Mich., in one of the most competitive House races on the map, NBC News projects.

The result marks a rare battleground race victory for the Democratic Party’s left flank, which has so far built its power in deep blue districts and cities.

The contest for Michigan’s 7th Congressional District was shaped by voter malaise with the economy under President Donald Trump and backlash to data centers. A co-founder of the Sunrise Movement, Lawrence centered his candidacy on opposition to local data center development and controversial Flock cameras while also pushing for tight restrictions on AI development.

He advanced to the general election after emerging from a divisive primary with less than 50% of the vote.

Follow live coverage

Rep. Tom Barrett, R-Mich. Tom Williams / CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty

Speaking with NBC News in September, Lawrence said the growing opposition to data center development was happening “at this moment in our history [where] the extreme concentration of power may be the single greatest threat that we face, and the place where it is concentrated is in these tech companies and their allies at the very heights of government.”

Lawrence, who came under fire for deleted social media posts that included writing “F--- isolation and the nuclear family domicile” during the pandemic, distanced himself from some past positions and said he let his Democratic Socialists of America membership “lapse” in July.

He said he was not campaigning as a DSA candidate because he believes “partisan and ideological labels … do a lot more to divide us than they do to bring people together.”

Barrett, a first-term congressman and Army veteran who previously served in the state Legislature, had cast Lawrence as being too far left for the swing district, which backed Trump in 2024 and was previously represented by Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich. Barrett won by 3 points in his 2024 race.

But as the environment worsened for Republicans, with voters souring on the economy and the war with Iran, Barrett moved to create some space between him and the president. He was an early Republican backer of war powers resolutions calling to limit the president’s powers in Iran. He also introduced data center legislation that would prohibit the federal government from overriding localities on data centers — an effort Lawrence said did not go far enough to regulate their development.

“I don’t agree with it,” Barrett told NBC News in September of Trump earlier remarking that the only reason a community wouldn’t want a data center is if they wanted to end up “backwards and poor.”

“I think that ultimately this decision has to rest with the people who live in those communities, and I respect that,” Barrett said.

The two battled over AI regulations at a debate last month, with Lawrence calling for a pause on AI advancements, pointing to whistleblowers raising alarms about the dangers of the technology, while Barrett talked up the need for “robust protections.” But Barrett said a pause would only empower American adversaries.

World.title: Democrats gain full control of five state governments, further expanding the party’s power
World.content:
Democrats gained total control of at least five state governments on Tuesday, giving the party a level of power it hasn’t held in some of those places in years.

The party won so-called trifectas — taking the governor’s office and both legislative chambers — in Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, according to The Associated Press.

The victories are the latest marker of an overwhelmingly successful midterm election for the party. In addition to sweeping control of both chambers of Congress, Democrats won a majority of governorships for the first time in 16 years, with Republicans long dominating at the state level.

Now, Democrats will have the ability to fundamentally change the local policy agenda, including in several presidential battleground states.

“This was the most significant night for state legislatures since the seismic Republican wave in 2010,” said Mandara Meyers, the executive director of The States Project, a Democratic-aligned group that works to build the party’s power in state legislatures.

The group was one of several to spend millions to boost Democratic gains in state legislative chambers.

Follow live coverage

In Wisconsin, Democrats clawed back full control of state government for the first time in 16 years, flipping the state Assembly and Senate while holding on to the governor’s mansion.

Those gains were partly the product of the state’s new legislative maps that went into effect after the state Supreme Court struck down the previous Republican-drawn lines in 2024. Democrats needed to flip two seats for a majority in the Senate and five in the Assembly but ended up with far more in both chambers.

In another key swing state, Pennsylvania, Democrats flipped far more than the three seats they needed in the state Senate to retake the chamber, while also expanding on what had been a one-seat edge in the state Assembly, handing the re-elected Gov. Josh Shapiro a powerful tool for his second term. It’s Democrats’ first trifecta in Pennsylvania since 1993.

Democrats also recaptured a trifecta in Michigan after losing it two years earlier, flipping control of the state House and padding their narrow majority in the state Senate. Meanwhile, Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson won the race to succeed term-limited Democratic Gov. Gretchen Whitmer.

In Minnesota, Democrats built sizable majorities in both legislative chambers, having needed only to flip one seat in the state House and protect a one-seat majority in the state Senate. Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar will be the state’s next governor, taking over for Gov. Tim Walz.

And in Nevada, Democrats held on to their existing control of both legislative chambers, while flipping the governorship blue with state Attorney General Aaron Ford’s win over GOP Gov. Joe Lombardo.

Democrats could still gain another trifecta in Arizona, where they haven’t held full control of state government in 60 years. State party leaders said they were on track to win both legislative chambers, though the AP has yet to project partisan control for either. Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs, meanwhile, won re-election.

The party also made notable inroads in traditionally Republican states.

In Texas, state Rep. Gina Hinojosa defeated GOP Gov. Greg Abbott, becoming the first Democratic governor to lead the state since 1995. Republicans had enjoyed complete control over state government since 2003.

As of Wednesday morning, Texas state Democrats had made significant gains in the state House, too — some state party leaders said control of the chamber was within reach — though the AP has not yet called control of that chamber. Republicans maintained control of the state Senate, according to the AP.

In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms won the race for governor, flipping the office blue for the first time in 24 years, while Democrats made major gains in the state House. The AP hasn’t called control of the state House but has projected that Republicans will maintain control of the state Senate.

Republicans had held a trifecta in Georgia since 2005.

In addition, Democratic gubernatorial victories in Iowa and Ohio broke up total GOP control of state government there.

Democrats also flipped control of the North Carolina state House for the first time in 16 years, the AP projected, while narrowly falling short of a majority in the state Senate.

Elsewhere, Democrats said they made enough legislative seat gains to break Republican supermajorities in chambers in South Carolina, Florida, Indiana, Kansas, Missouri and Ohio.

World.title: Democrats score key secretary of state wins ahead of the 2028 election
World.content:
Democrats won secretary of state contests in four presidential battlegrounds while making inroads in red territory, giving them election oversight authority in key states for the 2028 elections.

Democratic candidates maintained control of secretary of state offices in Arizona, Michigan and Nevada, while flipping the office in Georgia, all states that have been at the center of recent campaigns for the White House. And Democrats gained secretary of state control in the GOP-leaning states of Indiana and Ohio.

Follow live coverage

In Georgia, Democrat Penny Brown Reynolds will succeed Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger, who drew President Donald Trump’s ire for rebuffing his push to overturn the state’s 2020 election results. She defeated state Rep. Tim Fleming, a former aide to outgoing Republican Gov. Brian Kemp who was endorsed by Trump.

Reynolds, who is known for a family court television show and serving in the Biden administration, campaigned as a judge who would stand up to Trump while following the law in running state elections. Fleming did not go as far as other Republicans in claiming the 2020 election was stolen, but said there were “irregularities” and called for new mail voting restrictions.

In Michigan, Democratic Lt. Gov Garlin Gilchrist bested Macomb County Clerk Anthony Forlini, a Republican, to succeed Democratic Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, who won the state’s race for governor. Gilchrist had criticized Forlini for sharing voter data with the Trump administration and hiring a Jan. 6 protester to his office.

In Arizona and Nevada, incumbent Democrats Adrian Fontes and Cisco Aguilar fended off challenges from far-right Republicans whose careers were rooted in advancing election conspiracy theories, enjoying far better margins than they had in similar 2022 matchups.

And in Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa’s win in the governor’s race is also expected to give the party authority over the administration of state elections. Texas’ secretary of state is appointed by the governor, with concurrent terms.

Once an under-the-radar, downballot job, secretary of state has become a much more high-profile position amid a constant drumbeat of unfounded election fraud claims from Trump and his allies. All four battleground states saw challenges to the 2020 election results and secretaries of state in these and other states have faced a steady stream of lawsuits and threats.

In the final stretch of the midterm campaign, Democrats started targeting Indiana, Kansas, Ohio and Iowa for red-state gains. So far, they’ve won two of their targets and lost one.

Democratic state Rep. Allison Russo will be the next secretary of state of Ohio as her party also flipped Senate and gubernatorial seats in a state that has shifted to the right in recent years. Russo defeated Republican state Treasurer Robert Sprague.

In Indiana, Beau Bayh, a 30-year-old scion of a longtime Democratic family in the state, beat Republican state Rep. Max Engling. Engling had replaced Indiana’s Republican incumbent, Diego Morales, who was embroiled in allegations of corruption and ethics violations, at the party’s nominating convention.

Bayh spent more than $ 8.6 million on ads, according to AdImpact, campaigning heavily on fighting corruption. He ran at the top of the ticket in Indiana, which didn’t have any races for Senate or governor this year.

In Kansas, where voters haven’t elected a Democrat as secretary of state since 1948, the race between Democratic state Rep. Jennifer Day and Republican state Rep. Pat Proctor was too close to call, according to NBC News’ Decision Desk.

Democrats saw success elsewhere in the state, with pastor Adam Hamilton pulling off an upset over GOP Sen. Roger Marshall.

Top-of-the-ticket wins didn’t translate to secretary of state success everywhere.

In Iowa, Republican Secretary of State Paul Pate fended off a challenge from Democrat Ryan Peterman, even as Democrats won Senate and governor’s races in the state.

And In South Carolina, Republican Secretary of State Mark Hammond beat Democratic challenger Jason Belton, even as Democrat Annie Andrews prevailed in the Senate race.

World.title: Tuesday’s elections bring historic first for Black governors
World.content:
For the first time in U.S. history, multiple elected Black governors will serve at the same time after five wins in elections across the country.

They are Democrat Wes Moore, who won re-election in Maryland, Republican Rep. Byron Donalds in Florida, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia, Democrat David Crowley in Wisconsin and Democrat Aaron Ford in Nevada.

Before those wins, the only elected Black governors in U.S. history had been Moore; Deval Patrick, a Democrat who was elected Massachusetts’ governor in 2006; and Doug Wilder, a Democrat who was elected Virginia’s governor in 1989. None served simultaneously.

Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, overcame an enormous spending disadvantage to defeat Republican Rick Jackson, a wealthy healthcare executive who pumped more than $100 million of his own money into his campaign. She is the first woman and the first Black person to be elected governor of Georgia, and will be the first Black female governor in U.S. history.

Follow live updates on the midterm elections

In an interview with NBC News last month, Donalds said the history-making aspect of his candidacy was “very special.”

“From a larger perspective, there’s so much that has been talked about in politics over the last couple decades around race. Obviously, the country has had some real negative parts of our history surrounding race,” he said. “I’m humbled to be in this position, but I think it says a lot more about the state [of Florida] than it does about me.”

Others fell short in their races.

In South Carolina, another Black Democrat, state Rep. Jermaine Johnson, lost his state’s race for governor to Republican Alan Wilson.

On the Republican side, Rep. John James lost his governor’s race to Democrat Jocelyn Benson, and Minnesota state House Speaker Lisa Demuth lost the state’s gubernatorial contest to Democrat Amy Klobuchar.

World.title: Midterm elections could zap the data center buildout, experts say
World.content:
The Democrats' sweeping victories in the midterm elections on Tuesday could buoy opponents of data centers in some parts of the U.S. and slow the spread of the controversial facilities, according to Wall Street analysts.

As of Wednesday afternoon, voters had approved 38 ballot measures restricting data centers in communities across California, Illinois, Maine, Ohio, New York and other states, according to an analysis from political research firm Redbud Consulting. Residents in Harwood, North Dakota, were the only voters to approve a data center.

The election also elevates a number of state and gubernatorial candidates who made stricter regulation of data centers a key part of their campaigns.

The rapid development of data centers around the U.S. to help power artificial intelligence has provoked widespread public backlash. By a margin of more than 2-to-1, more Americans oppose than favor building a new data center in their area, a CBS News poll found this summer.

Focus on Texas

Franklin Templeton chief market strategist Stephen Dover predicted that the election results will lead to a "slowdown in data centers being built," bringing new regulations and costs for their developers.

"For tech investors, the big focus is will these midterm elections slow the pace of the planned 800 to 1,000 data centers across the U.S. fueling the AI Revolution," Yorkville Ives & Co. technology analyst Dan Ives said in a report. "The answer in our view is a clear YES."

Ives pointed to Texas, which accounts for 25% to 30% of the data center capacity expected to come online by 2030, as one state that could be affected. Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who defeated Republican incumbent Greg Abbott in the race for governor, proposed a temporary ban on data center construction during her campaign.

"Texas is the foundation of the AI buildout in the U.S.," Ives told CBS News.

Hinojosa's win over Abbott could stall the addition of 13 gigawatts of data-center power in Texas, according to Gordon Johnson, CEO and founder of the investment adviser GLJ Research.

Abbott had already suspended data center approvals, which makes it easy for Hinojosa to extend the moratorium.

"Texas already has a moratorium — Abbott built it. All the new governor has to do is keep it in place. She doesn't need a new law to keep data center permits frozen," Johnson told CBS News.

Keisha Lance Bottoms' gubernatorial victory in Georgia, the third-largest data center market, also has significant implications for the infrastructure buildout.

Bottoms, who campaigned on pausing new data center construction in the state, told CBS Mornings on Wednesday that she would immediately "sign an executive order for that pause, and then we will determine what else we need to do administratively to take that pause into effect."

Bottoms also said she plans to review tax incentives offered in Georgia that have spurred data center development.

"So, of course, we are going to have to take a look at what those agreements entail and determine what our remedies are to enact that pause, but I don't think we're going to get a lot of pushback across the state," she said. "Many local governments have already taken that first step."

Cooling an overheated sector

Market analyst Adam Crisafulli of Vital Knowledge noted that semiconductor, hardware and other stocks associated with data center construction fell sharply on Wednesday amid investor concerns over permitting delays.

Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management, thinks data center developers could face additional requirements to invest in electrical grids and potentially lose tax incentives, thereby raising their costs. She added in a research note that higher development costs for new facilities could "increase the value of existing infrastructure that is already powered, permitted, and operational."

Massive investment in data centers and the artificial intelligence sector more broadly has helped propel U.S. economic growth and drive stock market gains. In the long term, however, a slower data center buildout is unlikely to hamstring the economy, Dover of Franklin Templeton told CBS News.

"It's possible to argue that the AI trade and data center buildout was getting overheated, and this could dampen some of the excessive investment that might not have a good return on capital, which investors have questioned anyway," he said. "So unbridled expansion will be tempered a bit, but probably not a lot."

Although data center moratoriums may delay construction, they're unlikely to torpedo capital spending on AI or short-circuit broader growth, according to economists.

"A more restrictive stance toward data centers would stretch the timelines of future projects, and slower construction in the medium to long term wouldn't necessarily be a bad outcome for the macroeconomy," analysts with Oxford Economics said in a report.

World.title: Dow posts biggest gain of the year after Democrats sweep Congress
World.content:
The Dow Jones Industrial Average soared nearly 1,600 points, or 3%, on Wednesday, its biggest gain of the year, as investors digested the impact of the Democrats' sweeping victories in the midterm congressional elections.

Other indexes also jumped, with the broader S&P 500 climbing 120 points, or 1.6%, to close at 7,689 and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index gaining 1.4%.

"Investors are happy to have the midterms out of the way," market analyst Adam Crisafulli, head of Vital Knowledge, told investors in a report. "This was a major source of uncertainty, and putting it in the rear-view mirror removes a key obstacle heading into a very favorable time of year seasonally."

The shifting political winds could affect a range of issues that influence investment returns, from the pace of the data center buildout and cryptocurrency industry regulation to proposals to cap credit card interest rates.

At the same time, Wall Street analysts do not expect the outcome to derail a stock market being driven more by robust corporate profits and solid economic growth than by politics.

"The magnitude of the gains for the Democrats in the midterms does not change too much for the near-term policy outlook, given the party still lacks a filibuster-proof majority in the Senate and President Trump has veto power to block legislation," Stephen Brown of Capital Economics said in a note to investors.

Stocks of solar power companies, dollar stores and hospital owners helped lead the way as Wall Street tried to sort the winners from losers following the widespread losses for Republicans.

Investors, meanwhile, see risks ahead for Mr. Trump's social media company, the artificial intelligence sector and businesses owned by Elon Musk, who donated heavily to Republicans. Trump Media & Technology's stock price fell nearly 25% on Wednesday, while shares of Musk-owned SpaceX and Tesla sank 3.8% and 3.3%, respectively.

Gridlock good for stocks?

Investors also expect the election results to heighten gridlock in Congress, with Democratic lawmakers now in control of both the House and Senate, and Mr. Trump threatening to wield his veto power to block any legislation he opposes.

Political gridlock has historically been good for markets because it limits Congress' ability to pass sweeping tax and spending legislation, reducing the risk of volatility, according to Wall Street analysts.

Meanwhile, stocks have generally performed well following midterm elections. The S&P 500 stock index rose an average of 15.5% in the six months after the last 14 midterm races, dating back to 1970, according to figures from investment firm Edward Jones.

"Economic growth, inflation, interest rates and corporate earnings have historically mattered more to broad investment performance than the party composition of Congress, especially if the president and congressional leadership come from different parties," analysts with the Wells Fargo Investment Institute said in a report.

"We do not expect sweeping policy changes," they added. "More likely, in our view, is a split-government alignment on affordability, energy policy and opportunities from artificial intelligence."

Beyond the Beltway, the midterm electoral results could affect key issues for investors, such as the pace of data center construction, with enormous spending on artificial intelligence helping drive stocks to record highs this year while also raising concerns about a bubble in tech stocks.

"In divided government, the policy implications at the federal level may be limited, but data center policy decisions sit at the state and utility-commission level, making gubernatorial and utility races important alongside Congress, particularly Governor Abbott's loss in Texas," Jeff Buchbinder of LPL Research told investors.

"LPL Research continues to expect the buildout to occur, but strong performances by Democrats in key data center states (and pushback from the 'not in my backyard' folks) may slow it down some, potentially increasing regulatory pressure on AI infrastructure stocks including semiconductors, machinery and power generation," he added.

World.title: McDonald's plans to cook up cheaper menu items as sales slow
World.content:
McDonald's plans to offer more lower-priced menu items next year as it tries to lure inflation-weary customers struggling with the cost of living.

McDonald's CEO Christopher Kempczinski said Wednesday during a call with Wall Street analysts that the fast-food chain recently launched an eight-week pilot program to test new affordable menu options at 1,900 U.S. locations. The company is also testing "mix and match bundles" to see which will drive sales, he said.

McDonald's is aiming to launch the new offerings nationally in 2027, Kempczinski said.

The news came after McDonald's earnings report, released Wednesday, showed comparable sales growth of only 0.2% at U.S. locations from July to September, down from 2.4% during the same period last year. Overall foot traffic at the chain's U.S. stores was down 4.6% from a year ago, according to data from analytics platform Placer.ai.

Kempczinski acknowledged that the company has not done enough to meet the expectations of low-income diners, who are looking for "great entry-level value."

"We talked quite extensively about how [in] Q2 we didn't land that like we needed to," he told investors. "And so that's what we're in the midst of getting resolved right now and through testing."

His comments come the day after the U.S. midterms, where affordability concerns took center stage. Many candidates campaigned on addressing cost-of-living issues and bringing down gasoline prices, which have risen 38% since the start of the war in Iran, according to AAA data.

U.S. consumer spending has remained resilient even in the face of stubborn inflation, which remains stuck above the Federal Reserve's 2% target. However, economists note that lower-income consumers are feeling particularly strapped, as a larger share of their income goes toward expenses like gas.

Low-income consumers "are disproportionately feeling the effect of higher food and gasoline prices," Ryan Sweet, chief global economist at Oxford Economics, said on Wednesday during an event in New York City.

World.title: Huge space telescope plunges back to Earth after 22 years in orbit
World.content:
The Swift Observatory, a 1.5-ton NASA telescope that was launched more than two decades ago, has crashed back to Earth after an effort to rescue the wayward instrument failed earlier this year.

The roughly 3,200-pound observatory reentered Earth's atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. ET over the North Sumatra region of Indonesia, NASA said. Much of it burned up upon reentry. Some components are expected to survive reentry and may be found sprawled across hemispheres, NASA said.

The observatory's reentry path was tracked by NASA and the U.S. Space Force. NASA predicted its reentry time at around 3:30 a.m. ET on Nov. 4, with an 11-hour window of uncertainty on either side. NASA had previously said the "risk of harm coming to anyone on Earth is unlikely," placing the odds at about 1 in 2,100.

The Swift Observatory was sent into low-Earth orbit on Nov. 20, 2004 — almost exactly 22 years ago. The telescope's mission was to search for massive galactic explosions, including gamma-ray bursts and supernovas. The telescope was named for its ability to swerve rapidly toward such events.

The Swift Observatory NASA

The telescope was initially designed to run a two-year mission, but continued its operations until last month. Solar activity eventually dragged the telescope back down to Earth. Katalyst Space was contracted by NASA to mount a rescue of the telescope in July. The company dispatched a three-armed robot named Link to push the telescope back into place, but the robot ran into trouble shortly after launching. It was not able to get within seven miles of the telescope. The robot fell back to Earth in September. In August, it was decided that the Swift Observatory would be allowed to plunge back to Earth.

The telescope continued to return observations until late October, when NASA determined it was too low to remain steady. Its systems were shut down at that time.

In addition to observing more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts and 1,400 exploding stars, the Swift telescope was a "first responder" for the Hubble and Webb space telescopes, NASA said. Swift would issue alerts to those and other facilities, which would then more deeply investigate those observations.

"Swift has broadened our understanding of a wide variety of cosmic objects and events, from active galaxies powered by supermassive black holes and stars undergoing X-ray flares, to supernova explosions and comets and asteroids in our own solar system," NASA said in a blog post.

Scientists are still trying to figure out how to replace the work done by the Swift Observatory.

"We've known this day would come since before Swift was launched. At least in low-Earth orbit, what goes up must come down. And that end is catastrophic," Pennsylvania State University's John Nousek, an astronomer who led the control team, said on Monday.

"Our fervent hope is that the lessons learned by the successes of Swift can be applied to new generations of space missions to accelerate our discoveries about the universe," Nousek added.

World.title: Democrats' election rout is poised to reorder federal health policy
World.content:
Democrats' decisive sweep of the U.S. House and Senate in Tuesday's elections will reshape the direction of federal health policy — setting the stage for oversight investigations, a legislative push to reverse cuts to the Affordable Care Act and Medicaid, and a focus on lowering costs such as insurance premiums and drug prices.

The conclusive string of victories sets up Democrats to argue that voters — who said in preelection surveys that healthcare affordability was a top concern — have given them a clear mandate to overturn historic cuts President Trump and Republicans made to public healthcare programs.

The breadth of success, including wins by Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and other progressives, is likely to embolden some Democrats to forge ahead with ambitious policy proposals such as expanding Medicare, the federal insurance program for people age 65 and older, to cover all Americans. Their plan is to be positioned as the party that prioritizes lowering healthcare costs for the 2028 presidential election.

Party leaders, though, will need buy-in from Mr. Trump to advance any healthcare agenda. While he has veto power, he may be interested in brokering legislative deals as he seeks to cement his legacy and deflect fallout from investigations into his administration's handling of the war against Iran, mass deportations, contracting scandals, and other controversies.

Democrats were projected to win at least 237 of 435 seats in the House and at least 54 Senate seats as of Wednesday afternoon, according to The Associated Press. Several key races remained unresolved, including Senate contests in Alaska and Mississippi.

As election results continued coming out into early-morning Wednesday, Mr. Trump said in a phone interview with Politico that he had spoken with Democratic Party leaders and that voters had sent a message he must work with them "to make sure things go well for our country."

"I don't want to just be sitting there for two years vetoing everything," Mr. Trump said. "They want to see things happen, too."

But how Mr. Trump's new conciliatory position plays out in undoing GOP-led changes, such as new work requirements for many adults enrolled in Medicaid, the state-federal program for low-income and disabled people, remains to be seen. Republicans touted their overhaul of Medicaid and other changes to health programs wrought by their One Big Beautiful Bill Act as signature achievements in midterm campaigns.
