She said 72.43 billion pesos, or 61% of the total, has already been spent. 🎪 115 “Well-being Fairs” held across all 113 Michoacán municipalities: Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez said residents completed more than 1.1 million administrative procedures at the fairs over the past year, including ones that facilitated access to welfare programs.

Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez said residents completed more than 1.1 million administrative procedures at the fairs over the past year, including ones that facilitated access to welfare programs. 🛣️ 41 billion pesos invested in Michoacán highways: Infrastructure Minister Jesús Esteva said the government is upgrading 411 kilometers of highway, with the government and private sector investing more than 41 billion pesos (US $2.2 billion) in six projects.

Infrastructure Minister Jesús Esteva said the government is upgrading 411 kilometers of highway, with the government and private sector investing more than 41 billion pesos (US $2.2 billion) in six projects. 🏭 Work on Bajío Industrial Park to start this month: Deputy Economy Minister Luis Rosendo Gutiérrez said 9.3 billion pesos (US $498.5 million) will be invested in the park in Zinapécuaro, which will primarily cater to the agroindustrial and automotive sectors.

Deputy Economy Minister Luis Rosendo Gutiérrez said 9.3 billion pesos (US $498.5 million) will be invested in the park in Zinapécuaro, which will primarily cater to the agroindustrial and automotive sectors. 🎓 795,000 Michoacán students receive government scholarships: Education Minister Mario Delgado said primary, middle school, high school and university students all receive monetary assistance, funded with an investment of 5.7 billion pesos (around US $306 million).

Why today’s mañanera matters

A presentation on the progress made under “Plan Michoacán for Peace and Justice” over the past year was the central focus of President Sheinbaum’s Wednesday morning press conference.

The government devised the plan in response to the assassination of Uruapan Mayor Carlos Manzo on Nov. 1, 2025, and general insecurity in Michoacán.

At the start of her Wednesday mañanera, the president noted that today’s presentation would focus on progress in areas other than security. She said that an update on the security situation in Michoacán would be presented at her press conference next Tuesday.

Data presented at Sheinbaum’s Oct. 13 mañanera showed that homicides in Michoacán declined 40.3% in the first nine months of 2026 compared to the same period of last year.

The president was accompanied on Wednesday by various high-ranking officials, each of whom spoke briefly about Plan Michoacán initiatives.

Today’s mañanera allowed the government to both highlight progress on the plan and explain how funds have been spent. Sheinbaum characterizes her weekday press conferences as exercises in transparency, a principle she says is central to her administration.

115 ‘Well-being Fairs’ held in Michoacán

Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez reported that 115 “Ferías del Bienestar,” or “Well-being Fairs,” were held across all 113 municipalities of Michoacán over the past year.

She said that officials helped Michoacán residents complete more than 1.1 million trámites (administrative procedures) at the fairs, including ones that facilitated their access to government welfare programs.

Rodríguez also noted that Michoacán residents exchanged 673 firearms for cash over the past year under the Sí al Desarme, Sí a la Paz (Yes to Disarmament, Yes to Peace) program. Those exchanges, she said, will save lives.

Key advances under Plan Michoacán

Officials presented key advances under Plan Michoacán across a range of areas. Not all of the investment they outlined is directly linked to Plan Michoacán funding. Summarized below are the presentations made by 10 officials.

Deputy Economy Minister Luis Rosendo Gutiérrez reported that work will start this month on the Bajío Industrial Park in the municipality of Zinapécuaro. He said 9.3 billion pesos (US $498.5 million) will be invested in the project. The industrial park will primarily cater to the agroindustrial and automotive sectors.

Agriculture Minister Columba López reported that more than 177,000 residents of Michoacán are working in the government’s reforestation/employment program called Sembrando Vida (Sowing Life). She said the government is investing almost 2.2 billion pesos (US $117.9 million) in the program in Michoacán this year.

María Luisa Albores, director of the Mexican Food Security agency (Segalmex), reported that the government has purchased more than 63,000 tonnes of corn directly from some 2,400 small-scale farmers in Michoacán.

Environment Minister Alicia Bárcena reported that the government is investing 168.2 million pesos (US $9 million) in “sustainable forestry” projects in Michoacán.

Energy Minister Luz Elena González reported that more than 1,200 electricity projects have been completed in Michoacán, increasing electricity coverage to 99.99% of homes in the state. She said that 508 million pesos (US $27.2 million) were invested in the projects.

Tourism Minister Josefina Rodríguez reported that more than 2.46 million tourists visited Michoacán between January and August. She said tourist numbers increased 10.1% compared to the same period of last year. She said that tourism-related spending injected more than US $186 million into the Michoacán economy between January and August.

Infrastructure, Communications and Transport Minister Jesús Esteva reported that the government is upgrading 411 kilometers of highway in Michoacán. He said that the government and the private sector are investing more than 41 billion pesos (US $2.2 billion) in six highway projects in the state.

Welfare Minister Leticia Ramírez reported that the government is spending more than 30.4 billion pesos (US $1.6 billion) on welfare and social programs in Michoacán in 2026. She said that more than 1 million Michoacán residents benefit from the programs, which include pension schemes, educational scholarships and the distribution of fertilizer to farmers.

Education Minister Mario Delgado reported that over 795,000 students in Michoacán receive government scholarships. He said that primary school, middle school, high school and university students all receive monetary assistance. He said that the scholarships are funded with an investment of 5.7 billion pesos (around US $306 million).

IMSS Bienestar director Alejandro Svarch reported that a new hospital focused on the treatment of addictions had opened in Apatzingán. He also reported that a mental health center had opened in Huetamo. The combined investment in the two projects was 76.1 million pesos (US $3.6 million).

118 billion pesos in investment planned for Plan Michoacán by 2030

Presenting Plan Michoacán on Nov. 9, 2025, Sheinbaum described it as a “comprehensive strategy” and told reporters that it was based on 12 central tenets and included “more than 100 actions.”

Her presentation on Wednesday showed that there are, in fact, more than 2,500 Plan Michoacán “actions,” 1,680 of which have been “completed.” Sheinbaum said that represented progress of 67%.

She also said that 118 billion pesos (US $6.3 billion) is slated to be invested in Plan Michoacán between 2025 and 2030, the final year of her six-year term. That amount is more than double the 57-billion-peso investment that was originally announced.

Sheinbaum said that 72.43 billion pesos has already been spent on the plan. That amount represents 61% of the projected total.

Sheinbaum said that Plan Michoacán involves “very intense work” that is coordinated by the Interior Ministry. She also said that all of the federal government ministries have a “permanent presence” in Michoacán, one of 23 Mexican states governed by the Morena party.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: MND Local Puerto Vallarta: Tourists, traffic and turtles, oh my!
World.content:
Let me be the first to officially welcome you to tourist season in Puerto Vallarta! It’s the time of year when local entertainment ramps up, traffic jams up, and the checkout lines at Costco pile up.

But we may get a little help with traffic this season with the opening of the new Amado Nervo Bridge. It’s not just car traffic, but sea turtle traffic, too. Puerto Vallarta is in the thick of hatching season, when the newborn tortuguitas stumble their way from their nests to the sea by the hundreds, and you can help them on their journey.

And everyone is hoping for a more tranquil winter than last, when, on Feb. 22, members of the Jalisco New Generation cartel blocked traffic and burned cars and OXXO stores in the downtown area. The aftereffects of which have changed perceptions of safety here and abroad.

Read on to learn about how the city is working to restore tourist confidence and attract new visitors, the opening of a new commuter bridge, and sea turtle season.

Vallarta works to restore tourist confidence

Puerto Vallarta is working to revive tourism and attract new visitors amidst a backdrop of increased public perception of insecurity. According to the National Urban Public Safety survey, Vallartenses’ perception of insecurity has more than doubled since last year, rising from 24.7% in September 2025 to 53.6% in September 2026. While significantly up since this time last year, locals’ perception of insecurity has actually decreased since June, when it peaked at 65.4%.

The survey measures public perception of insecurity and doesn’t reflect actual crime rates. Puerto Vallarta remains one of the safer places to travel compared to other tourist destinations, and experiences less theft and violent crime than most U.S. cities of the same size. Also, the U.S. State Department, known for being expeditious about issuing travel warnings, has no current restrictions on travel to Vallarta.

But perception is everything, so the Vallarta tourism industry is working hard to win back traveler confidence and attract new visitors. This fall, representatives from the Puerto Vallarta Tourism Trust toured western states, hosting seminars for high-performing travel advisors in Arizona, Colorado and Utah, and welcomed tourism representatives from the U.S., Canada and other parts of Mexico to Vallarta. They even traveled to Poland, which will have direct weekly flights to Vallarta starting in December.

Despite February’s unrest, Puerto Vallarta remains one of the top destinations for vacationers in the world and is among the Top 10 global destinations for the Thanksgiving holiday, according to a recent survey by Allianz Partners. And if the traffic and Costco lines are any indication, we’ll have a healthy tourist season this year.

Amado Nervo Bridge opening

Here’s hoping a new commuter bridge between Banderas Bay and Puerto Vallarta will ease traffic on the busy Highway 200. The new Amado Nervo Bridge officially opened to cars on Oct. 28th. The bridge is located east of the main tourist corridor, connecting the towns of San Vicente and Ixtapa and surrounding communities, all of which previously had to use the 200 to get from one municipality to the next.

Local transportation officials estimate the bridge will cut as much as 40 minutes from the commute and ease congestion on Highway 200, especially between Mezcales and the Puerto Vallarta airport. The bridge is two kilometers long with three lanes in each direction and a bike lane. It’s a bit out of the way of the normal tourist route, but will hopefully direct more local traffic eastward and make traveling along the 200 smoother.

Turtles take to the sea

Hundreds of thousands of baby sea turtles are making their journey to the sea along Puerto Vallarta’s beaches. November is one of the best months to see them during the height of hatching season.

In Vallarta, a collaborative network of local community groups, grassroots non-profits, university researchers, government agencies, and beachfront resorts runs sea turtle camps along the coast. These camps protect eggs and ensure as many hatchlings as possible reach the sea. When mother turtles come ashore at night to dig nests and lay their eggs, the next morning conservationists remove them and place the eggs into manmade nests at the camps. This helps protect the eggs from predators and poachers. Not all nests are moved; camps only have capacity to protect so many. But still, they manage to save and release more than 150,000 baby turtles each year.

Turtle camps can be found at various spots along the coast of Banderas Bay, including the south end of Varadero beach in front of the Vidanta resort, Playa Holi in front of La Isla Mall, and Boca de Tomates turtle camp north of Bocanegra in the Marina. (Boca de Tomates took a beating with recent storms and could use support to rebuild.)

Camps often invite the public to witness and help with baby turtle releases. There are few things more precious and inspiring in nature than watching a baby sea turtle stumble its way into the surf. Crowds cheer and gasp as the little guys earnestly follow their instincts into the water, only to be washed back onto the sand time and time again until they finally make it out. I highly recommend you try to see a release when you visit.

Debbie Slobe is a writer and communications strategist based in Puerto Vallarta, Jalisco. She blogs at Mexpatmama.com and is a senior program director at Resource Media. Find her on Instagram and Facebook.

World.title: 38th Morelia Music Festival kicks off next week, highlighting artists from Asia
World.content:
The historic city of Morelia, Michoacán, is gearing up to host the 38th edition of the “Miguel Bernal Jiménez” Music Festival, which will take place from Nov. 13 to 22.

Featuring Asia as a guest region, the festival will feature representatives from China, Japan, India, Thailand, South Korea and Indonesia, in addition to the participation of artists and musical groups from 13 countries.

“It’s a must-see show,” head of the event Verónica Bernal told news outlet Crónica in an interview.

The festival will take place in different locations across the city, including cultural and religious landmarks like the Morelia Cultural Center, the Clavijero Cultural Center, the Roses Conservatory, the Shrine of Our Lady of Guadalupe and more.

The opening concert will feature the National Symphony Orchestra, conducted by Ludwig Carrasco, with violinist Yesong Sophie Lee as soloist. The performance will take place on Nov. 13 at 8 p.m. at the Teatro Morelos, one of the event’s primary venues.

The inaugural program includes music by Tan Dun, winner of an Academy Award and a Grammy for the soundtrack to the 2000 film “Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon”, in addition to the performance of El Chueco, a famous 20th-century ballet composed by the Mexican composer Miguel Bernal Jiménez, whose legacy gives this festival its name.

#musitecamx #ballet #guillermokeysarenas #miguelbernaljimenez #compositormexicano ♬ original sound – Fonoteca Nacional de México @fonotecanacional 𝙀𝙡 𝙘𝙝𝙪𝙚𝙘𝙤 es un ballet que utiliza elementos populares y religiosos para contar la historia de un niño paralítico que le teme al mundo exterior y que, tras soñar que supera sus miedos, despierta para disfrutar las procesiones que desfilan frente a la puerta de su casa. El argumento es del bailarín y coreógrafo Guillermo Keys-Arenas, que encargó la música al compositor Miguel Bernal Jiménez, y la obra se estrenó en el Teatro de Bellas Artes en 1951. Sin embargo, con el tiempo la música se independizó de la puesta en escena y es considerada por algunos la mejor partitura del compositor. Bernal Jiménez falleció el 26 de julio de 1956 pero su legado sigue vivo a través de su música, que la Fonoteca Nacional difunde a través de Musiteca.mx. Encuentra la grabación competa en el link denuestra biografía. Fotografía: Caracterización de el Chueco. Guillermo Keys-Arenas, Heterofonía, núm. 114-115, enero-diciembre de 1996, p. 87. México, INBA, Cenidim #FonotecaNacional

Miguel Bernal Jiménez (1910–1956) was an organist, researcher and teacher, originally from Morelia. He was a prominent figure in 20th-century Mexican sacred music and a pioneer in the research of music from the era of New Spain.

According to Festival Director Bernal, other events will also feature works by the composer.

Among the most anticipated performances is Carnaval Barroco by the French ensemble Le Poème Harmonique, which combines music, theater, dance and acrobatics. The show will be part of the celebrations marking 200 years of diplomatic relations between Mexico and France.

Additionally, violinist Lidia Baich and pianist Donka Angatscheva will commemorate the 125th anniversary of the resumption of diplomatic relations between Mexico and Austria.

Bernal said that nearly half of the activities will be free of charge, with a program that includes masterclasses, children’s performances and the traditional floral carpets of Patamban. Tickets can be purchased at a discount (through Nov. 6) here.

With reports from Excélsior and Mi Morelia

World.title: Will Pope Leo XIV visit Mexico in 2027?
World.content:
A potential visit by Pope Leo XIV to Mexico in 2027 caused confusion after statements by Mexican and Vatican officials were interpreted by Mexican media as confirmation of the trip. However, no official visit to the country has been announced.

The misunderstanding arose during a recent press conference by María Montserrat Alvarado, new Prefect of the Vatican Dicastery for Communication, in which she said that the pontiff would visit Our Lady of Guadalupe — a reference that was interpreted as an allusion to the Basilica of Guadalupe in Mexico City.

Later on Tuesday, when asked about the matter during a press conference, Mexico City Mayor Clara Brugada said that she had no confirmation of the visit. Still, she added that if it were to take place, it would be in 2027 on the occasion of the Guadalupan Jubilee Year.

“That is surely one of the reasons [of the Pope’s visit], and it will happen next year. We need to look at the dates, and we will provide an update right away,” she said.

The Guadalupan Jubilee Year began on Oct. 12 and is linked to the 50th anniversary of the consecration of the new Basilica of Guadalupe in Mexico City.

Noticing the confusion, Televisa’s Vatican correspondent Valentina Alazraki clarified Wednesday morning that the Vatican’s spokesperson was referring to the Parish of Our Lady of Guadalupe in Casavalle, Uruguay.

#Actualización | La jefa del Gobierno capitalino, Clara Brugada, calificó como una buena noticia la visita que realizaría el papa León XIV a México. Sin embargo, momentos después se aclaró que en realidad se trata de la parroquia de la Virgen de Guadalupe en Uruguay. 👇 https://t.co/4cDfTySBYR — MVS Noticias (@MVSNoticias) November 3, 2026

“According to Vatican spokesperson Matteo Bruni, Montse Alvarado was not referring to the Basilica of the Virgin of Guadalupe in Mexico City, but rather to the parish in Casavalle, Uruguay. Therefore, there was no confirmation of a papal visit to Mexico,” Alazraki wrote on her X account.

In a later post, Alazraki said that according to several Vatican sources, “it is very clear that Pope Leo does indeed want to go to Mexico” and visit the Basilica of Guadalupe in Mexico City.

However, “there is nothing concrete, neither regarding the date nor the program. There is only the intention,” she stated.

Confusion over the Pope’s visit to Mexico comes days before his upcoming Apostolic Journey to Latin America, which will include visits to Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru between Nov. 6 and 17.

With reports from El Sol de México

World.content:

MEXICO · POLITICS

Key Facts The country Mexico’s lower house of Congress, the Chamber of Deputies, writes the national budget each autumn.

What happened About 250 retired Chamber workers blocked every entrance on Wednesday 4 November 2026.

The offer A one-time payment of 56,000 pesos (about US$3,000) ended the blockade.

What is next Deputies meet again on Monday 9 November, and talks with the retirees resume on Thursday 12 November.

Power Index Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 in Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 71.4 points (October 2026 edition).

Mexico’s lower house of Congress lost a working day on Wednesday 4 November 2026 because its own retired staff blocked the gates. About 250 retired workers and union members of the Chamber of Deputies closed every pedestrian and vehicle entrance to the Legislative Palace of San Lázaro, the Chamber’s seat in Mexico City.

The Chamber’s president, Raúl Bolaños-Cacho Cué, cancelled the full session planned for 11 a.m. and opened talks instead. The blockade ended at about 1 p.m. after more than eight hours, and deputies return on Monday 9 November.

For US readers, the stoppage matters because the same Chamber must approve Mexico’s 2027 federal budget, which shapes the peso and the bonds that US funds hold. Mexico is also one of the biggest trading partners of the United States, so its budget calendar reaches well beyond Mexico City.

Alignment group: Hedging. Watch21 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.7 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

What Happened

The protesters are retired workers and union members of the Chamber itself, not pensioners from the wider public. They arrived early on Wednesday and closed all access, so deputies and staff could not reach the building.

Bolaños-Cacho said it was his duty to guarantee safety and to find a solution through dialogue. He announced a talks table for 11:45 a.m., and the retirees were received by him and Fernando Castro Trenti, who heads the Chamber’s administration committee.

Why the Retirees Protested

The retirees want the Chamber to restore benefits that stopped in April 2026. They point to a clause of the benefits agreement between the Chamber and its union, which gives them support on top of the state pension they receive from ISSSTE, the pension fund for government workers.

Their list of demands also includes food parcels, annual eyeglass support and annual transport assistance. They say the 2027 budget must set aside enough money to keep these benefits going.

What the Chamber Offered

The Chamber offered a one-time payment of 56,000 pesos (about US$3,000 at 18.60 pesos per US dollar), equal to four months of support. Of the roughly 250 protesters, 248 accepted it, and they lifted the blockade at about 1 p.m. after meeting the Chamber’s leaders for more than an hour.

Both sides agreed to meet again on Thursday 12 November. The announcements did not say whether the monthly benefits will return in 2027.

What Comes Next

The full Chamber meets again on Monday 9 November at 3 p.m. Other business set for this week, such as the call to choose the next president of the National Electoral Institute (INE), the body that runs Mexico’s elections, now waits for that session. The Chamber must approve the federal budget for 2027 by 15 November under Article 74 of the Mexican Constitution.

It already passed the 2027 revenue law in October, and the Senate approved it on 27 October.

What It Means for You

If you hold Mexican peso bonds or stocks through US funds, one cancelled session changes little, but the budget vote is the real test. The peso traded near 18.60 per US dollar on Wednesday, so 1,000 pesos were worth about US$54.

Travellers to Mexico City should expect occasional protests near government buildings while labour disputes with public workers continue. Check local advisories before visiting the area around San Lázaro.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether the monthly benefits will return in 2027, since the payment is a one-time offer. The full terms of the payment were not confirmed.

It is also unclear whether the retirees will block the building again if the 12 November talks fail. Nor is it known whether the lost day will delay the 2027 budget vote.

How Much Did the Chamber Offer the Retirees?

When Does the Chamber Meet Again?

The full Chamber resumes on Monday 9 November at 3 p.m. Talks with the retirees continue on Thursday 12 November.

Does the Blockade Affect Mexico’s 2027 Budget?

The Chamber must approve the budget by 15 November under Article 74 of the Constitution. It is not known whether the lost day will delay the vote.

World.title: Suriname Stays on EU Air Safety Blacklist
World.content:
File photo, December 2015. The Paramaribo waterfront seen across the Suriname River. (Photo: Dan Sloan, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

SURINAME · AVIATION

Key Facts The country Suriname is a small nation on South America’s north coast, next to French Guiana.

What happened On 3 November 2026, President Jennifer Simons met aviation officials about the European Union (EU) ban.

The ban Airlines certified in Suriname have been barred from flying to the EU since 3 June 2025.

The outlook Suriname’s aviation chief says there is no quick fix for the problems.

Power Index

Suriname will stay on the European Union’s air safety blacklist for now, and its aviation chief says there is no quick fix. President Jennifer Simons met aviation officials of a United Nations agency on Tuesday 3 November 2026 to speed up the recovery.

For US readers, the ban matters because it restricts Surinamese-certified airlines on routes to Europe and to nearby French Guiana. Our guide to Suriname’s economic key players explains why the country is drawing so much foreign interest.

What Happened

Simons met officials of the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), the United Nations agency that sets global flight-safety rules, at the Presidential Cabinet. Transport Minister Raymond Landveld, presidential aviation adviser Faizel Baarn and Anjulio Wolf, director of the Civil Aviation Safety Authority Suriname (CASAS), the national regulator, also took part.

The talks covered what support CASAS needs from the government and further work with ICAO and SRVSOP, a regional aviation-safety body. The government says a recovery plan and preventive measures have been drawn up and submitted, and that a preliminary report was assessed positively.

Why the Ban Exists

The European Commission, the EU’s executive arm, put all air carriers certified in Suriname on its Air Safety List on Tuesday 3 June 2025. It named a shortage of qualified personnel, weak oversight of flight operations and aircraft airworthiness, and non-compliance with international safety standards.

The decision rested on a unanimous opinion of EU member-state aviation experts, who met in Brussels from 13 to 15 May 2025. The Commission said it stands ready to support Suriname’s efforts to meet the standards.

No Quick Fix

Wolf said there is “no quick fix” for the problem, because structural weaknesses in Suriname’s oversight system built up over very long periods. He said a thorough approach and careful planning are needed to repair them for good.

The government says its approved recovery plan can now move into a faster implementation phase. No date for removal from the list has been announced, and the decision rests with the European Commission.

What It Means for You

If you plan to visit Suriname or work there, expect limits on direct connections that depend on Surinamese-certified airlines flying to the Netherlands or French Guiana. Check with your airline which carrier and aircraft will operate your ticket before you book.

The ban does not stop US airlines or flights from the United States, because it covers only carriers certified in Suriname. For investors tied to Suriname’s oil boom, such as the GranMorgu offshore oil project, covered in our earlier report, slow progress on aviation safety is a reminder that the country’s institutions are still catching up with its ambitions.

What Is Not Known

It is not known when the Commission will review Suriname’s case, or what proof it will want before lifting the ban. Details of the recovery plan and the preliminary report are not public in the official statements.

It is also unclear how many Surinamese flights have been cut or moved to leased aircraft from approved carriers. No cost figure for the repairs has been given.

More: Suriname news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why Is Suriname on the EU Air Safety List?

The European Commission listed all Suriname-certified airlines on 3 June 2025. It cited too few qualified staff, weak oversight and non-compliance with international safety standards.

Can I Still Fly From the US to Suriname?

The ban covers only airlines certified in Suriname, and only for EU operations. Flights by carriers from other countries are not affected by it.

When Will Suriname Leave the List?

No date has been announced. Suriname’s aviation chief says there is no quick fix, and the European Commission makes the final decision.

What Did President Simons Do on 3 November?

She met ICAO, the UN aviation agency, and Surinamese aviation officials. The goal was to speed up the recovery plan.

World.content:

KENYA · TELECOMS · REGULATION

Key Facts The country Kenya, in East Africa, wants to change how its telecom firms pay for radio airwaves.

What happened Kenya’s communications ministry published a revised draft law in November 2026 ending instalments.

The change Licence fees would be paid in full up front, ending instalments above 1 billion shillings (US$7.7 million).

The dates Comments close Tuesday 17 November 2026; an online forum meets Wednesday 25 November.

What to watch It is only a draft, so operators and the public can still push for changes.

Kenya wants mobile phone companies to pay for their radio airwaves all at once instead of over many years. The Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy put the change into a draft law that it put out for public comment in early November 2026.

Free daily brief — no card needed Get every Africa story in one morning email We build you a personalized brief around the topics you follow — free for 7 days. Love it? Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time.

For US readers, the draft matters because Safaricom, Kenya’s largest mobile operator by subscribers, and its rivals depend on airwaves for 4G and 5G. Paying up front would raise the cash a company needs before it can launch new services.

What the Draft Says

The draft is the Kenya Information and Communications (Amendment) Bill, 2026, and it runs to about 90 pages. Clause 11 changes section 25A of the current law, which covers how licence fees are paid.

Today, section 25A lets the Communications Authority of Kenya, the telecom regulator, accept airwave (spectrum) fees in equal instalments over up to 10 years. That option applies when the fee is above 1 billion shillings (about US$7.7 million), and the applicant must be Kenyan or at least 51% Kenyan-owned.

The draft deletes subsections (3), (4) and (5) of section 25A, which hold those instalment rules. The bill’s own explanation says the effect is that every applicant must pay the prescribed licence fees in full before the grant of a licence.

Unsubscribe with one click at any time; see our privacy policy. Your checklist is ready. Download the PDF checklist

Why Airwaves Cost So Much

Spectrum is the range of radio frequencies that carries phone calls, mobile data and 5G signals. A government licenses it to operators, and the fees can reach billions of shillings for a large block.

Under the old rule, a buyer that also promised to build at least 500 base stations (masts that carry mobile signals) in three years could spread the bill over a decade. If that buyer lost its local ownership, the full balance fell due at once.

What Else Is in the Bill

The spectrum clause is one of many changes, so the fee rule may not be the main fight. The draft would also raise several fines, including the maximum for running a telecom network without a licence from 1 million to 5 million shillings (about US$7,700 to US$38,500).

It would add type approval for electronic equipment, meant to curb substandard or counterfeit devices. It would also repeal section 29, a rule on improper use of a telecom system that the High Court declared unconstitutional in 2016.

The Calendar for Comments

The ministry says a multi-stakeholder committee prepared the draft after public consultations, and that this is a revised version. Written comments are due by Tuesday 17 November 2026, using a template in the public notice.

A virtual validation forum follows on Wednesday 25 November 2026, from 9:00 a.m. to noon East Africa Time. As a bill, it still needs to pass Parliament.

What It Means for You

If you own shares in Safaricom through its major shareholder, South Africa’s Vodacom, or in the listed telecom group Airtel Africa, a rule that raises up-front costs could squeeze cash for network spending. The effect depends on how much spectrum each firm buys and when.

Travellers and expats in Kenya will not see a change soon, because the draft is only a proposal. Over time, higher entry costs could slow new 5G coverage, or push firms to build in big cities first.

The shilling traded near 129.8 per US dollar on 4 November 2026, so 1,000 shillings are worth about US$7.70. That rate is the basis for the dollar figures in this article.

What Is Not Known

The ministry has not said why it wants to end instalments, and the draft does not name any operator. It is also unknown whether Parliament will keep the clause as written.

Public information does not show which operators have used the instalment option. The draft has no transitional clause for licences already granted on instalments.

More: Kenya news in English, every day from The Rio Times. Related: how Kenya charges telecoms for spectrum, the court case over spectrum fees and Airtel Kenya’s 5G airwaves deal.

Frequently Asked Questions

What Does Kenya’s Draft Law Change for Airwave Fees?

It would delete the rule that lets Kenya’s regulator accept payment in instalments over up to 10 years. Every applicant would pay the full licence fee before the licence is granted.

Has the Draft Become Law Yet?

No, the ministry has only published a draft bill for comment, and Parliament has not passed it. Comments are due by Tuesday 17 November 2026.

Who Could Be Affected by Upfront Payment?

Any operator seeking airwaves with a fee above 1 billion shillings (about US$7.7 million), the threshold in today’s law. Smaller firms with less cash on hand could feel it most.

How Can the Public Comment on the Draft?

Written comments go to the email address in the ministry’s public notice by Tuesday 17 November 2026. A virtual forum follows on Wednesday 25 November from 9:00 a.m. to noon East Africa Time.

Sources: Communications Authority of Kenya, draft Kenya Information and Communications (Amendment) Bill, 2026, November 2026; Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy, public notice on validation of the draft bill, November 2026; Kenya Information and Communications Act, section 25A; RT, USD/KES exchange rate, 4 November 2026.

DOMINICAN REPUBLIC · SECURITY

Key Facts The country The Dominican Republic shares Hispaniola with Haiti, where armed gangs rule.

What happened Two Dominican ministers toured four border crossings on Wednesday 4 November 2026.

The support Santo Domingo gives El Salvador’s troops in Haiti logistics, intelligence, equipment and medical care.

The border The defence minister said the frontier is calm, with about 11,000 Dominican troops posted along it.

The missing Four Salvadoran soldiers have been missing near Port-au-Prince since Sunday 18 October 2026.

The Dominican Republic is quietly backing El Salvador’s military push against armed gangs in neighbouring Haiti, two of its ministers said on Wednesday 4 November 2026. The help covers logistics, intelligence, equipment and medical care for Salvadoran troops.

For US readers, the story matters because Haiti’s collapse is a main driver of Caribbean migration and a security worry for a Dominican Republic that many Americans visit. Our guide to security in the Dominican Republic explains the wider picture.

What Happened

José Ignacio Paliza, the Minister of the Presidency in President Luis Abinader’s government, and Lieutenant General Carlos Antonio Fernández Onofre, the Minister of Defence, visited the crossings at Dajabón, Elías Piña, Jimaní and Pedernales. They were joined by the commanders of the air force, army and navy and by Cesfront, the Dominican land border-security corps.

Paliza said Santo Domingo provides El Salvador with logistical support, information, intelligence, military equipment and, when needed, medical assistance. He added that the government’s action must be prudent and timely, and must follow international procedures.

Why El Salvador Is in Haiti

President Nayib Bukele of El Salvador has sent more than 2,000 soldiers to Haiti. They serve in the Gang Suppression Force, a United Nations-authorised international force that replaced a Kenya-led mission to fight Haiti’s armed gangs.

Four Salvadoran soldiers disappeared after an ambush outside Port-au-Prince, the Haitian capital, on Sunday 18 October 2026. They are still missing more than two weeks later, and finding them is the main stated reason for the larger deployment.

A Calm Border, Officials Say

Fernández Onofre said the frontier is “totally calm” and that the gangs sit where they were a year ago, around Mirebalais in central Haiti and Croix-des-Bouquets on the outskirts of Port-au-Prince. He said about 11,000 Dominican soldiers are posted along the border, reinforced by two extra battalions in late October.

Trade and authorised crossings continue under permanent security watch. No closure was mentioned in the ministers’ statements.

What It Means for You

If you travel to Santo Domingo, Punta Cana or Puerto Plata, nothing in Wednesday’s statements changes entry rules or flight plans. The tension is concentrated along the land border, which most visitors never cross.

If you follow Haiti as an investor, aid donor or voter, the Dominican role shows that the effort against the gangs now runs through several neighbours. A tougher campaign can push more Haitians toward the Dominican border and, over time, toward the United States.

What Is Not Known

It is not known how many Salvadoran troops or how much equipment move through Dominican territory, or what the support costs. The ministers gave no figures and did not say whether Dominican personnel will operate outside the country.

It is also unknown whether the four missing Salvadoran soldiers are alive. Bukele has disputed reports that remains found near Port-au-Prince were theirs.

Frequently Asked Questions

What Is the Dominican Republic Doing in Haiti?

It is not sending troops into Haiti. Ministers say it gives El Salvador’s forces logistics, information, technical intelligence, military equipment and medical help.

Has the Dominican Republic Closed Its Border With Haiti?

No closure was announced on Wednesday 4 November 2026. Trade and authorised travel continue under permanent security watch.

Why Are Salvadoran Soldiers in Haiti?

More than 2,000 Salvadoran troops are in Haiti to fight armed gangs. They are also searching for four soldiers missing since Sunday 18 October 2026.

Does This Affect Travel to the Dominican Republic?

The ministers described the border as calm, and no change to travel rules was announced. Check your government’s travel advisory before any trip near the frontier.

COLOMBIA · ENERGY

Key Facts The country Colombia, a South American oil exporter, wants to restart oil and gas projects that have stalled.

What happened On Wednesday 4 November 2026 the National Hydrocarbons Agency (ANH) unveiled a plan to restart stalled drilling contracts.

The price tag The agency says reviving the industry needs close to US$10 billion in new investment.

The timing It expects the first quarter of 2027 to be the turning point for that spending.

Colombia’s state oil agency told investors on Wednesday 4 November 2026 how it plans to get stalled oil and gas projects moving again. Ernesto Forero, president of the National Hydrocarbons Agency (ANH), which grants and oversees drilling contracts, said reviving the industry would need close to US$10 billion.

For US readers, the plan shows whether Colombia can attract foreign oil investors and secure more gas at home. Our report on the Rescue Law, the government’s fiscal rescue bill, explains the tax incentives that the oil plan leans on.

What Happened

Forero spoke at the IX Oil, Gas and Energy Summit in Cartagena, which runs from 4 to 6 November. He appeared with Frank Pearl, president of the Colombian Petroleum Association (ACP), the industry’s main trade group.

He described three fronts. The first is removing the causes that keep several contracts suspended, the second is adding incentives for large investments through the Rescue Law, and the third is sending clear institutional signals so private companies can find financing.

Forero invited companies to submit projects that raise output from existing fields. He said current oil prices make new investment easier to justify.

The Steps Already Taken

In August 2026 the ANH created a specialised team, the Strategic Group for Gas Projects Acceleration, to clear bottlenecks that keep new gas from reaching the market. It brings together legal, technical, environmental, social and contract experts who work directly with operators.

The agency has also reserved almost 20 million hectares across 12 basins for studies, a first step before new exploration areas can be offered. It says it now uses technical roundtables and an inter-sector hydrocarbons committee to deal with security, transport and community issues.

What the Industry Wants

Industry groups led by the ACP want the Rescue Law to remove a surtax on oil income and to offer long-term tax stability for large projects. They say the effective tax rate on oil extraction is about 50%, made up of a 35% base rate and a surtax of up to 15%.

The groups also warn that Colombia now imports about one third of the gas sold. The government has to weigh those demands against its own plan to cut spending and calm worries about public debt.

What It Means for You

If you own shares or bonds of Colombian energy companies, the key signal to watch is whether Congress keeps the oil incentives when it votes on the Rescue Law before the session ends on 16 December. A clear tax rule would make it easier for companies to commit money in early 2027.

For consumers, more gas output would reduce reliance on imports, which Colombia has used to cover shortfalls. Travellers will not see any change from this announcement.

What Is Not Known

It is not known which suspended contracts will restart first, or how many companies will bring new projects. The agency has not published a list of projects or a date for each step.

Whether Congress will accept the tax incentives is also open, and the US$10 billion figure is the agency’s estimate rather than a signed commitment. Oil prices, which Forero called favourable, can also change quickly.

Frequently Asked Questions

What Did Colombia’s Oil Agency Announce on 4 November 2026?

The National Hydrocarbons Agency presented a three-part plan: unblock suspended contracts, add incentives through the Rescue Law and signal support for private financing. It says the industry needs close to US$10 billion.

When Does the Agency Expect New Oil Investment?

It expects the first quarter of 2027 to be the turning point for new investment. No date has been set for individual projects.

What Is the Rescue Law and Why Does It Matter for Oil?

It is the government’s fiscal rescue bill, filed on 29 October 2026. The agency says it contains incentives for large investments, including in energy.

Does Colombia Still Import Gas?

Industry groups say imported gas now covers about one third of domestic demand. The agency’s team for gas projects aims to bring new local gas to market faster.

World.title: South Africa’s 10-Party Coalition Explained
World.content:
SOUTH AFRICA · ANALYSIS

Key Facts What is happening South Africans voted on Wednesday, 4 November 2026, for councils in all 257 municipalities. Results are due within seven days.

Why it matters The African National Congress (ANC) lost its majority in 2024 and now governs with the Democratic Alliance (DA).

The numbers In 2024 the ANC won 159 of 400 seats and the DA 87, so the ANC needed partners.

What it means for you US holders of rand (South African currency) assets should watch whether the ANC-DA pact holds before 19 November.

South Africa’s national government is a ten-party coalition, and its stability rests on the partnership between the ANC and the DA. Today’s local elections, the first nationwide vote since the coalition formed in June 2024, show how far that partnership reaches into city halls.

Free daily brief — no card needed Get every Africa story in one morning email We build you a personalized brief around the topics you follow — free for 7 days. Love it? Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time.

South Africa elects its municipal councils today, Wednesday 4 November 2026, in 257 municipalities. This analysis explains how coalitions work from the national Government of National Unity (GNU) down to city halls, and why they so often break, building on the Rio Times Africa Intelligence Brief.

From Majority Rule to the Government of National Unity

From 1994 until 2024 the African National Congress (ANC), the party of Nelson Mandela, held a majority in the National Assembly, the 400-seat lower house of Parliament. On 29 May 2024 it won 159 seats with 40.18% of the vote.

A governing party needs 201 seats, so the ANC was 42 short. On 14 June 2024 the ANC and the Democratic Alliance (DA), until then the main opposition party, signed a statement of intent to form a Government of National Unity (GNU).

Cyril Ramaphosa, the ANC leader, was re-elected president by the National Assembly on 14 June 2024. By late June the GNU had ten parties, among them the Inkatha Freedom Party (IFP), the Patriotic Alliance (PA) and six smaller parties.

Those six are GOOD, Rise Mzansi, Al Jama-ah, the Pan Africanist Congress, the United Democratic Movement and the Freedom Front Plus. The 2024 result for the six largest parties was as follows, with seats counted out of 400.

ANC: 159 seats, 40.18% of the vote

DA: 87 seats, 21.8%

MK Party (uMkhonto weSizwe, founded by former president Jacob Zuma): 58 seats

Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF), a left-wing party: 39 seats, 9.52%

IFP: 17 seats, 3.85%

PA: 9 seats

The MK Party and the EFF are outside the GNU and sit in opposition. The MK Party took 45.35% of the vote in KwaZulu-Natal in the 2024 provincial election and won 37 of 80 seats.

That made it the largest party in the province that is home to Durban. The partnership has already been adjusted once.

On 30 June 2026 Ramaphosa changed the national executive after consulting the DA’s leadership. Willem Aucamp of the DA became Agriculture Minister, and David Maynier of the DA became Minister of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment.

File photo. Johannesburg, one of the eight big cities (metros) where mayors are chosen after the count. photo. Central Johannesburg seen from a high tower, with the city centre streets below.

The Parties and What Each Wants

The GNU is an ANC-led partnership, and the DA is its largest partner. Each party below is described by its role, using only what is confirmed for 2026.

ANC: the largest party, with 159 seats and the senior partner in the GNU. Ramaphosa is president and Paul Mashatile is deputy president.

the largest party, with 159 seats and the senior partner in the GNU. Ramaphosa is president and Paul Mashatile is deputy president. DA: the second-largest party, with 87 seats, a GNU member and the governing party in Cape Town. Geordin Hill-Lewis is federal leader, and Leon Schreiber is the DA minister of Home Affairs.

the second-largest party, with 87 seats, a GNU member and the governing party in Cape Town. Geordin Hill-Lewis is federal leader, and Leon Schreiber is the DA minister of Home Affairs. MK Party: an opposition party with 58 seats, led by Jacob Zuma.

an opposition party with 58 seats, led by Jacob Zuma. EFF: an opposition party with 39 seats, led by Julius Malema, its founder.

an opposition party with 39 seats, led by Julius Malema, its founder. IFP: an early GNU partner with 17 seats, led by Velenkosini Hlabisa, who is also the minister of Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs (COGTA), the ministry that oversees local government.

an early GNU partner with 17 seats, led by Velenkosini Hlabisa, who is also the minister of Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs (COGTA), the ministry that oversees local government. PA: an early GNU partner with 9 seats.

an early GNU partner with 9 seats. Freedom Front Plus: a GNU member since June 2024, with 6 seats.

a GNU member since June 2024, with 6 seats. ActionSA: a party with 6 seats outside the GNU, whose candidate Herman Mashaba, a former Johannesburg mayor, is a candidate for mayor of Johannesburg.

Hill-Lewis was elected DA federal leader at a congress in Midrand on 12 April 2026. He succeeded John Steenhuisen, who did not seek re-election and is now Deputy Minister of Trade, Industry and Competition.

Why Municipal Coalitions Break

Councils Have No Binding Rulebook

Councils elect their mayors and speakers at their first sittings, so a party without a majority must bargain for every post. South Africa has no binding coalition framework in law yet, which leaves those deals to the parties themselves.

In the 2021 local elections the ANC won 45.59% of the vote, the DA 21.62% and the EFF 10.32%. The ANC’s 40.18% in the 2024 national vote was lower than that 2021 council share, so it enters this contest with less room to spare.

The Reform Bill

The Local Government: Municipal Structures Amendment Bill (B23-2026) is before Parliament. According to Parliament, it proposes these changes:

mandatory written coalition agreements

longer timeframes for calling first council meetings, electing speakers and appointing mayoral committees

new rules on voting methods and on removing municipal office-bearers

a requirement that councillors who become office-bearers have relevant experience, skills or qualifications

Parliament’s committee on Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs is taking public comment until Friday, 27 November 2026.

What 4 November Could Change

The Size of the Vote

The contest covers 257 municipalities: 8 metros (the big cities), 44 districts and 205 local councils. There are 10,526 council seats.

More than 29 million voters are registered. The Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC), the independent election body, certified 136,790 candidates, against 95,427 in 2021.

Three Scenarios

These are scenarios, not forecasts, and no official results had been published when this was written. Mayors of the eight metros, including Johannesburg, where ActionSA’s Herman Mashaba is a candidate, will be chosen only after the count.

In the first scenario the ANC holds most metros and the DA keeps Cape Town, which would leave the GNU largely as it is. Both parties would then keep a reason to stay together in the national government.

In the second scenario the DA gains ground and the MK Party does well in Durban, which would force new alliances and test the ANC and DA relationship nationally. The MK Party’s 45.35% in KwaZulu-Natal in 2024 shows the size of its base there.

In the third scenario many councils are hung, meaning no party has a majority, and coalition talks drag on. Until the reform bill passes, the parties would negotiate under today’s rules.

What It Means for You

Markets look at coalition risk through three prices: the rand, South African government bonds and Johannesburg-listed shares. We found no verified post-vote price move at the time of writing.

The South African Reserve Bank, led by Governor Lesetja Kganyago, raised its repo rate (the main policy rate) by 25 basis points to 7.00% on 28 May 2026 and held it on 23 July. It added another 25 basis points to reach 7.25% on 23 September, and Kganyago said rates are expected to stay broadly stable for the rest of this year.

The Reserve Bank’s next rate decision is on 19 November 2026. Unemployment stood at 33.6% in the second quarter of 2026, with youth unemployment at 47.4%, according to Statistics South Africa, the national statistics agency.

A US reader with emerging-market bond funds, rand exposure or mining shares should treat council coalitions as one input beside rates and commodities.

What Is Not Known

No official results had been published when this analysis was written. Who will run the eight metros depends on coalition talks after the count.

No post-vote market moves were available either. The final form of the reform bill is also not known.

What to Watch

5 November 2026: the first market reaction in the rand and government bonds.

the first market reaction in the rand and government bonds. By 11 November 2026: the legal deadline for the Electoral Commission to declare results.

the legal deadline for the Electoral Commission to declare results. After the count: mayoral votes in the eight metros, including Johannesburg, Tshwane, eThekwini (Durban) and Nelson Mandela Bay.

mayoral votes in the eight metros, including Johannesburg, Tshwane, eThekwini (Durban) and Nelson Mandela Bay. 19 November 2026: the Reserve Bank’s rate decision.

the Reserve Bank’s rate decision. 27 November 2026: the deadline for public comment on bill B23-2026.

the deadline for public comment on bill B23-2026. 2029: the next national election, after the five-year parliamentary term.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is South Africa’s Government of National Unity?

It is a ten-party coalition formed in June 2024 after the African National Congress (ANC) lost its majority. The ANC won 159 of the 400 National Assembly seats in the 2024 election, 42 short of a majority.

Which parties are in the coalition?

The ANC, the Democratic Alliance (DA), the Inkatha Freedom Party (IFP) and the Patriotic Alliance (PA) are in it, joined by GOOD, Rise Mzansi, Al Jama-ah, the Pan Africanist Congress, the United Democratic Movement and the Freedom Front Plus. The MK Party and the Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF) are outside it.

Why do South African municipal coalitions collapse?

Councils elect mayors by vote, and South Africa has no binding coalition framework in law yet. A party without a majority must therefore bargain for every post, and those deals rest on trust alone.

What would the coalition bill change?

Bill B23-2026 proposes mandatory written coalition agreements and longer timeframes for constituting councils. Parliament’s committee takes public comment until 27 November 2026.

When will the local election results be known?

The Electoral Commission (IEC) must declare results within seven days, so by 11 November 2026. In 2021 it declared them on 4 November, three days after the 1 November vote.

What should US investors watch after the vote?

Watch the rand, South African government bonds and whether the DA and ANC stay together in the GNU. The Reserve Bank’s next rate decision is on 19 November 2026.

PUERTO RICO · IMMIGRATION

Key Facts The place San Juan is the capital of Puerto Rico, a US territory whose residents are US citizens.

What happened Mayor Miguel Romero Lugo met the island’s top federal investigator and demanded detailed arrest data.

The demand He wants arrest numbers, legal grounds, releases and advance notice to the city.

The stance City police will not assist immigration enforcement but will keep fighting crime with federal agents.

What is next The mayor wants a written federal reply to the letter he sent last week.

The mayor of San Juan, Miguel Romero Lugo, has asked federal immigration agents to explain who they arrested in his city’s neighbourhoods and why. He made the demand in a meeting with the local chief of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the criminal-investigation arm of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and published it in a written statement on Tuesday 3 November 2026.

Free daily brief — no card needed Get every Caribbean story in one morning email We build you a personalized brief around the topics you follow — free for 7 days. Love it? Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time.

For US readers, the story tests how far federal deportation drives can go in a place where every resident is a US citizen. Our earlier report on the first condemnations of the raids explains how the operations began.

What Happened

Federal agents carried out immigration operations in San Juan communities such as Barrio Obrero and Villa Palmeras, starting on Thursday 22 October 2026. The mayor cited complaints of intimidation, long guns, interventions in religious spaces and action against people who documented the arrests.

On Monday 26 October the mayor ordered the Municipal Police not to take part. A week later he met Rebecca González Ramos, who heads HSI in Puerto Rico, and repeated that federal authority "must be accompanied at all times by respect for human dignity and the constitutional rights of all people."

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Puerto Rico Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

What the Mayor Wants

Romero Lugo asked for a detailed list of the arrests: how many people were held, on what grounds, and how many were freed after their immigration status was checked. He also asked agents to separate people with criminal records or charges from those stopped only over their immigration status.

He said the data are needed "to know the scope of the operations and to assess their impact on our communities." He also wants the city told when operations happen, so the city’s Immigrant Assistance Office, a municipal unit that guides affected families, can help them.

The mayor said González Ramos told him the recent street operations were carried out by Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO), the ICE branch that arrests and deports people, based in Miami, Florida. He asked for a direct contact there and a written answer to the letter he sent federal authorities the week before.

According to the mayor, González Ramos said she would pass on the need for "communication mechanisms that help prevent conflicts" during such operations. She had said a week earlier that HSI does not lead such operations on the island.

A Line Between Cooperation and Enforcement

The mayor repeated that city police and city offices will not take part in or support immigration control. At the same time, the city says it will keep working with federal agencies on crime and other public-safety matters.

That split matters in a territory where local and federal officers work the same streets. It also shows how local and federal officials can disagree on immigration while still sharing crime work.

What It Means for You

If you travel to San Juan, nothing changes for US citizens: no passport is needed and you do not clear immigration. The dispute is about street operations in specific neighbourhoods, not about visitors.

For US investors and employers on the island, the story is a reminder that federal enforcement can reach communities where many immigrants live and work. The mayor’s data demand could shape how much the public learns about each operation.

What Is Not Known

It is not known how many people were detained in the latest operations, which is why the mayor asks for the figures. We found no public federal answer to his written request as of Wednesday 4 November 2026.

It is also unclear whether the operations will continue, whether the city will be warned in advance, and whether any official investigation of the complaints will open. The mayor has called for one, and we found no announcement of it.

More: Puerto Rico news in English, every day from The Rio Times. See also who holds power in Puerto Rico.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who Is Miguel Romero Lugo?

He is the mayor of San Juan, the capital of Puerto Rico. He ordered city police on Monday 26 October 2026 not to take part in immigration enforcement.

What Did the Mayor Ask Federal Agents For?

He asked for the number of people detained, the legal grounds for each operation and how many were released after status checks. He also asked for a contact point and advance notice to the city.

Are Puerto Ricans Affected by These Arrests?

Puerto Ricans are US citizens by birth, and US citizens cannot lawfully be deported. Critics worry that citizens can still be stopped during street operations, which is why the mayor wants records of each intervention.

Will San Juan Police Help Federal Agents?

Not with immigration control. The mayor says police will keep working with federal agencies on crime and other public-safety matters.

COLOMBIA · ECONOMY

Key Facts The country Colombia, a South American economy with a new conservative president, Abelardo de la Espriella.

What happened Commerce Minister Mauricio Gómez Amín said Colombia will sign a trade deal with Japan.

The date Signing is set for Sunday 20 December 2026, after nearly 15 years of stalled talks.

What comes next Under Colombian procedure, Congress and the Constitutional Court, which reviews treaties, must still weigh in.

Power Index Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 51.9 points (October 2026 edition).

Colombia will sign a long-awaited trade pact with Japan on Sunday 20 December 2026, Commerce Minister Mauricio Gómez Amín announced this week from Madrid. The treaty, called an Economic Partnership Agreement, is Japan’s version of a free-trade deal.

Free daily brief — no card needed Get every Colombia story in one morning email We build you a personalized brief around the topics you follow — free for 7 days. Love it? Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time.

For US readers, the pact matters because Japanese carmakers, machinery makers and investors would gain easier access to a market where US firms already trade under a preferential agreement in force since 2012. Our guide to Colombia’s key players explains who is steering the policy.

What Happened

Gómez Amín, who runs the ministry that handles trade and industry, said four months of talks cleared the blockage in a negotiation that had been frozen for nearly 15 years. He said the treaty should open new agribusiness markets, ease technology transfer and draw foreign investment in the energy transition and electric mobility.

Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (BB-); 26 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.8 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The minister said the aim is to open markets for Colombian products and create new opportunities for farms and industry. The government has not yet published the text of the agreement.

How the Talks Restarted

The restart began in late August. On Thursday 27 August 2026, Gómez Amín met Japan’s Foreign Minister, Toshimitsu Motegi, in Tokyo, and both governments told their technical teams to continue talks aimed at reviving the negotiation, according to the Colombian trade ministry.

On Monday 31 August the president said real progress had come within the first 15 days of his government. The minister also met Toyota, the Japanese carmaker, and Toshiba, the electronics group, and the president said Colombia is working so Mazda, another Japanese carmaker, can return to assembling vehicles in the country.

What the Deal Is Meant to Do

An Economic Partnership Agreement lowers tariffs on goods and usually adds rules on investment, services and customs. The Colombian government says this one targets agribusiness exports, technology transfer and clean-energy and electric-mobility investment.

The minister also confirmed that Colombia will take part in GREEN×EXPO 2027, a horticultural fair in Yokohama. Which tariffs would fall, and how fast, has not been made public.

The Road to Ratification

Signing is only one step, because under Colombian procedure treaties go to Congress and then to the Constitutional Court, the court that checks them against the constitution. Japan is also expected to complete its own approval.

No ratification timetable has been announced. Colombia is also pursuing separate trade goals in Washington, as we reported in our story on Colombia’s push to end a US tariff.

What It Means for You

If you invest in Colombia through US funds, a Japan pact signals that the new government wants more trade partners beyond the United States. Japanese car and parts makers could become stronger competitors to US suppliers in Colombia once tariffs fall.

Travellers and importers need not change plans, because nothing changes until the treaty is ratified and in force. Coffee and flower buyers should watch whether Japan lowers its own tariffs, since that would pull Colombian farm exports toward Asia.

What Is Not Known

The text, the tariff schedule and the list of products covered have not been published. It is also not known where the signing will take place, who will sign for Japan, or whether Japan has confirmed the date.

The government has not said how long ratification will take. It has also not said whether every chapter of the text is fully closed.

More: Colombia news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What Is Colombia Signing With Japan?

An Economic Partnership Agreement, a trade treaty that lowers tariffs and sets rules for investment. Colombia says it will sign on Sunday 20 December 2026.

Why Did Talks Take Nearly 15 Years?

Negotiations stalled for years before the new government restarted them in August 2026. Officials say four months of technical talks removed the blockage.

Does the Deal Take Effect on 20 December?

No. Signing starts the approval process, which under Colombian procedure includes Congress and the Constitutional Court before the treaty can take effect.

Does the Deal Affect US Exporters?

It could add Japanese competition in Colombia once tariffs fall. US firms already trade with Colombia under a trade agreement in force since 2012.

Sources: Ministry of Commerce, Industry and Tourism of Colombia, Colombia and Japan reactivate EPA negotiation, 27 August 2026; Ministry of Commerce, Industry and Tourism, statement by the president on Japan, 31 August 2026; statements by Commerce Minister Mauricio Gómez Amín, Madrid, 4 November 2026.
