World.title: Hard truths
World.content:
TUFTON... we must obtain more value from the investments we have already made (Photo: JIS)

THE latest review of Jamaica’s public health sector presents a mixed bag of progress and troubling setbacks, with improvements in infrastructure and staffing overshadowed by soaring medicine costs, weaknesses in primary health care, and persistently high maternal and neonatal deaths.

Most alarming is the finding that complications from non-communicable diseases (NCDs) account for nearly four in every five deaths in Jamaica, while too many patients are turning up at hospitals with conditions already at an advanced stage.

The findings are contained in the Jamaica Health Public Expenditure Review, prepared by the World Bank at the request of the Planning Institute of Jamaica (PIOJ) and the Ministry of Health and Wellness, covering the years 2016 to 2022.

Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton, who presented aspects of the report, along with the Government’s response, to Parliament on Tuesday, did not shy away from the findings, describing the review as “candid” and declaring that the Government accepts its conclusions.

“The review asks how much Jamaica spends on health, how well that money is spent, and what results it buys for our people,” Tufton explained.

He noted that the review measures Jamaica’s progress against the World Bank’s 2017 review, and compares the island’s performance with countries of similar demographic profiles.

He told Parliament that NCDs cause close to 80 per cent of deaths, maternal and neonatal mortality remain too high, and Jamaica’s per capita health expenditure is still below that of comparable countries, including Brazil, Grenada, Guyana, St Lucia, Dominica, Suriname, and Colombia.

Too much of the country’s health care spending, he acknowledged, is also being channelled into expensive late-stage hospital care, while medicine costs have risen rapidly.

“We need more nurses and more doctors in our health centres. And our service level agreements with the regional health authorities are not yet used to their full potential to hold the system accountable,” Tufton acknowledged.

According to the minister, “None of these findings comes as a surprise to the ministry. They validate the internal assessment that the ministry itself undertook, which led to the development of Vision for Health 2030, our 10-year strategic plan.

“That assessment told us that a health system built for acute and infectious disease must be reoriented towards prevention, primary healthcare and the management of chronic illness; that our workforce must grow and be deployed where it is needed most; that our facilities need sustained investment and maintenance; and that we need stronger governance and accountability for results,” said Tufton.

He posited that, working independently, the bank has reached the same conclusions.

“That tells us that we have diagnosed the problem correctly and that we are on the right road,” he said before reminding of the steps the ministry has taken over the past 10 years to address each of the bank’s findings.

“The ministry has not waited. Over the past decade we have acted on each of these fronts,” said Tufton.

On the matter of prevention, he reminded of the ‘Jamaica Moves’ programme launched in 2017 to tackle physical inactivity, poor diet, and the risk factors for NCDs. He also reminded of the ‘Know Your Numbers’ campaign, which encourages Jamaicans to have annual health checks and understand what he values mean for their health status.

On primary care, Tufton said the health and wellness ministry adopted the Primary Health Care Policy and, through the Health Systems Strengthening Programme, with support from the Inter-American Development Bank and the European Union, was upgrading health centres into comprehensive facilities. These include the Greater Portmore Health Centre, and redeveloping Spanish Town Hospital.

“On mothers and children, the Programme for the Reduction of Maternal and Child Mortality strengthened high-dependency and neonatal care in our hospitals; and the Western Child and Adolescent Hospital in Montego Bay, a gift of the People’s Republic of China, will be the first hospital of its kind in the English-speaking Caribbean,” said Tufton.

“On infrastructure, we have rehabilitated the Cornwall Regional Hospital and, following Hurricane Melissa, we are working with the National Reconstruction and Resilience Authority to rebuild the Black River, Falmouth, and Noel Holmes hospitals to a more resilient standard,” he added.

Tufton told the Parliament that the National Health Fund (NHF) integrated the NHF Card and the Jamaica Drugs for the Elderly Programme in 2020, simplifying access for patients.

Regarding human resources, he said “The review rightly identifies people as the foundation of any health system.” He said the ministry is focused on training more health care workers, retaining those already employed, and deploying them to primary care and underserved communities.

Tufton argued that the review records real progress, and he asked his fellow lawmakers to note it. He also stressed that Jamaica stands out in the region for the priority it places on health, highlighting that by 2021/22 the ministry’s spending had reached 16 per cent of central government expenditure, a larger share than almost every other Caribbean country.

Tufton also pointed out that the burden on households has fallen as the Government now finances 68 per cent of current health spending, up from below 40 per cent in 2012. He said out-of-pocket payments have fallen to 15 per cent, below the international threshold of 20 per cent.

He also cited investment in health facilities, sharing that capital spending more than doubled in real terms between 2015/16 and 2019/20, while spending on the maintenance and upgrading of facilities rose by 150 per cent.

Additionally, Tufton noted that more Jamaicans were getting their medicines, with NHF prescriptions rising from 1.5 million to 2.7 million, enrolment growing by 86 per cent, and prescription fill rates growing from 85 to 92 per cent.

Tufton said the health workforce has grown, with 1,996 posts for medical officers established since 2016.

“Of note is that there has been a 30 per cent increase in doctors in primary care, in keeping with the reform of primary health care, moving from 338 in 2023 to 432 in 2025.

Arguing that the World Bank’s central message is that money alone is not enough, Tufton said, “We must obtain more value from the investments we have already made”.

Opposition spokesman on health Dr Alfred Dawes latched on to that point, telling Tufton, “As I listened the minister’s presentation, it just drives home the point that we have been making — spending more money on health does not equate to better health care.”

World.title: Utility cables hobble SPARK project
World.content:
President of Greenwood Citizens Association Trevor Burnett, Jr indicates a section of unfinished road in his community.

GREENWOOD, St James — Utility cables have emerged as the latest obstacle delaying the completion of a Shared Prosperity through Accelerated Improvement to Our Road Network (SPARK) project in Greenwood, St James.

Contractors have been unable to complete the rehabilitation of just under one-mile of road leading into the community as they await relocation of the underground wires.

“The reason why the Greenwood project has not been completed is that there are some telecommunications cables that are there. We have made requests to the telecommunications company that is responsible for those cables to move them,” minister without portfolio in the Ministry of Economic Growth and Job Creation Robert Morgan, told the Jamaica Observer Tuesday.

He has responsibility for works.

“We can’t move them because if we move them, then they might get damaged and a large portion of the area would be without telecommunications services,” the minister added.

The Greenwood road is among several in St James earmarked for rehabilitation under the government’s $45-billion SPARK programme. However while other roads — including some on which work began later — have seen varying levels of completion, the Greenwood project remains unfinished.

The incomplete section stretches approximately half-a-kilometre from the community’s entrance off the highway to a section of Greenwood Avenue.

“We are really trying to work with the telecommunications company to remove those cables — I think some of them are fibre-optic cables — so we can finish the road,” Morgan continued.

Work began on the road late last year but the project has been plagued by delays, which the minister acknowledged. While most of the repairs have been done and drainage installed, the last portion has lagged for about six months. China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC), the contractor undertaking the project, has completed approximately 90 per cent of the work.

“I know the residents have been challenged. Because initially we had a water line issue where we had to instal new pipes and now that the road is pretty much paved that little section there is a challenge to the residents; so we are working on it,” Morgan assured.

For now, sections of the unfinished road remain open for drainage works, with caution signs placed in the area to alert motorists and pedestrians to potential hazards.

President of the Greenwood Citizens’ Association Trevor Burnett, Jr said he had been given a similar explanation for the delay.

“CHEC came out, I think August 1st, and said they were going to put in a new drain so that we don’t have any more flooding and as they started to dig, Flow cables and fibres underground started to be impacted,” he shared.

“We got Flow involved and so we are waiting on Flow now to complete their leg. They are supposed to move the fibre from underground, temporarily, and put it on poles so that CHEC can get to install the drain,” Burnett, Jr added.

Already concerned about the delay, the association president said he is also worried that there may be additional challenges ahead if the relevant parties fail to properly coordinate their work.

“After they remove the underground cables and put them on the post and CHEC completes their road paving, will Flow have to dig up the road again in order to bury back their fibre?” he asked.

“We need to know if they can work in conjunction with each other. My thought process is that Flow or CHEC would have put in some pipes alongside the drain so that Flow can just insert their fibres inside of it and we have a smooth sailing going forward,” Burnett, Jr explained.

He said he has been seeking answers but had yet to receive any substantial response.

Meanwhile, residents continue to contend with the inconvenience caused by the unfinished project.

“When it rains, it’s horrible, it’s flooded and you can’t get in and out most of the time. Pedestrians have to be using alternative routes, we have to be creating detour roads for pedestrians to go in and out of the community,” Burnett, Jr said.

He said CHEC had placed marl on the road as a temporary measure. However, the recent dry spell has turned the area into a dust bowl for those travelling through the community.

Residents said the situation continued to disrupt their daily lives and urgently needs to be addressed.

“When it rains it’s a problem and when it’s dry, it’s a dust nuisance; every day I have a cold,” complained Madge-Neil Burnett, who owns Greenwood Plaza.

She said the conditions have also affected her business.

“My thing them spoil up. Some of them we clean and sell [but] a lot of it we have to throw them away,” she lamented.

World.title: Masicka brings it home with Forever 1NE
World.content:
Minister of Culture and Entertainment Olivia “Babsy” Grange is out to support Masicka at the launch of his upcoming Forever 1NE concert held at D’Ferrano Restaurant & Lounge Rooftop on Monday night. (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

Portmore, his birthplace and the community that helped shape his journey, will take centre stage in a defining moment for Masicka when he brings his Forever 1NE music festival to Caymanas Park on December 19.

For the dancehall star, the occasion represents more than the staging of a major concert; it is an opportunity to give back to the place he calls home, while demonstrating the possibilities that open up when Jamaican artistes take ownership of their success and create opportunities on their own terms.

“This a mi place, Portmore; yah so mi birth, so dis a history,” Masicka declared at Monday night’s official media launch at D’Ferrano Restaurant & Lounge Rooftop, where sponsors, government officials, music industry stakeholders, and fans gathered to celebrate the undertaking.

The entertainer, who has spent more than a decade establishing himself as one of dancehall’s leading voices, was visibly at home as he addressed the gathering, expressing gratitude to the team working behind the scenes to bring the festival to fruition.

“Big up mi team, because this wouldn’t possible without dem; dem work hard. It’s a great feeling to host this in the community weh mi come from. With everything weh mi achieve inna mi career, me feel like a di right place to give back to,” he said.

It is a sentiment that resonates beyond the festivities planned for December. Portmore has long been said to be a breeding ground for Jamaican musical talent, and Masicka’s return as an internationally recognised act, now leading his own festival, is a moment of considerable significance for the municipality.

Minister of state in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade and Member of Parliament for St Catherine East Central Alando Terrelonge captured that pride in his address, welcoming the entertainer back to the community that helped shape his career.

“The truth is that we always say home is where the heart is, but tonight, home is where music is, and Masicka, I want to say welcome home,” Terrelonge said. “For years Portmore has been the incubator for Jamaica’s rawest, most undeniable talent. It is the community that shaped Masicka’s career, and to see him return to Portmore as an international headliner, commanding his own festival for the first time in his hometown, it fills every single Portmore resident with pride.”

Terrelonge praised Masicka as a master lyricist and storyteller whose career reflects patience, dedication. and growth. He also highlighted the potential benefits of the festival for the surrounding community, including increased commercial activity, job creation, and greater tourism visibility.

For him, December 19 represents an opportunity to celebrate not only Masicka’s achievements, but also the ability of Jamaican artistes to headline major productions at home.

“It’s celebrating a homecoming and proving that when possible, our own Jamaican musicians can headline their own concerts,” he said.

Dominic Bell, communications manager at J Wray & Nephew, which is partnering with the festival through Magnum Tonic Wine, pointed to the work behind Masicka’s success and the significance of the moment for the genre.

“Magnum’s Forever 1NE music festival will provide the manifestation of over 15 years of hard work from Masicka, garnering local and international acclaim,” Bell said. “As a lover of dancehall, this is exactly what the culture needs right now.”

Minister of Culture and Sport Olivia “Babsy” Grange, in welcoming the Forever 1NE initiative, commended Masicka for his discipline and for remaining focused on his music.

“I want to congratulate him for the example that he has been setting, the focus on the music. Him not ‘chatty chatty’ and run up him mouth and get himself into problems, him focus on him music, and that is what I admire so much about him,” Grange said.

She added that artistes have an important role to play in creating opportunities for the wider music industry, noting that Masicka and his team were taking that responsibility seriously through the festival.

“Music is entertainment, but it’s also a business,” she said, encouraging fans to support the artiste while reminding him of the responsibility that comes with their continued backing.

Minister of State in the Ministry of Industry, Investment and Commerce Delano Seiveright said the festival could help reinforce the municipality’s importance beyond its reputation as a residential community.

“Masicka is a game-changer and he is showing us what game-changing looks like,” Seiveright said. “Portmore is important to us. Over 200,000 people live in Portmore. It’s not just a residential community, it’s a place for business, a place for retail, and it’s going to become a place again for major events.”

Caymanas Park, the festival venue, is central to that ambition. Gary Peart, of Supreme Ventures, operators of Caymanas Park, said the property was poised to broaden its identity beyond horse racing and establish itself as a major entertainment destination.

“Everybody sees Caymanas as horse racing, the reality is that it’s going to be the biggest entertainment place in Jamaica,” Peart said, inviting patrons to witness a different side of the venue when Forever 1NE takes place.

Chief executive officer of Main Event Entertainment Group Solomon Sharpe, himself a Portmore native, said considerable work was already under way to deliver a production worthy of the occasion.

“We really want to put on a good production. Masicka is the biggest, baddest thing around town, and at Main Event we will try our best to keep up with him,” Sharpe said.

He disclosed that the team had already conducted six or seven site visits and reworked the venue layout several times, with an extensive range of production elements being considered.

The scale of the preparations is matched by a line-up designed to bring together some of dancehall and reggae’s distinctive voices. Joining Masicka on December 19 will be Dexta Daps, Shaneil Muir, and I Wayne, with additional surprise guests expected to make appearances.

And while the night’s full musical offering remains under wraps, those at Monday’s launch received a brief preview of what Masicka has in store. His performance was short but powerful, offering a taste of the commanding stage presence that has helped propel him to the forefront of the genre.

Masicka promised that the December staging would be anything but ordinary.

“December 19 nah go normal. Me and mi musical bredda dem ago create a pandemonium,” he declared.

World.title: What’s bad for Trump is good for Le Pen
World.content:
Anger at the rising cost of living spells danger for incumbents everywhere.

Beware the angry voter. That’s the message Europeans are taking from the crushing defeat suffered by Donald Trump’s Republicans in the U.S. midterm election.

The fury over the cost of living that helped propel the U.S. president to power has now turned against him. And with elections looming in heavyweight EU countries like Spain, Italy, France, Greece and Poland, Trump’s fate is a warning for incumbents across the continent.

Growing anger over rising prices and unaffordable housing is likely to spell trouble for Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who has already faced waves of protests over the cost of fuel.





The blowback in the U.S. shows what happens when right-wing populist leaders take charge and then don’t deliver on their promises, said Irene Tinagli, an Italian member of the European Parliament from the opposition Democratic Party.

“Trump came up with the promise of lowering the cost of living. He was attacking the previous administration for the inflation. He promised to bring back quality jobs,” Tinagli said. “This didn’t happen.”

Surveys show voters focused on economic concerns, said Mathieu Gallard, research director at polling firm Ipsos.

Demonstrators protest against rising housing prices in Barcelona on Oct. 5, 2026. | Manaure Quintero/AFP via Getty Images

In Spain, affordability is already a major issue in the campaign for an election scheduled for Nov. 29. Most polls predict the far-right Vox party, which has been accusing Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez of failing to meet citizens’ basic needs, will gain enough seats to enter into government for the first time as a coalition partner to the conservative People’s Party.

Whatever their political stripes, incumbents are vulnerable, Gallard said.

“The far-right or radical right [leaders], when they arrive in power, find themselves in the same situation as traditional parties and have the same difficulties,” he added, pointing to this year’s defeat of Hungary’s Viktor Orbán and a sharp drop in support for the far-right Sweden Democrats.





For insurgents like France’s Marine Le Pen and her far-right National Rally party, however, voter discontent offers opportunity.

The cost of living “will be the major issue in the campaign,” said Alexandre Loubet, a lawmaker for the National Rally and a key architect of Le Pen’s economic platform. “The advantage [for us] is that we are very consistent on this issue. It’s a bit like immigration — we are already in people’s minds on these subjects.”

Le Pen, who is the frontrunner in next spring’s presidential race, has long made cost-of-living a central issue for her platform and is capitalizing on the government’s current economic and fiscal woes.

She made affordable housing a central theme in her first campaign appearance and has doubled down on her promises to shield pensioners from upcoming budget squeezes. The far-right veteran is also campaigning on lowering energy taxes, brushing aside criticism that her proposals are unaffordable.

The blocked entrance of the Saint-Sernin high school in Toulouse on Nov.2, 2026. | Matthieu Rondel/AFP via Getty Images

At her party congress last week, Le Pen pushed a message of change and hope, adopting her rival President Emmanuel Macron’s catchword, “Renaissance,” as her campaign motto.

The positive tone “was intentional,” said Loubet. “There’s a sense of gloom in the country. We need to offer a little hope, a vision, a direction.”

The recent protest movements that have swept Spain, France, Italy and, to a lesser extent, Germany, have centered around complaints about the cost of living, especially for the young. They echo anger in the U.S., where polls showed young Americans felt their economic situation was deteriorating as the country headed in the wrong direction.





“The affordability debate in the United States breaks on class lines,” said Penny Naas, a senior vice president at the transatlantic think tank German Marshall Fund. “If you’re an American and you are not well off and energy plays a much bigger part in your household income, you’re feeling much more hurt by the current situation.”

“There are some similarities with what’s going on in Europe,” she added, pointing at school protests in France that started in the relatively poor outskirts of cities.

So far, centrist candidates have struggled to find the right messaging on the issue. Le Pen’s top centrist challenger, former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe, has struggled to gain traction with a pitch centered on economic realism.

A protest to demand more funding for schools and support for housing, on Oct. 30, 2026 in Rome. Filippo Monteforte/AFP via Getty Images

In Germany, Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservative Christian Democrats are also feeling the squeeze after suffering a series of electoral defeats, losing to the far right in eastern states and the radical left in Berlin.

“What this election shows is that if you want to win the hearts and minds of citizens, you cannot fight populism by trying to be the defender of the status quo,” said Sigrid Friis, a 32-year-old member of the European Parliament from the Danish Social Liberal Party.

“Those who have won this campaign are the young, the progressives, the forces that really are the forces of change,” she added.

World.title: Spanish rail infrastructure chief steps down after Toledo train crash
World.content:
Huge cranes lift one of the wrecked carriages of a train crash between a Renfe AVE train and an Iryo train, two days after the deadly accident in Urda, in the province of Toledo on October 30, 2026. | Oscar del Pozo/AFP via Getty Images

It marks the second resignation related to the disaster in just 24 hours.

⁠Adif President Luis Pedro Marco de la Peña has submitted his resignation to Spain’s new transport minister, Carlos Cuerpo.

Adif, responsible for Spain’s rail infrastructure, signaling and traffic control, is under intense scrutiny after last week’s devastating crash near Urda, Toledo, that claimed 69 lives. De la Peña's resignation was first reported by local media, and confirmed by a Spanish government official in a text message.

This marks Cuerpo’s first notable action since stepping into the ministry after former Transport Minister Oscar Puente’s resignation Tuesday night. Puente left his post following a marathon hearing before Congress’ Permanent Deputation, where both allies and opponents urged him to resign.

World.title: Hungary releases secret police files from communist era
World.content:
Documents are pictured in the historical archives of the Hungarian State Security in Budapest on Sept. 29, 2026. | Péter Kőhalmi/AFP via Getty Images

The files reveal the names of the socialist regime’s informant network, 70 years after the Soviet Union crushed the Hungarian revolution of 1956.

Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s key campaign promise to release files containing the socialist regime’s informant network has finally come to fruition after decades of debate.

The government on Wednesday gave citizens access to previously restricted files, allowing them to search online for ancestors’ names, 70 years after the Soviet Union crushed the Hungarian revolution of 1956. The files’ release had proved particularly controversial as the names mentioned in them were not necessarily actual informants, but sometimes just “persons of interest” to the regime.

In a public address Wednesday, Magyar urged citizens to “treat this long overdue publication of documents with dignity and humanity” as “many families will now face difficult information” regarding their personal history.

World.title: MEPs fear fundamental rights will take a hit under plans to expand EU border agency
World.content:
While member state authorities would still take decisions on returns, the EU border agency will become “responsible for return-related support from the beginning to the end, from A to Z,” Brunner said.

Under the Commission plan, Frontex could also help deport people from EU countries to hubs in countries outside the bloc, and from those hubs to third countries, the commissioner confirmed.

Centrist and left-leaning lawmakers said they were worried that the expanded mandate and scope would come with larger fundamental rights pitfalls.

“How will we guarantee that Frontex will comply with EU law while they have to obey the laws of third countries, where there is a completely different legal framework in place?” the Greens’ Tineke Strik, a Dutch MEP, asked the commissioner. “I really think that this modality will clearly lead to the risk of more fundamental rights violations,” she added.

Socialists and Democrats MEP Murielle Laurent, from France, asked: “To what extent can Europe externalize its migration policy while also externalizing its human rights defense policy?” She warned that “a more powerful EU agency is also an agency that should have more careful oversight.”

Brunner insisted that Frontex already has to meet firm fundamental rights obligations, and that those remain in place under the Commission’s plans.

Frontex would only assist non-EU countries in returns under an international agreement that lays out fundamental rights safeguards, he said. The Parliament would have to sign off on any such agreement, he added.

World.title: Midterms : 5 points que l’Europe doit surveiller après l’écrasante victoire des démocrates face à Trump
World.content:
Ces résultats impliquent probablement de futures enquêtes sur la guerre en Iran, le fonctionnement du FBI et, bien sûr, les business de la famille Trump. Pour se faire une idée de leur magnitude sur le plan politique : c’est comme si vous aviez le scandale du Whitewater de Bill Clinton et la première procédure de destitution contre Donald Trump réunis, avec en prime l’affaire Iran-Contra pour pimenter le tout.

Quel sera l’impact de ces bouleversements politiques majeurs sur l’Europe ? Des prix de l’énergie à la guerre en Ukraine, l’avenir du continent dépend en grande partie de ce qui se passe à Washington. Voici cinq points à surveiller.

L’Europe risque de faire les frais de la frustration de Trump

Certains observateurs chevronnés estiment que cela n’est pas seulement possible, mais hautement probable. “Nous devons nous préparer non pas à des relations transatlantiques plus harmonieuses, mais à plus d’animosité et à encore davantage d’exigences de la part de Trump envers l’Europe”, a averti Wolfgang Ischinger, un diplomate allemand expérimenté qui a présidé pendant de longues années la Conférence de Munich sur la sécurité.

Les démocrates auront davantage d’occasions de s’opposer à Donald Trump via des procédures budgétaires et en se montrant plus fermes lors des auditions de contrôle et des enquêtes. Ils commenceront probablement aussi à imposer des conditions plus strictes aux projets de loi souhaités par la Maison-Blanche.

Mais le président américain dispose d’une marge de manœuvre constitutionnelle considérable en matière de politique étrangère, de diplomatie et de sécurité nationale — ainsi qu’en matière de politique commerciale. Et Donald Trump s’en est ouvertement emparé en recourant à des décrets et en mettant au point des stratégies juridiques inédites et controversées pour contourner le Congrès.

“[Trump] est à la tête des forces armées. Il a la main sur les droits de douane et les accords commerciaux. Il dispose d’une tribune influente. Même si les démocrates remportent les deux chambres, il peut opposer son veto aux projets de loi”, a énuméré Phil Gordon, ex-conseiller à la sécurité nationale de l’ancienne vice-présidente Kamala Harris, auprès de Brussels Playbook.

World.title: Mélenchon a-t-il déjà son ticket pour le second tour ?
World.content:
La France insoumise s’est réjouie de la défaite de Donald Trump lors des élections de mi-mandat aux Etats-Unis, y voyant la possibilité de “faire reculer l’extrême droite”. Toute coïncidence avec la situation française n’est pas fortuite, alors que le scénario d’un second tour opposant Marine Le Pen à Jean-Luc Mélenchon devient de plus en plus probable, sondage après sondage. Pourquoi les Insoumis se sentent-ils pousser des ailes ? Ont-ils raison d’y croire ? Cela oblige-t-il les candidats de la droite et du centre à redéfinir leur stratégie ? Anthony Lattier en discute avec Victor Goury-Laffont, journaliste à POLITICO, et Marcelo Wesfreid, directeur adjoint de la rédaction.

World.title: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle to visit EU Parliament
World.content:
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle visit the Community Recording Studio in Nottingham, England on Oct. 15, 2026. | Pool photo by Joe Giddens via Getty Images

Couple will be in Brussels to talk about online child safety.

BRUSSELS — Prince Harry and Meghan Markle will visit the European Parliament next week to discuss online child safety, according to an email sent to lawmakers and seen by POLITICO.

Visiting Brussels for the first time as a couple, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex will on Tuesday join Parliament President Roberta Metsola in opening an exhibition honoring “the memory of children whose lives were lost in connection with online harms.”

Prince Harry will then discuss with Commissioner Dubravka Šuica, experts and lawmakers “how we can turn legislative commitments into effective safeguards for children, including through safer design, stronger enforcement, and clear accountability for technology companies,” the email reads.

The event is being hosted by Spanish center-right lawmaker Antonio López-Istúriz White, who is the vice president of the Parliament’s intergroup on children’s rights. In September, the European Commission proposed the EU Kids Act, which includes restrictions on social media use for minors.

“The decisions we take on AI, platform design and the enforcement of online safeguards will shape the digital environments in which children grow up. This responsibility cuts across parliamentary committees and policy areas; the experiences of children and families should inform and guide our work throughout,” Lopéz wrote in his invitation to other lawmakers.

World.title: Metsola tells MEPs not to rely on AI when drafting laws
World.content:
“No matter how AI may be used in a parliament, the responsibility is still [with] those who are elected,” she said.

Secretary-General Alessandro Chiocchetti said at the same event that Parliament is building its own AI tool for sensitive work, hosted on its internal infrastructure.

As POLITICO reported in July, commercial AI models, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Meta’s Llama, can still be used for less sensitive tasks.

Parliament officials have warned of a surge in AI-written amendments, including some that reference laws that don't exist. Chiocchetti cited the case of an MEP who turned to AI for legal advice and got a wrong answer. “Our jurists took two days just to prove ChatGPT wrong,” he said.

The administration will submit new guidelines on using AI to senior leaders “very soon,” Chiocchetti said. Existing guidelines for staff date from 2024.

“Basically it boils down to three things: be open about using artificial intelligence, meaning if they use it, they have to say it as the rules require; never put sensitive material into a public tool; and check everything before it leaves your desk because it is your name on it,” Chiocchetti said.

He added he wants to use AI to help sort through thousands of amendments. But the drafting and consideration of laws need to remain with MEPs, as “the risk is indeed that we delegate the political debate to a chatbot.”

“Every text we vote has to be one that people wrote, checked, and are willing to defend. Anyone reading a new regulation should be able to find out who decided and hold them responsible.”

World.title: Spain: Madrid hosts 30th Ibero-American Summit with 22-nation bloc
World.content:
World leaders gathered at Madrid's Teatro Real on Wednesday evening as King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia inaugurated the 30th Ibero-American Summit. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez greeted arriving delegations from the 22-member community.

 

Despite the ceremonial welcome, only 10 countries were represented by their heads of state or government. Argentina's Javier Milei, Chile's José Antonio Kast and Guatemala's Bernardo Arévalo were among the seven Latin American presidents present.

Brazil's Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Mexico's Claudia Sheinbaum and Venezuela's acting president Delcy Rodríguez stayed away, highlighting political divisions ahead of Spain's general election on 29 November.

UN chief António Guterres and European Council President António Costa joined the gathering, while Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky travelled to Madrid for separate talks.

Thursday's programme includes the plenary session and official photograph at the Royal Collections Gallery, as Spain mourns 69 victims of last week's train disaster.

World.title: Zelenski makes surprise visit to Madrid for talks with Sánchez and Latin American leaders
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrived in Madrid on Wednesday for a series of high-level meetings coinciding with the Ibero-American Summit. His visit, which was kept secret for security reasons until his plane landed, includes a schedule of meetings with international leaders over the summit's two days.

 

Zelenskyy will take part in a meeting on Thursday with several of the leaders who have travelled to the capital, among them UN Secretary-General António Guterres and European Council President António Costa.

The presence of the Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez is also expected, along with other Ibero-American representatives. Besides this meeting, the Ukrainian president will hold bilateral talks with Sánchez and with Spanish King Felipe VI.

Holding the summit in Madrid is also an opportunity for Kyiv to strengthen its contacts with Latin American countries, a region where the war triggered by the Russian invasion continues to generate opposing positions. According to government sources, Zelenskyy plans to hold meetings with representatives of several of the 22 Ibero-American delegations present in the capital.

Zelenskyy to meet country leaders in a heated context

Zelenskyy confirmed his arrival on social media, saying "our top priority is strengthening Ukraine's air defences, protecting our people, and expanding defence cooperation and production."

"Further support steps are being prepared," the Ukrainian president added, without providing details on the measures or the leaders he would meet.

The far-right presidents of Argentina and Chile, Javier Milei and Jose Antonio Kast, as well as Bolivian conservative Rodrigo Paz, are among the Latin American heads of state in the Spanish capital.

Two weeks ago, Milei made a visit to Madrid where he called Sanchez a "disgraceful dictator" and urged Spaniards to "kick out" his Socialists in the election.

The firebrand libertarian has made several unofficial visits to Spain since becoming Argentina's president in 2023, but has never met Sanchez, instead supporting the conservative and far-right opposition as well as launching into long diatribes against socialism.

The Ibero-American format has lost influence in recent years, and reversing that trend is the key goal of the group's 30th summit in Madrid.

At the last summit, held in Ecuador in 2024, a historically low four heads of state turned up and the divided participants failed to adopt a final declaration.

This year, the seven Latin American presidents in attendance will illustrate the region's tilt to the right after a slew of electoral victories for allies of Trump.

Further complicating the scene for Sanchez is the absence of his leftist allies in Latin America's powerhouses: Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum and Brazil's newly re-elected veteran Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.

'The best response is an open economy,' Felipe VI

Against a backdrop of economic uncertainty and international tensions, Felipe VI argued for an open economy and a move away from protectionism. "The best response does not lie in protectionism, but in an open economy based on equal rules for everyone," he told Ibero-American business leaders gathered in Madrid.

The Spanish King rejected the idea that the response should be to close off the national economies or raise trade barriers. Instead, he advocated greater openness and cooperation between countries that share values and objectives. In this regard, he highlighted the potential of Ibero-America as a space to deepen ties and generate new economic opportunities.

The region has, he stressed, significant energy resources and strategic raw materials, including critical minerals and rare earths, which could place it in a prominent position in the new international economic landscape. To make the most of these opportunities, Felipe VI stressed the importance of having "stable environments, legal certainty and solid, transparent institutions".

These are conditions he considers essential for attracting investment and building trust. "Trust is one of our most valuable assets and, allow me to say, also one of those we can most easily lose", he said.

Finally, the Monarch stressed the importance of continuing to tighten ties between the European Union and Latin America and the Caribbean, a relationship he sees as essential for tackling today's economic challenges and seizing the opportunities offered by a rapidly changing international landscape.

Albares defends the Ibero-American Summit amid absences

It fell to the Foreign Minister, José Manuel Albares, to play down the empty seats. "It is absolutely not a forum in decline," he insisted on Wednesday before the foreign ministers' meeting. His argument is that all 22 countries have someone in Madrid, at least their foreign minister, and that those who are not coming either rarely travel or are facing internal problems that prevent them from being away for several days.

Absent, among others, are Lula da Silva, Claudia Sheinbaum and Delcy Rodríguez, and with them several of the presidents closest to Sánchez, who instead finds himself alongside Chilean José Antonio Kast and Milei, at the opposite end of the political spectrum. Albares chose to look back. Only three heads of state attended the Cuenca meeting in 2024, and compared with that, ten seems a success to him.

On the ideological clash, the minister said the community had always been diverse in the political colour of its governments and that its strength lay in putting a common voice above differences he regarded as temporary. The Ibero-American Secretary-General, Andrés Allamand, describes it as "the summit of reaffirmation".

World.title: Indra to lead Spanish alliance guarding Europe's undersea infrastructure
World.content:
In France, seven leading technology companies, with Indra at the forefront alongside SAES, UTEK, Aragon Photonics, Iqua Robotics, FYLA and Sateliot, joined forces in Paris on Wednesday to address one of the greatest vulnerabilities in international security: shielding the seabed.

 

During the Euronaval trade fair, senior industry executives signed a strategic agreement to develop the SIPRIS initiative, a project intended to give Spain technological sovereignty in the protection and continuous surveillance of cables and critical infrastructure under water.

Indra will lead coordination of the ecosystem and will take on overall system integration through its Seadef architecture and the sovereign artificial intelligence platform IndraMind, reinforced by the use of unmanned aerial drones.

For Ana Belén Buendía, the company’s naval director, Sipris responds to the "urgent need" to monitor the underwater environment in order to give Europe technological sovereignty. She stressed that the alliance between leading Spanish firms will make it possible to build a comprehensive solution and position the national industry at the forefront of a sector that is undergoing a strategic boom.

Drones, fibre and satellites to shield the seabed

The other partners will deploy a multidisciplinary technological network to secure the marine environment. SAES will contribute its sensors and sonar processing for threat detection, while autonomous control will be shared between UTEK, responsible for surface vehicles (USV), and Iqua Robotics, focused on unmanned submarines (UUV) for infrastructure inspection.

Anomaly detection via fibre optics will be handled by Aragon Photonics, supported by FYLA’s underwater optical communications and Sateliot’s satellite coverage.

This alliance lays the foundation for a modular, scalable industrial ecosystem, designed to progressively integrate new players, technology centres and SMEs from the sector.

The project will now move straight into field testing before its launch on the market. With this step, Spain scores a major coup in the defence industry and joins the small club of powers capable of protecting their own infrastructure beneath the sea.

World.title: Hungary: communist-era files released, up to 60,000 former agents revealed
World.content:
In spite of Hungary's democratic transition in 1990, efforts to disclose communist-era archives have repeatedly failed, with critics blaming successive governments' reluctance to implicate public figures across the political spectrum.

 

Hungary's Prime Minister Peter Magyar ended this stall with a bill in September to grant unrestricted access for the public to the records for the first time.

"After 36 years, we are finally fulfilling what was once one of the key promises of the 1990 regime change — a promise that was later denied and lied about," Magyar told a media briefing at the state security archives.

"For decades, restrictions on public access provided opportunities for political hysteria, blackmail, the exertion of pressure, and silencing," he said.

Public figures featured in registry

Politicians, clergy members and TV personalities' names appeared in the registries. But a "large proportion" of the informants were "people who did not make their mark on national public life," said Bendeguz Gergo Cseh, the head of the archive.

The government will set up hotlines offering emotional support and counselling for those affected by the revelations.

"Following today's disclosure, a great many families will be confronted with information that is difficult for them to bear," Magyar said, asking people to treat the disclosure with "dignity and humanity."

Various types of documents disclosed

Under the law on the full disclosure of the previous regime’s secret service activities, four types of state security records dating from before 1990 will be made freely accessible to anyone.

On Wednesday morning, the three of these became accessible on the nyitottaktak.hu (source in Hungarian) website.

The "6 card" is the registration sheet for a network member. It contains the agent’s identifying data, including name, place and date of birth, mother’s name and occupation, but also the main details of the agent’s activity. Among them, the circumstances and motivations that led to them becoming an agent and how long they remained a network member.

A register of recruitment between 1957 and 1962 and a database of former agents' personal data and code names were also released. In total, estimates suggest 50,000 to 60,000 agent names were made public over all this document disclosure.

The public has free access since Wednesday to this data via a search tool that can filter by birth data, by name, place and date of birth, as well as by code name, across all types of records that have been made public.

A second batch of files with further detail on about 9,000 informants will be released in February.

Around 150,000 agents during communist era

Hungary was under one-party communist rule between 1949 and 1989 that repressed dissent.

Much like in East Germany and other parts of the Soviet-led Eastern Bloc during the Cold War, authorities employed an extensive network of informants to monitor public sentiment.

Individuals, often recruited through coercion, were tasked with reporting on colleagues, friends and even relatives for signs of disloyalty towards the regime.

Estimates suggest that secret police employed around 150,000 agents in total over the four decades of the Mátyás Rákosi (1952-1953) and János Kádár (1956-1988) regimes.

But only about one-third of their names are known, and detailed, substantive information exists for only about 10% of them. Many records were lost in 1956 and during the anti-Soviet change of regime, and the remainder was kept until 1997 in the Ministry of Interior, until the creation of ÁBTL’s predecessor, the Historical Office.

Entrance of the Historical Archives of the Hungarian State Security in Budapest’s 6th district in Eötvös Street - 28 December 2022. MTI/Róka László

Cseh Gergő Bendegúz, director general of the Historical Archives of State Security Services (ÁBTL), told the Hungarian press agency MTI that there are about ten thousand files, comprising many hundreds of thousands of pages in total.

Responding to a question on how reliable and complete the documents are, Cseh Gergő Bendegúz underlined that the content of state security records is not necessarily true in every case and is certainly very incomplete.

'Better late than never'

Debates over opening the archives have dogged Hungarian politics since the fall of communism. In 2002, weeks after becoming prime minister, socialist politician Peter Medgyessy became embroiled in a scandal after it was revealed that he had worked as a communist-era secret agent.

The case prompted fresh calls for transparency, and parliament adopted a law in 2003 that allowed individuals who had been monitored to learn who had reported on them.

The release was "better late than never," said historian Laszlo Eorsi from the 1956 Institute Foundation.

"We are getting access to much more information than before about who the authorities have recruited and how the security apparatus worked back then," he said.

But historians have cautioned against judging anyone just because their names are on the list of informants.

"I know of quite a few examples when someone was recruited, but they did not make a report, but in fact took a huge risk by turning against the authorities. Some even could be considered proper heroes," Eorsi stressed.

World.title: Euronews owner pushes for enlargement of EU to 'reunite the continent'
World.content:
Euronews owner and chairman Pedro Vargas David argued in favour of the rapid enlargement of the European Union at the Euronews Enlargement Summit on Tuesday, as it welcomed policymakers, political leaders, experts and business representatives to Brussels.

 

"Let us in as fast as you can, we will show you once inside, we are worthy members of the EU," he said, voicing the demand of many candidate countries to the EU including Albania, Georgia, Serbia and Ukraine.

As more nations than ever want to join the bloc, candidate countries have divided support within their population. Albania is leading with 92% of its people supporting EU accession, while Turkey and Serbia have the lowest support from their people to join the EU, respectively 46% and 31%.

Beyond Europe's borders, he also praised Armenia's and Georgia's candidacy as their "populations are European by culture and tradition."

David wondered if for some candidates the above numbers were "too low", pointing out responsibilities: "Are we doing all we can to counter the narratives of our opponents? [...] Are our EU ambassadors in the candidate countries not too many times seen as the spokespeople of everything that is wrong and not the promoters of the good cases?"

Euronews Enlargement Summit 2026, 3 November 2026, Brussels. Euronews

The 'Gibraltar model' of accession for the Western Balkans

Pedro Vargas David declared his support for a "Gibraltar model for a swift application of Schengen" for Western Balkan nations, referring to the idea of allowing a fast-tracked membership status with "potential changes to the rights and obligations" of member states, such as veto limitations, voting powers and access to certain programmes.

He called for a debate to take place on the issue, "in particular in the Council and also in the Parliament.

David underlined how recent elections were carried out in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia as arguments in favour of this: "democratic elections, perfect, surely not, but no one doubts that the result reflected the will of the people."

He then expressed his support for a rapid enlargement of the EU: "We can either step up our game and move fast, or continue to be tangled in our old positions. We have a historical opportunity, but make no mistake, if we miss it, others will not."

Georgian PM Irakli Kobakhidze (left) with Euronews Chairman Pedro Vargas David (second right) and Euronews CEO & Editorial Director Claus Strunz (right) in Brussels 3 Nov 2026 Euronews

EU citizens support enlargement by a narrow majority

Almost 53% of European Union citizens support enlargement, with divided endorsements among EU countries. In Sweden, 79% of people support it, while France staggers at a low 35%.

David sees a solution to raise support for enlargement: "More than 2/3 of Europeans say they don’t know enough and want to be more informed. These Europeans are ready to change their views if they get the right information. And that is the responsibility of political leaders, but also the responsibility of the media. The responsibility of Euronews."

He also called for the UK to rejoin the EU: "In next year’s summit, let’s make sure we have the United Kingdom back at the table. I said a month ago, if GB News was Brexit TV, let Euronews be the Rejoin TV. Mistakes can always be made, but they can also be corrected. We, as Europeans, are poorer and weaker without the UK, and so is the UK without Europe."

Some 60% of British people want to rejoin the EU, "bring that Union Jack back to Brussels ASAP," he urged.

World.title: MEPs debate EU enlargement at Euronews Summit in Brussels
World.content:
From the Western Balkans to the Southern Caucasus and Europe’s eastern flank, the Euronews Enlargement Summit revealed a European Union closer to expansion than at any point in the past decade – but also the political obstacles that could still derail it.

 

In this edition of The Ring, Estonian MEP Riho Terras from the European People's Party (EPP) and his Italian counterpart Pasquale Tridico from The Left went through all the arguments discussed at the event.

Leaders gathered in Brussels to discuss candidate countries’ ambitions to join the EU, and whether the bloc is ready to admit them as the prospect of expansion looks more real than it has in years.

From Ukraine and Georgia to Montenegro and Armenia, each country faces its own mix of political sensitivities, painstaking reforms and diplomatic hurdles. Progress can be swift, but setbacks can be equally dramatic.

This episode of The Ring is hosted by Stefan Grobe, produced by Luis Albertos and Amaia Echevarria, and edited by Vassilis Glynos.

Watch it in the player above.

World.title: Bob Dylan meets Pope Leo XIV in the Vatican, with music, faith and a rosary gift
World.content:
"Knocking on Heaven's Door": in 1997 Bob Dylan sang Knockin' on Heaven's Door in front of John Paul II. Almost thirty years later, the American singer songwriter is back in the Vatican, this time to meet Pope Leo XIV. It is an encounter that intertwines music, spirituality and a commitment to peace, centred on an artist who has spanned generations and has even inspired Popes' speeches.

 

The musician, 85, winner of the Nobel Prize for Literature, was received on Wednesday afternoon in the Apostolic Palace. The meeting was described on social media by Father Antonio Spadaro, who accompanied Dylan together with Andrea Monda, editor of L'Osservatore Romano.

"Today I accompanied Bob Dylan to see Pope Leo. Not without the emotion of experiencing a meeting that has the flavour of history and the feeling that, at every step in the Apostolic Palace, anything could have happened!", wrote Spadaro, posting two photographs of the singer next to the Pope.

Black sweatshirt, hood pulled over his head: in Rome for a stop on his tour (on Thursday evening he will take to the stage at the Palazzo dello Sport), Dylan stays true to his persona and stages an encounter that brings together two icons, even if they belong to very different worlds.

The audience was brief, with greetings and a few exchanges. Leo XIV gave the musician a rosary, while Dylan responded with a copy of Chronicles - Volume 1, his autobiography.

Bob Dylan and Pope Leo, the common thread of peace and music

The meeting did not come out of nowhere. Last July the Pope had in fact quoted Dylan in the preface to the book from the Vatican publishing house, Libreria Editrice Vaticana, Disarmata e disarmante. La pace è un dono, edited by journalist Alessandro Banfi.

The words he chose were those of Go Away You Bomb (Vai via, bomba), a protest lyric written by the musician in 1963, at the height of the Cold War: "I hate you because man made you and man owns you and man handles you".

A composition against the nuclear threat, it stayed out of the spotlight for a long time: the song has never been recorded or officially released on Dylan's albums. The original manuscript was only found in 2013. Leo XIV used it to issue a warning against rearmament and the risk of a new nuclear escalation.

Dylan became famous in the 1960s also thanks to songs such as Masters of War and Blowin' in the Wind, associated with anti-war protests and the struggle for civil rights. His position, however, is more nuanced than that of an absolute pacifist: in 2001 he said he did not consider himself a pacifist and defended the right to self-defence.

From John Paul II to Leo XIV: Dylan has met a Pope before

This is not the first time Dylan has appeared before a Pope. In 1997 the singer songwriter took part in the National Eucharistic Congress in Bologna, where he performed in front of John Paul II and around 300,000 young people.

After playing three songs, including Knockin' on Heaven's Door, Dylan took off his cowboy hat, climbed the steps of the papal stage and shook Karol Wojtyla's hand.

American pop legend Bob Dylan steps down from the stage after greeting Pope John Paul II at the end of his performance in Bologna on 27 September 1997 AP Photo

On that occasion too, music acted as a bridge between the world of rock and that of the Church. In his address to young people, John Paul II quoted Blowin' in the Wind, one of the musician's masterpieces: "You ask me: how many roads must a man walk down before you can call him a man?".

The Polish Pope replied with his own interpretation: "Only one. There is only one road for man, and it is that of Jesus Christ".

Bob Dylan's faith, between conversion and gospel songs

Spirituality is another central dimension of his career. Raised in a Jewish family, Dylan went through a profound religious turning point at the end of the 1970s, after recounting a spiritual experience that led him to draw closer to Christianity.

In 1979 he released Slow Train Coming, followed by Saved and Shot of Love: three albums in which Christian faith and the language of gospel openly entered his music. In the following years he returned to a more varied repertoire, without abandoning religious references.

In a more recent interview Dylan reiterated that he is a religious person, that he often reads the Scriptures, meditates and prays.

Leo XIV and music: "Singing belongs to those who love"

For Leo XIV too, music is much more than an accompaniment to prayer. In the first year of his pontificate the Pope has repeatedly emphasised its communicative and spiritual power: we have heard him sing the Regina Caeli and the Pater Noster in Latin, and watch with deep involvement the songs of the communities he has met during his travels.

At the Jubilee for choirs and choral groups, in November 2025, Leo described music as a gift of the great civilisations, capable of expressing what we carry deep in our hearts. Singing, he explained, brings together mind, feelings, body and soul. And quoting Saint Augustine he recalled: "Cantare amantis est", that is, "singing is characteristic of one who loves".

World.title: Brazil: Santa Claus School celebrates graduation at Christ the Redeemer
World.content:
Christmas came early to Rio de Janeiro on Tuesday, when 55 graduates of the Escola de Papai Noel do Brasil gathered beneath Christ the Redeemer to mark the end of their training. Dressed in red suits and white beards, the new Santas sang carols as they rode the Corcovado mountain railway to the statue, then climbed the final steps for a ceremony that included a blessing and the presentation of diplomas.

 

The free course, open to men aged 50 and over with naturally white or grey hair and beards, runs for a month of Tuesday afternoon classes covering acting, improvisation, diction, posture, make-up, costume and beard care, plus Brazilian Sign Language. It was founded in 1993 by the actors Limachem Cherem and Conrado Freitas, with the costume designer Fátima Tavares Cherem, in the basement of Cherem's house in Vila Isabel.

More than 1,000 Santas have passed through the school in 33 years, along with about 300 Noeletes, its female equivalent. Many graduates are retirees earning extra income at shopping centres, hospitals and parties; some, such as the lorry driver Marinezio Teixeira de Oliveira, come back for a second certificate.

World.title: Democrats take House and Senate from Republicans in US midterm rout
World.content:
Democrats will control both chambers of Congress after flipping seats in Republican strongholds across the US in an election seen as a repudiation of President Donald Trump.

By late Tuesday night, it was clear that Democrats had succeeded in turning the 2026 US midterm elections into the so-called "blue wave" that had been predicted by pollsters.

But by Wednesday morning, the scale of the victory had turned into a "blue tsunami," surprising even the most optimistic political pundits.

In January, Democrats are set to have a commanding majority of at least 237 to 139 in the House and a 54 to 44 advantage in the Senate.

Democratic candidates flipped seven highly competitive Senate seats, including in what have for decades been reliably Republican districts in "red" states.

Texas voted in James Talarico as its first Democratic Senator since 1988, while electing a Democratic governor, Gina Hinojosa, for the first time in over 30 years.

The heartland state of Kansas, where farmers have been hit by high diesel prices and tariffs, will send a Democrat, Adam Hamilton, to the US Senate for the first time in over 90 years.

Other surprise wins in Republican strongholds included Iowa, South Carolina, and Ohio.

Big Democrat victory in US midterm elections To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

According to data analyzed by the New York Times, the 2026 Democrats came in at a 13 point margin of victory over the Republicans for the popular vote in the House, the largest such margin since 1976 seen in the wake of the Watergate scandal that shattered the presidency of Republican Richard Nixon two years prior.

Democrats also saw large gains in almost every voter group compared with the 2024 presidential election that put Trump in the White House, indicating the breadth of the political swing away from Republicans.

The full scale of the Democrat majority in both chambers may not be known until later Wednesday or Thursday as some races are still too close to call, or take longer to count ballots.

Democrats promise change, buoyed by Trump's unpopularity

The midterms were seen as a referendum on President Donald Trump, who had historically low approval ratings of around 38% ahead of election day.

Trump had campaigned relentlessly in the weeks leading up to the election, in what often turned into meandering speeches to dwindling crowds.

Democrats were able to capitalize on Trump's unpopular policies like the war in Iran and ensuing record-high fuel costs, which compounded a growing affordability crisis while the president was seen as enriching himself.

On Wednesday, Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries said his party was focusing "relentlessly on affordability and on accountability."

"The days of the House of Representatives functioning like a wholly-owned subsidiary of the Trump administration are over," said Jeffries, who could become the first Black speaker of the House in January.

Democrats say they are ready to launch a 100-day agenda to lower costs for fuel, groceries and healthcare, while conducting vast oversight and investigations into Trump and his administration.

When asked about the option of impeaching Trump or cabinet members for breaking laws while in office, Jeffries said Democrats were not focusing on that for now.

The margin of victory in the Senate is still not a two-thirds supermajority, with which Democrats alone could vote to convict in cases of impeachment, or override presidential vetoes.

Even as a lame duck president for the remaining two years of his term, Trump still has the power of the executive at his disposal, which comes with broad sway, especially in foreign policy.

Midterms put US political divide on display To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

GOP blame game begins

Despite for months claiming that Democrats would cheat to win the election, Trump did not dispute the Republican blowout. Instead, he claimed that Republicans would have won had his name been on the ballot.

Nevertheless, Trump said he would be willing to work with Democrats, while at the same time promised to use veto power to block legislation.

In remarks on Wednesday outside of his ballroom construction site at the White House, Trump appeared to admit that the economic impacts of the Iran war had cost the Republican Party.

Trump preferred to speak more about ballroom project than the midterms on Wednesday Image: Evan Vucci/REUTERS

"I think it's largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term," Trump said.

Earlier Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance was more direct, saying the Iran war was the "reason we lost."

However, Trump spent the majority of the time in front of reporters on Wednesday talking about his ballroom project.

"It's going to be not only one of the biggest, but it'll be the most beautiful ballroom I think anywhere in the world," he said.

World.title: Bavarian politician Hubert Aiwanger found dead in Berlin hotel
World.content:
Aiwanger was Bavaria's Economy Minister and the chairman of the right-wing populist Free Voters Party. The circumstances surrounding his death are still unclear.

Bavarian politician Hubert Aiwanger was found dead in a hotel in Berlin on Wednesday, the German capital's public prosecutor's office said.

Aiwanger was Bavaria's deputy premier, economy minister and the chairman of the right-wing populist Free Voters party. He was 55 years old.

What do we know about Hubert Aiwanger's death?

The circumstances surrounding Aiwanger's death are still unclear. Police and prosecutors in the German capital have launched an investigation.

On Wednesday evening, investigators said the goal is to "determine the specific cause of death and the circumstances surrounding it, as well as to rule out any possible foul play."

Aiwanger had been feeling unwell on Wednesday, German tabloid Bild reported.

He had been scheduled to deliver a speech at the opening of his party's Berlin office, but canceled his appearance due to health reasons, German news agency dpa reported.

Aiwanger's body was found on Wednesday evening at the "Neuer Fritz" Hotel on Friedrichstrasse in Berlin-Mitte, according to Bild.

Bavarian state premier, the Christian Social Union's Markus Söder, has said he is "deeply shocked" by the news of his deputy's death.

"The sudden death of Hubert Aiwanger is an absolute tragedy," Söder said in a post on X.

"Our thoughts are now first and foremost with his family and his children. We mourn with them and pray for them."

Who was Hubert Aiwanger?

Born in Lower Bavaria in southern Germany, Aiwanger was elected to the Bavarian State Parliament in 2008 with the Free Voters and became their parliamentary group leader.

In 2018, his party formed a coalition with the center-right CSU, the Bavarian sister party of the ruling Christian Democratic Union (CDU). Aiwanger held the role of the state's Minister of Economic Affairs and deputy state premier.

Aiwanger was the face of the Free Voters in Bavaria and across Germany, and was known for his combative approach.

He was unable to replicate his political success at the state level, however, as the Free Voters never won enough seats to enter the Bundestag, Germany's federal parliament.

Aiwanger was viewed as a polarizing figure in Bavaria Image: Frank Hoermann/SvenSimon/picture alliance

In the weeks before state elections in 2023, Aiwanger became embroiled in a national scandal when the Süddeutsche Zeitung reported that he had written an antisemitic leaflet during high school in the 1980s, which included references to Nazi-era atrocities such as Auschwitz.

He is survived by two children. He was not married but lived with Tanja Schweiger, a district administrator for the Free Voters.

World.title: Winners, losers, the EU: Five takeaways from the US midterms
World.content:
Donald Trump's Republicans suffered a crushing defeat in Tuesday's midterm elections, with the Democrats wresting control of Congress. What does this mean for US politics and the world?

The Democrats not only made significant gains in Tuesday's midterm elections but also took control of both chambers of Congress. Here are five insights that can be drawn from this moment.

1. US democracy is alive and well

The storming of the Capitol, attempts to change the rules of the electoral process, a spate of presidential executive orders to bypass Congress and many more examples sparked concerns that the US' vaunted democracy was being transformed into an authoritarian system under Donald Trump. But the country's democratic institutions have proven more resilient than many had feared.

Many voters were driven by their opposition to Trump's desire to rule with unfettered power. Instead they want to see country's institutional safeguards strengthened.

A post-election survey by news agency Associated Press found that about 30% of voters thought the state of democracy was the country's biggest problem . About 70% felt that Congress was not doing enough to provide checks and balances on the president.

This midterm result sends a clear signal that voters want stronger parliamentary oversight. President Trump could of course continue trying to govern through executive orders, bypassing Congress. But Congress sets the budget.

This means the Democrats, who now control Congress, can deny the president the funds he needs for his political initiatives. They can also set up investigative committees, which puts the Trump government under considerable pressure to justify its actions.

2. The Democrats can still win elections

For a long time, the Democratic Party lacked compelling leadership, a unified approach and a clear answer as to how it intends to win votes. Tuesday's election proves the party is still a political force to be reckoned with.

Its gains in many Republican strongholds are nothing short of sensational. The party was even able to score victories in Texas and South Carolina. In Kansas, the Democrats won a Senate seat for the first time since 1932.

The midterms have also put the spotlight on a new generation of Democrats: Younger politicians, some of them noticeably more progressive, who could chart a fresh course for the party.

Take, for instance, the Democratic Socialists of America, or DSA, an organization which is considerably more left-wing than the Democratic Party itself. At least five candidates endorsed by the DSA have been elected to the House of Representatives.

James Talarico becames the first Democrat to win a Senate seat for Texas Senate in over 30 years Image: Eric Gay/AP Photo/picture alliance

The DSA advocate for strong welfare policies that focus on affordable housing, health care and workers' rights. They also want to see greater checks on the power of large corporations.

"The argument was always that these folks can't win on a national stage," Brandon Bohrn, an expert on trans-Atlantic relations at the Bertelsmann Foundation, told DW. Now some of them have defied the odds and actually won, potentially sparking an internal debate about what the Democrats stand for and how they plan to win voters in the 2028 presidential election, Bohrn said.

3. The Republicans face a fierce internal battle over the party's future

Donald Trump has already made it clear that he does not hold himself responsible for this midterms defeat, taking to Truth Social to deflect any blame.

Yet not everyone in the Republican party is likely to agree. Critics of Trump who had been sidelined may feel emboldened to speak up again. The question as to whether the Republicans should abandon Trumpism will be almost impossible to ignore.

By law, Donald Trump cannot run for a third term in the 2028 presidential race so Republicans will have to think about who can. But who will take the lead? And more importantly: On what policy platform?

Tuesday's election defeat will likely accelerate this debate, making a power struggle over the Republicans' political future inevitable.

4. For Iran's leadership, Trump's defeat is good news

The war against Iran and resulting economic hardships have cost the Republicans many votes. The cost of living, in particular, was a key issue for many American voters.

The consequences of the Iran war have primarily driven up energy prices. This is likely to significantly increase domestic pressure on Trump to reach a lasting agreement with Iran.

Trump does seem keen to cut foreign policy costs, especially in areas where it has been politically controversial for his party. Shortly before the midterms, he announced that he no longer intends to provide billions in military aid to Israel. This was in relation to a deal that was meant to expire in two years anyway.

5. What the election outcome could mean for Europe

Ian Lesser, an expert on US foreign and security policy at the German Marshall Fund, believes that the midterm elections could also impact trans-Atlantic relations. "This actually makes a big difference for Europe in a number of different important ways," Lesser told DW.

Trump has not shown great enthusiasm for NATO Image: Yves Herman/REUTERS

The Democrats could try to reinvigorate dialogue between Europe and the US, Lesser suggests. After all, with control of Congress, the Democrats have more say on Trump's NATO policy, can influence budget decisions and military funding, and can complicate planned cuts to US support. Europe and the US may even cooperate on climate and environmental issues.

"Simply restoring a degree of trust and predictability, however we get to that, makes a big difference," Lesser said.

Not all differences will be resolved overnight though.

"Tariffs are a little tricky because there are clearly vested interests in the US in keeping some of this in place," Lesser concluded. "But in terms of new and very aggressive tariff measures, I think Congress would absolutely push back against that, on both sides of the aisle, actually."

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: 36 years later: Hungary opens Communist-era secret service files
World.content:
Decades after the end of Soviet rule, Hungary is releasing all its secret service files. The disclosure is sparking fresh debate about informants, guilt and responsibility.

On November 4, 1956, tens of thousands of Soviet soldiers and tanks swept into Hungary, brutally suppressing the country's anti-Communist uprising. Decades of dictatorship followed, relying on Hungary's brutal secret police to keep the system in place.

Events on Nov. 4 this year represent something of a reckoning with this dark chapter of Hungarian history.

Prime Minister Peter Magyar's government is ordering the full release of the country's secret police "agent files," which contain the names of Hungarian state security informants, some of whom cooperated out of their own volition even as others passed on information unwittingly.

In 1956, Hungarians tried to stop Soviet tanks with cobble stone barricades Image: AP Photo/picture alliance

Magyar and his Tisza party had previously promised to make the "agent files" public if elected. Their release is an historic event, as it comes after over three decades of heated debate over how to handle such sensitive files. The decision to publish is also sure to spark further debate on Communist-era guilt and responsibility.

Release opposed for years

Hungarians have been calling for the release of the files for years. After the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989 and the end of Soviet rule, civil rights activists and smaller Hungarian political parties said the files should be released. Demands for their publication were expressed repeatedly over following decades.

Yet Hungary's first post-Communist prime minister Jozsef Antall, a conservative, rejected the idea as did Viktor Orban's long-ruling Fidesz party. The latter blocked efforts to open the files, voting more than 30 times against such plans since 2010, according to Hungarian news platform Telex.

A partial release of state security files did occur in the 1990s, when the Hungarian parliament passed the so-called "agents law" in 1994. This required members of the government, members of parliament and certain public servants to undergo background checks to determine whether they had ever worked for the former state security services.

From 1997, Hungarian citizens have been able to view their own files and in 2003, permissions were expanded. But they have never been able to find out the names of informants.

The law relevant to the files contained provisions that were open to broad interpretation, which allowed government agencies such as the Ministry of Interior to prevent the transfer of files from the secret police to the Historical Archives of the Hungarian State Security, or ABTL, if they believed it would compromise national security.

Such a selective release of files not only prevented Hungarian society from learning the truth about its state security service, it also made it possible for files to be exploited in political power struggles, for example, by leaking compromising information about politicians to the public.

Viktor Orban's Fidesz party never supported making the 'agent files' public Image: Balint Szentgallay/NurPhoto/picture alliance

One such case involved former Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Medgyessy, who was exposed by the Fidesz-affiliated daily Magyar Nemzet in 2002 for having worked as a Communist-era secret agent.

Political fallout expected

Magyar's government is putting an end to this. From Nov. 4, databases containing all the names of, and key information about, informants will be made available online.

Additional databases will be released as well. They include one of the most extensive databases on individuals recruited to work for the Hungarian state security agency. Confidentiality provisions set out in the old "agent law" have also been scaled back, meaning significantly more files will likely be accessible in the future.

The upcoming release of data on up to 60,000 out of an estimated 150,000 secret police informants could have major political consequences. Even so, ABTL director Bendeguz Gergo Cseh recently cautioned that, "you can't believe everything the state security agencies and their files claim." Many documents were incomplete and not fully reliable and many files had been destroyed, he said.

Others are also skeptical about the release. Historian Janos M. Rainer, an expert on Hungary's dictatorship, told Telex that the publication would have made sense right after the fall of the regime. Releasing the files after all these years is more of a symbolic gesture, he argued.

Meanwhile historian Krisztian Ungvary, who has researched the state security files extensively, welcomes the upcoming publication. It will allow historians to pursue new research and society to engage in fresh debates, Ungvary told DW. He believes Hungary will benefit from such reflection, as "societal lies inevitably lead to a strained relationship with politics and the price we paid for that was 16 years of Fidesz rule."

Defendants are questioned by a judge in Budapest on March 9, 1957, during the first show trial held after the 1956 Hungarian uprising Image: MTI/picture alliance

Political reckoning
