World.title: Sabah suffers defeat to Viking in Champions League
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 5. Azerbaijani club Sabah suffered a heavy defeat in the fourth round of the UEFA Champions League league phase.

Valdas Dambrauskas' side lost 4-1 away to Norway's Viking.

The match was held at Lyse Arena in Stavanger.

As a result, Sabah have suffered their third defeat in four league-phase matches of the Champions League and remain on three points.

World.title: Android's market share in Azerbaijan falls to 54.9% in October
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 5. The Android operating system’s market share in Azerbaijan has declined.

According to Trend’s calculations based on data from the Global Stats analytics platform, as of the end of October 2026, Android’s share of the Azerbaijani market fell by 1.55 percentage points compared to the previous month, reaching 54.9%.

Nevertheless, Android retained its leading position among operating systems in Azerbaijan. Microsoft Windows took second place, with its market share declining by 0.16 percentage points over the month to 29.51%.

iOS ranked third with a market share of 11.71%. Compared to September, this figure increased by 1.23 percentage points.

According to data from Global Stats, as of the end of October 2026, Android also retained its leadership in the global operating system market. Microsoft Windows took second place, and iOS took third.

According to information published on Android's official website, Android 17 is the current major version of the operating system. Google continues to release updates for this version. On October 2, 2026, Android 17 QPR 3 Beta 1 was released, marking the latest quarterly update for supported devices.

"As we continue to build on the initial release of Android 17, we are updating the platform by addressing identified issues and implementing improvements that will subsequently become available on supported devices. These updates are released quarterly as part of the Quarterly Platform Releases (QPR) program and become available both in AOSP and on Google Pixel devices as part of Feature Drops.

Although these updates do not contain API changes that affect app functionality, we provide images of the latest QPR beta versions so that developers can test their apps on these builds if necessary. This is particularly relevant when planning to implement new features that could impact the user experience," the statement reads.

World.title: Chronicles of Victory: November 5, 2020
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 5. The Azerbaijani Army launched a counter-offensive operation, later called the "Iron Fist", on September 27, 2020, in response to the large-scale provocation of the Armenian armed forces along the frontline.

The 44-day second Karabakh war ended with the liberation of Azerbaijan’s territories from nearly 30-year Armenian occupation and the restoration of territorial integrity.

Chronicle of the 40th day of the Second Karabakh War:

- President Aliyev gave an interview to the Spanish EFE news agency.

- The fighting continued mainly in the direction of Aghdara and Khojavand.

- Armenia violated ceasefire on the state border with Azerbaijan

- Armenian armed forces shelled Goranboy, Tartar, and Aghjabadi.

- A person injured as a result of Armenian aggression died in Barda.

- The number of Azerbaijani civilians killed as a result of the Armenian aggression reached 92.

- Armenian armed forces shelled the villages of Tartar and Aghdam districts.

- A video of new military equipment abandoned by Armenian armed forces on the battlefield was released.

- Video of the liberated villages of Fuzuli and Khojavand districts was released.

- Video of the destruction of the Armenian military infrastructure in Tonashen village was released.

- Armenian military column was ambushed and destroyed near Aghdara.

- The battery of the 41st artillery regiment of Armenian armed forces was destroyed.

World.title: Azerbaijani Parliament Committee discusses draft state budget for 2027 (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 4. On November 4, the Milli Majlis (parliament) Committee on Economic Policy, Industry and Entrepreneurship discussed the draft law “On the State Budget of the Republic of Azerbaijan for 2027.”

As reported by the Public Relations and Press Department of the Milli Majlis, the meeting was attended by committee members, representatives of political parties represented in parliament, as well as heads and representatives of relevant government agencies.

Opening the meeting, Chairman of the Committee on Economic Policy, Industry and Entrepreneurship Azer Amiraslanov said that the 2027 budget package had been submitted to the Milli Majlis in accordance with the procedure established by law, while the Chamber of Accounts had prepared its opinions on the budget documents.

Speaking about the key parameters of the 2027 state budget, the committee chairman noted that budget revenues are projected at 39.2 billion manats and expenditures at 42.4 billion manats. This represents a 1.7% increase in both revenues and expenditures compared to the approved 2026 budget. The upper limit of the state budget deficit is set at approximately 3.2 billion manats.

He emphasized that the budget package provides a solid financial foundation for implementing the initiatives put forward by President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev, the state programs defined by him, and the strategic objectives facing the country. It was noted that the budget package reflects a further strengthening of the state's social policy next year. This is evidenced by the fact that 18.7 billion manats, or 44.2% of total expenditures, are allocated to social purposes. This amount is 1.6 billion manats, or 9.2%, higher than the 2026 figure. At the same time, the state budget also prioritizes national security and defense. Capital expenditures in the 2027 state budget are set at 13.8 billion manats, or 32.5% of total expenditures.

Speaking about the importance of ensuring budget sustainability, the committee chairman noted that full compliance with budget rules, increasing the share of non-oil revenues to more than 60% of budget receipts in 2027, covering 90.1% of current expenditures through non-oil and gas revenues, and reducing the transfer from the State Oil Fund by 935 million manats are the main factors reflecting qualitative changes in the budget.

Finance Minister Sahil Babayev then presented the draft law “On the State Budget of the Republic of Azerbaijan for 2027” and the documents included in the budget package.

The minister noted that under the leadership of the head of state, the country's socio-economic development is being ensured across all areas. Azerbaijan is transforming into a powerful and more economically developed state, better able to ensure the well-being of its population. The framework for ongoing structural, institutional, economic and social reforms is also envisaged for the coming period, both in the state budget and within the medium-term expenditure framework.

He said that the main principles of the 2027 budget policy, developed under the leadership of President Ilham Aliyev, include supporting sustainable economic growth, maintaining macroeconomic stability, fully financing measures to improve public welfare and support the social sector, strengthening defense capabilities and ensuring security, developing the Karabakh and East Zangezur economic regions, expanding the use of digital technologies and innovation, supporting the development of education and healthcare, complying with the budget rule while maintaining fiscal discipline, ensuring targeted and efficient execution of budget expenditures through the State Treasury, and further accelerating the development of the real sector of the economy.

Regarding the key macroeconomic indicators for 2027, it was noted that the country's gross domestic product (GDP) is projected to reach 141 billion manats next year, representing real growth of 2.7% compared to 2026. GDP in the non-oil and gas sector is forecast at 109.1 billion manats, indicating real growth of 4.4% compared to 2026. The average annual price of a barrel of crude oil for next year is set at $65. Average annual inflation is projected at 5.3%.

Currently, total public debt stands at 23.9 billion manats, down 2.8% compared to the beginning of this year. Of the total debt portfolio, 16.2 billion manats account for domestic public debt and 7.7 billion manats for external public debt. As of October 1 this year, strategic foreign exchange reserves had reached $89.4 billion. Next year's revenues of the State Oil Fund are projected at $7.8 billion, expenditures at $7.1 billion, and transfers from the Fund at $7 billion.

It was noted that one of the key priorities of budget policy is to further reduce dependence on oil. To this end, the Azerbaijani government is implementing consistent and targeted measures. Next year, the ratio of the consolidated budget's non-oil primary deficit to non-oil GDP is expected to stand at 17.1%, while the share of non-oil revenues in the consolidated budget is projected to reach 64.5%.

The minister noted that budget expenditures had been structured in line with the country's socio-economic needs. According to him, consolidated budget expenditures will amount to 46.2% of non-oil GDP. Capital expenditures will account for 32.5% of the state budget. Education and healthcare expenditures will reach 3.6% and 1.5% of GDP, respectively. Next year, allocations to the agricultural sector will amount to 15.8% of agricultural GDP.

It was also reported that the dependence of districts on subsidies would be fully eliminated in next year's state budget. The subsidy allocated to Nakhchivan will be reduced by 13.6 million manats, or 6.4%, compared to the current year.

S. Babayev noted that consolidated budget revenues would reach 47.6 billion manats next year, an increase of 2.6 billion manats, or 5.9%, compared to 2026. The share of revenues in GDP will reach 33.8%, 1.2 percentage points higher than the 2026 figure. The share of non-oil revenues in the consolidated budget will reach 64.5%, up 1.5 percentage points compared to the current year.

State budget revenues are projected to increase by 645 million manats compared to the current year. Their share in GDP is forecast at 27.8%.

Non-oil sector revenues are expected to amount to 23.8 billion manats, or 60.6% of total revenues. The ratio of non-oil revenues to non-oil GDP will stand at 21.8%. Oil sector revenues will amount to 15.5 billion manats, or 39.4% of total budget revenues.

Meanwhile, receipts through the State Tax Service are expected to reach 18.4 billion manats, or 47% of total revenues, representing an increase of 1.5 billion manats, or 9%, compared to the current year. Receipts through the State Customs Committee will amount to 6.9 billion manats, or 17.1% of budget revenues, while transfers from the State Oil Fund will total 11.9 billion manats, or 30.3% of budget receipts.

Next year, dividend revenues from state-owned enterprises are projected at 872 million manats, revenues from paid services provided by budget-funded organizations at 949 million manats, and other revenues at 484 million manats.

The minister then presented information on next year's consolidated and state budget expenditures. It was noted that consolidated budget expenditures are projected at 50.4 billion manats, 1.5 billion manats higher than in the current year.

State budget expenditures are set at 42.4 billion manats, an increase of 696.4 million manats, or 1.7%, compared to the current year. They will account for 30.1% of GDP and 38.9% of non-oil GDP.

In the structure of state budget expenditures, current expenditures are projected at 26.4 billion manats, or 62.3% of total expenditures. Socially oriented expenditures will amount to 18.7 billion manats, or 44.2%. Capital expenditures are projected at 13.8 billion manats. Public debt servicing costs are estimated at 2.2 billion manats. The finance minister also presented expenditure figures by functional classification of the budget.

Chairman of the Central Bank Taleh Kazimov then addressed the meeting.

According to him, despite the challenging global situation, economic growth continued in Azerbaijan during the first nine months of 2026. During this period, GDP increased by 1.5%, while the non-oil and gas sector grew by 2.6%. The country's foreign trade surplus amounted to $10.5 billion, while strategic foreign exchange reserves increased by 5.1%, reaching $89.4 billion.

It was noted that this year, monetary policy, through monetary conditions, was also aimed at keeping inflation within the target range. Exchange rate stability was maintained in the foreign exchange market during the reporting period of 2026.

It was also emphasized that the expansion of banking sector assets during 2026 contributed to supporting economic activity. In particular, over the 10-month period, banking sector assets increased by 15.1%, reaching 65.7 billion manats. In addition, insurance premiums rose by 8% in the first nine months of this year compared to the same period last year, while insurance payouts increased by 29%. Total trading turnover in the securities market amounted to 35 billion manats. The overall volume of stock market transactions increased ninefold, reaching 2.6 billion manats.

T. Kazimov then presented forecasts regarding the expected macroeconomic policy for 2027. According to the Central Bank's projections, the country's GDP will grow by 2.3% in 2027, while non-oil and gas GDP will increase by 4.3%. The current account surplus is projected at $5.4 billion, while annual inflation is forecast at 5.9%.

Commenting on the 2027 budget draft, he generally gave a positive assessment of the presented macro-fiscal framework for 2027 and the medium-term period. He noted that conservative growth and optimization of public expenditures, a gradual reduction in oil transfers, an increase in the share of non-oil sources in budget revenues, and keeping the budget deficit and public debt at manageable levels contribute to strengthening fiscal sustainability.

Head of Staff of the Ministry of Economy Elvin Jamalov then addressed the meeting. He spoke about the qualitative changes that had taken place in the economy during the reporting period.

It was reported that private sector investment in fixed capital amounted to 14.7 billion manats, increasing by 10.9% in real terms. Private investment in the non-oil and gas sector grew by approximately 21%. It was also noted that the main drivers of growth in the non-oil and gas sector were non-oil industry, logistics and digital services.

At the same time, it was emphasized that the full execution of state budget expenditures, including capital expenditures, by the end of the year is an important factor affecting the pace of economic growth.

Excluding the State Oil Fund's gold transactions, non-oil and gas exports increased by 20.5% over the first nine months, reaching $3.2 billion, of which 60% accounted for industrial products. The foreign trade surplus, excluding the Fund's gold transactions, increased by 25%, reaching $7.1 billion.

It was noted that tax revenue targets for the first nine months of this year were fulfilled by 107.2%, including 102.9% in the non-oil and gas sector. At the same time, 80.6% of the annual forecast had already been achieved. Tax revenues increased by 9.4%, while taxes collected from the non-oil and gas sector rose by 12.6%.

At the committee meeting, Chairman of the Chamber of Accounts Vugar Gulmammadov presented the Chamber's opinion on the draft state budget of the Republic of Azerbaijan for 2027. It was noted that the draft law, prepared in accordance with legislation, had been analyzed article by article, revealing the need to improve certain provisions.

Vugar Gulmammadov said that, unlike previous years, the explanatory section of the budget package provided a more specific definition of fiscal risk, while the degree of impact and probability of occurrence of such risks had been assessed in line with international recommendations.

During the discussion, the deputy chairman of the Committee on Economic Policy, Industry and Entrepreneurship, other MPs, and representatives of political parties also spoke. They shared their views, assessments and proposals regarding next year's state budget draft and raised a number of questions.

Finance Minister Sahil Babayev, Central Bank Chairman Taleh Kazimov, Chairman of the State Customs Committee Shahin Baghirov, Executive Director of the State Oil Fund Israfil Mammadov, Head of Staff of the Ministry of Economy Elvin Jamalov, and Chairman of the Chamber of Accounts Vugar Gulmammadov provided explanations on the issues raised during the speeches.

Following the discussions, the draft law “On the State Budget of the Republic of Azerbaijan for 2027” was recommended for consideration by the Milli Majlis at a plenary session in its first reading.

World.title: Azerbaijani gymnasts make successful start at world championships (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 4. The World Championships in trampoline gymnastics and tumbling are being held in Nanjing, China, from November 4 to 8.

As reported by the Azerbaijan Gymnastics Federation, members of the Azerbaijani national team are also competing for medals at the prestigious event, which has brought together the world's top gymnasts.

Azerbaijan is represented in the mixed synchronized trampoline event by 2026 World Cup series winners Seljan Mahsudova and Mahsud Mahsudov. Mahsud Mahsudov and Huseyn Abbasov, who also hold the same title, will compete in the men's synchronized event. In addition, Seljan Mahsudova and Mahsud Mahsudov will showcase their skills in the individual event.

The national tumbling team includes two-time world champions in the team event Mikhail Malkin, Tofiq Aliyev, Adil Hajizade and Alexey Karatashov. The experienced gymnasts are determined to achieve further success in both individual and team competitions.

It should be noted that Alexey Karatashov is making his World Championships debut in the senior category.

The first qualification day of the championships brought successful results for Azerbaijani gymnasts. Competing in the mixed synchronized trampoline event, Seljan Mahsudova and Mahsud Mahsudov scored 50.250 points to secure their places in the semifinals.

Azerbaijan's tumbling representatives also delivered confident performances. Tofiq Aliyev topped the qualification round with a score of 59.500 points, advancing to the next stage. Mikhail Malkin, scoring 57.100 points, finished fourth and qualified for the second qualification round.

Azerbaijani gymnasts also achieved a successful result in the team competition. The national tumbling team scored a total of 87.200 points, topped the standings and secured a place in the final.

On November 5, the individual trampoline events will get underway. This time, Seljan Mahsudova and Mahsud Mahsudov will represent Azerbaijan in the individual competitions.

World.title: Greens senator Jordon Steele-John's ex-partner charged with stalking
World.content:
A 40-year-old woman is due to appear in court today, charged with aggravated stalking of Western Australian Greens senator Jordon Steele-John.

Police will allege the Perth woman was a former partner of Senator Steele-John.

Detectives from the WA Police Family Violence Investigation Squad said they charged the Perth woman with one count each of "aggravated stalking with intent to intimidate" and "demanding property by written threats".

The woman will appear before the Perth Magistrates Court today.

Senator Steele-John took leave from the parliament in October after a group of current and former party staffers wrote to Greens leader David Shoebridge about "multiple allegations of serious misconduct" by Senator Steele-John relating to "his behaviour in the presence of women".

Senator Steele-John has denied the allegations, including in a lengthy and since-deleted letter posted to social media.

An independent inquiry into the allegations has been commissioned by the WA branch of the Greens.

Senator Shoebridge has previously said leave was appropriate in the circumstances and he would not prejudge the inquiry.

World.title: Mount Morgan residents welcome new water pipeline after drought
World.content:
Mount Morgan retiree Christina O'Leary is no stranger to a drought.

The 85-year-old, who's lived in the old goldmining town for most of her life, remembers her father carting buckets of water from the public well to keep her mother's parched garden alive during prolonged periods of dry weather.

"Don't ask me what I did yesterday but I can still see Dad walking down there," she said.

The town of Mount Morgan, 40 kilometres south-west of Rockhampton, had traditionally relied on water from the No 7 Dam and domestic rainwater tanks for its supply.

Long-term resident Christine O'Leary has lived through multiple droughts. (ABC Capricornia: Jacob Gamble)

"I can still remember when I was a little kid … bathing in the [used laundry] water," she said.

Due to a lack of rain, the dam levels dropped in 2021, as low as 10 per cent, and residents were placed on the maximum level-6 water restrictions.

"[The town] was very dry and desolate looking, almost desert-looking," Ms O'Leary said.

The council had to cart water to Mount Morgan from 2021 to 2024, due to a prolonged drought. (ABC Capricornia: Jasmine Hines)

Rockhampton Regional Council resorted to trucking water into town at a cost of $17,000 a day.

The harsh water restrictions were in place for three years, until 2024.

Ms O'Leary said being "conscious" of water use had become a way of life — but residents are hopeful that's now changed.

This week, representatives from all levels of government announced a long-awaited $88 million pipeline project had been completed, bringing treated water from a Rockhampton reservoir.

The pipeline will see the local dam transition to purely recreational use and promises to deliver more reliable supply.

Glen Kelly said the years of drought were tough on Mount Morgan residents. (ABC Capricornia: Jacob Gamble)

"Rocky's bathtub is a lot bigger [than the Mount Morgan No7 Dam]," state member for Mirani Glen Kelly said.

"When you have reliable, safe water, it doesn't just help industry or [the] likes of our hospital or [the] likes of the businesses in Mount Morgan.

"It supports the communities, the people that live in that town."

Mount Morgan residents have campaigned for a permanent water supply for years. (Image: Vanessa Jarrett)

'Water security is everything'

Mount Morgan was once a bustling hub in central Queensland, generating enormous wealth from the goldmine.

The town experienced an exodus after the mine closed in 1990, but a revival operation has sparked hope for future employment prospects.

Resident Kirra Swain has been campaigning for years for the town to have its own water pipeline and said it would deliver more certainty for future residents.

"Along with the pipeline, the mine was always a pipe dream … a lot of locals never thought it would happen," she said.

" The pipeline is a massive, massive bonus to our town and we're so grateful that it's finally come to fruition. "

The art gallery manager said much of the town's social and economic livelihood was dependent on the dam.

"We've got our little art gallery … it relies on tourism [and] the dam is a massive drawcard for that," she said.

"Water security is everything in a small town like this."

Regional water infrastructure struggles

While Mount Morgan residents welcomed the announcement, other regional towns continue to face repeated water restrictions due to drought and aging infrastructure.

Isaac Regional Council has been forced to issue multiple different warnings and water restrictions to Clermont residents since August, after a run of water infrastructure failures.

Most recently, rainfall and run-off into the Theresa Creek Dam affected the raw water quality and the Clermont Water Treatment Plant had trouble treating and processing the water.

In a notice published on Wednesday, the plant said it was producing treated water again but residents were still asked to conserve water were possible.

Specialist divers had been on site and were undertaking further work on the dam's intake structure.

In Far North Queensland, the Northern Peninsula Area Regional Council last month began shutting off water to its communities for 12 hours from 9pm due to "dangerously low" reservoir levels and aging infrastructure.

At the same time, its mayor and councillors lobbied the federal government for more funding to upgrade water infrastructure

The new pipeline was jointly funded by the local council and state and federal governments. (ABC Capricornia: Jacob Gamble)

Queensland Minister for Water Ann Leahy acknowledged that water insecurity was an ongoing issue for regional communities, but said the government was listening to local councils.

"Trying to find people like water engineers for regional communities is always a challenge," she said.

"The cost increases [are a challenge] as well."

World.title: Breaking: Retailer's future in doubt as David Jones calls in administrators
World.content:
Australian retailer David Jones has been placed into administration.

The 188-year-old department store's collapse comes after negotiations with key landlord Westfield broke down.

The department store's chief executive is addressing staff this morning at the company's Melbourne headquarters.

The retailer is behind on rental payments and its collapse will leave staff and suppliers such as fashion brands in the dark.

It is expected to rationalise store numbers, with it currently having 38 sites.

McGrath Nicol have been appointed as voluntary administrators and separately its secured lender Hilco has appointed Christopher Hill, David McGrath and Joanne Dunn of FTI Consulting as Joint and Several Receivers and Managers.

The union that represents retail workers, the Shop, Distributive and Allied (SDA) Employees Association, said its immediate focus was on keeping as many people in jobs as possible.

The outlook for shoppers if David Jones goes under If David Jones goes belly-up, consumers could be out of pocket. Here's what the experts say shoppers should consider to avoid a Christmas nightmare.

National secretary Gerard Dwyer said the SDA was seeking to "protect and prioritise" the legal and financial entitlements of any workers affected by redundancies.

The union said it was pursuing two key objectives: preserving jobs wherever possible, and ensuring workers received all entitlements owed to them if positions were lost.

Mr Dwyer said the SDA welcomed the federal government's payday super reforms, arguing they would help protect workers from losing up to three months of unpaid superannuation in the event of a company collapse.

World.title: Cyber attack hits French blood banks but no blood products compromised
World.content:
The refrigerators at three regional blood banks in France were hit by a cyber attack overnight from Sunday into Monday, at the same time hackers struck supermarkets from Sweden to Belgium.

"Several regional facilities of the French Blood Establishment (EFS) were affected by a cybersecurity incident that impacted certain cold storage room monitoring and control systems," the health ministry said in a statement.

French food retailers targeted by hackers Several major food retailers in France are targeted by hackers who raised fridge temperatures to 50 degrees Celsius.

The incident had no effect on blood supplies, EFS spokesperson Charley Dubois said.

"We have staff round the clock since blood can be needed at any time. They were warned about the problems by alerts and moved the blood to other refrigerators that were not connected," she said.

Around the same time, hackers tampered with refrigerators at stores in eight European countries, forcing retailers to discard large quantities of food, in an attack that echoed an incident affecting dozens of supermarkets in France three weeks earlier.

The situation was under control on Wednesday, local time, the health ministry said, adding that remote access to the affected refrigerators had been disabled.

Investigations are underway into how the attack was carried out, what equipment may have been affected and when systems can safely return to service.

The attack followed a similar incident in France last month when police said hackers seized control of cooling units at hundreds of supermarkets, causing fires and food losses.

The French Blood Establishment, whose headquarters are pictured here, says the cyber attack was thwarted before it could do any damage. (AP: Christophe Ena)

The incidents have raised concerns in the European Union about previously unknown vulnerabilities in connected infrastructure amid growing security tensions since Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

Reuters

World.title: Crocodile's day trip to popular resort island sparks commotion
World.content:
A saltwater crocodile has caused a commotion at one of Queensland's most popular tourist islands, forcing snorkellers out of the water and a resort to ramp up safety precautions.

A 2-metre croc was spotted close to the shore of Fitzroy Island, 29 kilometres off Cairns, on Monday, prompting resort and ferry staff to issue warnings and erect signage.

Far North Queensland is famous for its crocodiles, but sightings near the island are rare, with the last known occasion at the popular snorkelling and swimming spot nearly two years ago.

Fitzroy Island National Park is a 45-minute boat trip from Cairns and is popular with locals and tourists. (Supplied: Colliers)

Bundaberg-based sailor Mark Fletcher was among those who saw the crocodile while his yacht was anchored off the island on Monday.

He was in the water to inspect a faulty propeller when he heard people screaming from the shore.

"[I] got back on the boat and there were some people standing on the staircase who had a full view of the ocean, and they were screaming out, 'Crocodile, crocodile,'" Mr Fletcher said.

He took his dinghy to the beach to investigate and was told the crocodile had been heading towards him, before changing course towards two snorkellers who got out of the water after hearing the yelling.

"I didn't really know it was in the water when I was in the water," Mr Fletcher said.

" It was only after I thought about it that I could have been in a bit of strife. "

Safely back on his yacht, Mr Fletcher saw the croc pop up again a short distance away.

"It just floated along the beach, about 20 metres off, looking at people — people standing up at the back of the beach like crows on a power line — and it just floated past, not a worry in the world," he said.

'Crazy experience'

Scottish tourist Kyle O'Shea, 23, described seeing the crocodile as "surreal" and a "core memory" that would stay with him forever.

He and his girlfriend travelled to the island on Monday after flying from their home in Glasgow to fulfil their dream of visiting Australia.

As the couple lined up at the Cairns marina to board their ferry to the island, a crew member advised a crocodile had been spotted that morning.

"And then when we were on the boat heading to the island, they also told us again that there was a crocodile," Mr O'Shea said.

" They said that you can still go in the water, it's up to you, but they advise not to. "

Upon arriving at the island, they encountered more warnings from staff and on freshly erected signage.

Warning signs will remain on the island for seven days after a sighting. (Supplied: Kyle O'Shea)

Mr O'Shea said he and his girlfriend were initially a bit disappointed their snorkelling plans had been "ruined".

"Once we get told there's a crocodile, [my partner was] just like, 'No, not a chance,'" he said.

But he said their disappointment was soon eclipsed by the excitement of seeing the crocodile "bobbing on the waves" as they were sitting on some rocks near the shore.

"Somebody pointed over and I was like, 'Oh, what's she pointing at?'" Mr O'Shea said.

"You could see everything, you could see the tail with the spikes on it.

" It was a surreal experience for me, just a crazy experience … I think crocodiles are amazing. "

'Rare' sighting prompts safety measures

In a statement, Fitzroy Island Resort said crocodile sightings near its shores were "rare", but it was treating the incident seriously.

It said the resort had reinforced existing safety and communication procedures, including regular shoreline inspections, ongoing checks from its vessels and regular communication with resort guests, day-tour operators and passengers.

"Although these sightings are uncommon, we are well equipped to manage them and will continue to monitor the situation closely, continuing regular contact with Parks and Wildlife authorities and following their advice," general manager Dallas Bickle said.

Queensland's Environment Department confirmed it was investigating the sighting and was continuing to monitor the area.

Mr Bickle said the crocodile was thought to be a young male searching for new territory during breeding season and had not been seen again near the island since Monday night.

He said it was the second sighting he had dealt with in his three years in the role, the last one being in late 2024.

The crocodile was a holiday highlight for Scottish tourists Kyle O'Shea and Chelsea Kerr. (Supplied: Kyle O'Shea)

Both Mr Fletcher and Mr O'Shea said they were satisfied with the resort's handling of the situation and its efforts to warn guests.

Mr O'Shea said the experience had not deterred him from returning to Australia.

"If anything, it's inspired me to come back because Cairns is a lovely place and I just love crocodiles," he said.

World.title: Outback town abandoned after council 'drops the ball'
World.content:
Sharing a house with her adult children, 57-year-old Waluwarra woman Michele Belia just wants to go home.

"I'm living in town here in Mount Isa, but I want to go back," she said.

Ms Belia's home in Urandangi, about two hours' drive south-west of Mount Isa, was one of about 15 homes destroyed in March 2023 when more than 7 metres of floodwaters inundated the town.

Urandangi was barely visible in the floods that inundated the region in March 2023. (Supplied: Tobermorey Station)

A lack of suitable housing and drinking water is stopping her and the other residents from returning.

For Ms Belia, there was the added pain of being away from where her family was buried and where she built her life.

"My brother's there, my mum, and all my cousins, my auntie and my uncle are there [buried]," she said.

"[In 2003], I bought a block [at Urandangi] … I said to my mum, 'I'm going back home,' and Mum said, 'I'm coming too, I'm following you'.

"I thought she was joking, but she chucked all her gear in the car, and she came with me. She was so happy to be home."

Previously a teacher aide at Urandangi State School, Michele Belia says she had built a life in the regional town. (ABC News: Tim Little)

A forgotten town

Sitting on the banks of the Georgina River, near the Queensland–Northern Territory border, Urandangi was established in 1885 as an outpost for cattle drovers.

At its peak in the 1930s and 40s, the town was home to as many as 400 people, but the rise of cars and the decline of large-scale droving saw its population dwindle.

By 2023, about 20 permanent residents remained, with the outpost regularly accommodating up to 50 people who travelled between Urandangi and Alpurrurulam in the Northern Territory.

The Urandangi Hotel glued the town together, serving as the grocery store, post office and only pub for more than 300 kilometres.

A slow-moving tropical low brought heavy rain across the Georgina catchment in 2023. (Supplied: Tobermorey Station)

But in March that year, torrential rain across the catchment saw the Georgina River rise to more than 7 metres, forcing the evacuation of the entire community.

The devastating event, which authorities said was on par with the 1974 record flood, was three months after another major peak.

Today, little remains of the historic town.

The severe water damage destroyed about half of the town’s 40-odd homes and buildings.

None are habitable.

No residents are currently living in the outback town; its displaced people are dotted across Brisbane, Boulia and Mount Isa.

Urandangi residents are pushing local, state and federal governments to try to reopen their town. (ABC News: Tim Little)

The local state school was one of the few buildings to survive.

In a statement, the Department of Education said Urandangi State School, which had eight students enrolled in 2023, was in working condition and could be reopened if needed.

'We dropped the ball'

Disconnected from the grid and two hours' drive from the nearest health clinic, Urandangi's isolation makes delivering essential services an expensive exercise.

Before the floods, Boulia Shire Council provided regular rubbish collection, treated bore water and sewerage services to the remote community.

But from December 2024, the council stopped supplying drinking water and most other services to the deserted township.

Mayor Rick Britton said bacterial testing required to maintain a safe drinking water supply was too difficult for the resource-strapped council.

He estimated restoring services would cost about $500,000 a year.

Boulia Shire Council Mayor Rick Britton said the floodwaters were very slow moving. (ABC News: Leonie Mellor)

"We've dropped the ball on the traditional owners … but our capacity to keep that township and deliver those services is very limited," he said.

With 500 ratepayers across the shire's 61,000 square kilometres, Cr Britton said tough decisions had to be made.

Boulia Shire Council continues to maintain the airstrip and cemetery. (Supplied: Boulia Shire Council)

"Even trying to get a permanent employee to live there [is impossible] … the lack of water, lack of electricity, lack of normal liveability," he said.

"We're willing to sit at the table, but it's got to be funded by either the state or federal government to the cent."

A federal government spokesperson said state and local authorities were responsible for coordinating water infrastructure.

"State and territory governments are primarily responsible for managing water within their jurisdictions and for bringing forward water infrastructure proposals to the federal government for funding consideration through the National Water Grid Fund," they said.

A spokesperson for Queensland's Minister for Local Government, Ann Leahy, said nearly $9 million was given to the Boulia Shire after the 2023 flooding from disaster recovery arrangements, including $35,000 to drill a new bore in Urandangi.

'Shouldn't be fighting for water'

Regardless of the new bore, Cr Britton said the costs lay with the treatment regime the council needed to follow to make water potable.

For Ms Belia and the other 18 residents wanting to go home, access to water remained the biggest barrier.

"I'm not going back until they put the water back on," she said.

Residents and visitors were taken by helicopter to a nearby airstrip and flown via light aircraft to Mount Isa during the flooding. (Supplied)

Frustrated at the lack of progress, they turned to Mount Isa-based Indigenous advocacy group Camp Fire Healing for help.

Director Markeesh De Busch accused all levels of government of abandoning the community.

She said the upheaval, more than three years later, was "causing so much bloody grief".

Residents have turned to Mount Isa-based Indigenous community group Camp Fire Healing to help have their voices heard. (ABC News: Tim Little)

"Boulia Shire Council needs to take responsibility and allow these people, Waluwarra people, the dignity and respect to go home," Ms De Busch said.

"We as Aboriginal people are the owners of this land, but yet we can't even get water."

With no funding agreement or timeline for restoring services, Ms De Busch said the township was being erased.

"We shouldn't be fighting for water, for our people. That's not fair; it's 2026."

World.title: 'Australia's loneliest echidna' no longer solo after trail-cam discoveries
World.content:
Ranger Tasha Cooper had been learning how to trap feral cats on an island off Tasmania when she came across a discovery that sent her scrambling for her radio.

Curled up in the cage was an echidna — or trimanya in palawa kani, the language of Tasmania's Aboriginal people.

The species had not been encountered in person on the Bass Strait island in decades.

An echidna that wandered into a cage used to trap feral cats. (Supplied: Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre)

Trail cameras have since recorded echidnas at four separate locations across the island. (Supplied: Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre)

"The excitement was overwhelming. I didn't know if I was going to cry or scream or what," Ms Cooper said.

"Just to see this trimanya curled up trying to push his way out of this cage, there were just no words for it," she said.

'Australia's loneliest echidna' spotted on trail camera

An echidna dubbed "Australia's loneliest" by WWF after it was spotted on a trail camera on Lungtalanana in November 2023. (Supplied: Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre)

Lungtalanana, also known as Clarke Island, is in the Furneaux group of islands off Tasmania's north-east coast.

About 8,230 hectares in size, the island returned to Aboriginal ownership in 2005.

Pakana rangers are working to restore the island through land management practices, including weed removal, cultural burning and remote wildlife monitoring.

In 2023, a trail camera recorded two images of an echidna, captured months apart.

Increased echidna sightings across the island have excited conservation crews. (Supplied: Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre)

Due to the high number of images to review, the photos were not discovered until 2024.

It marked the first time the species had been spotted on Lungtalanana/Clarke Island in decades, and came after fears that a 2014 bushfire that burnt through 80 per cent of the island had wiped them out.

The rewilding program hopes to restore Lungatalanana/Clarke Island's vegetation, 98 per cent of which was destroyed in the 2014 bushfire. (Supplied: WWF Australia/Chris Crerar)

Conservationist group WWF Australia, which supports the island's Aboriginal-led restoration project, had labelled the echidna as "Australia's loneliest".

Following the discovery, trail camera surveillance was boosted, with an image of an echidna recorded in 2025, and a further three this year.

But it was not until Ms Cooper's encounter in September that an echidna was spotted out in the field.

Pakana ranger Tasha Cooper was overcome with excitement when she discovered an echidna in a cat trap. (Supplied: Tasha Cooper)

To determine whether the images were of a single active individual or multiple echidnas, rangers contacted University of Tasmania echidna expert Stewart Nicol.

Professor Nicol said that due to the "cryptic" nature of echidnas, it was difficult to estimate population numbers without tracking them.

"Given the size of the island that they're working on, and the fact that there's been about four or five sightings now, I'd be surprised if there were fewer than a dozen of them.

"There'd probably be more than 20 or 30 echidnas there, probably even more," Professor Nicol said.

Associate Professor Stewart Nicol tracking echidnas on a separate project. (936 ABC Hobart: Carol Rääbus)

Ambitious whole-island rewilding project

The discovery comes after the Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre last month launched the Lungtalanana Restoration Project.

Clarke Island to have wombats again in rewilding project Indigenous land managers are hoping to repatriate ecologically and culturally significant species to lungtalanana island, but feral cat predation and a lack of funding are standing in their way.

Along with the removal of invasive species and native wildlife tracking, the project is working to repair habitat and return locally extinct species such as Bass Strait wombats, Bennett's wallabies and long-nosed potoroos.

It will also create training and work opportunities for Palawa people while strengthening culture and connection to country.

It is that hoped at least six species wiped out by invasive predators, land clearing and catastrophic bushfires can be re-established on Lungtalanana/Clarke Island.

"It's going to be a huge win for us, for the Palawa community," Ms Cooper said.

Healthy Country ranger Tooarn Brown said the priority was the removal of feral cats.

"We want to make sure they're gone before we start doing any major rehabilitation," he said.

Mr Brown said the confirmation of an echidna population on the island was encouraging and showed restoration efforts were having an impact.

"It means that our management of the island, in both the native plants in the program and when it comes to getting rid of predators, are coming together and creating enough of a system where those small animals don't feel the need to just hide away," he said.

World.title: LIV Golf future in doubt as premier says Australia event likely cancelled
World.content:
The future of LIV Golf appears to be in serious doubt after reports that BC Partners, which provides financing to middle-market companies, is dropping its bid to relaunch the league.

The Financial Times reported that the private capital firm withdrew its support due to a failure to secure sufficient player commitments.

LIV Golf files for bankruptcy LIV Golf files for bankruptcy, flagging a restructure with a massive loan from the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia.

The professional men's golf league, a competitor to the PGA Tour, filed for bankruptcy protection in New Jersey in September as part of a restructuring after Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF), which has invested more than $US5 ⁠billion ($7 billion) in LIV since its launch in 2022, announced it was ending its financial backing after the 2026 season.

BC Partners's decision came as a deadline loomed to show there was enough player support to hold a tournament series in 2027, the FT said, citing people directly familiar with the matter.

The firm and LIV Golf did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment.

LIV has held four annual tournaments in Adelaide, starting in 2023, and was supposed to host an event next March at the Kooyonga Golf Club.

However, South Australia Premier Peter Malinauskas told 891 ABC Adelaide this morning that media reports suggest LIV's future, in his state at least, is over.

"I haven't had any official confirmation from LIV themselves, but I saw a report this morning, and it feels like it's game, set and match as far as I can tell," he said.

LIV Golf has died on a flawed premise and a broken promise While Adelaide showed just how good LIV Golf could be, the flawed premise of the breakaway tournament always spelled trouble.

"That's because BC Partners, that is the funders of LIV 2.0, I guess, have arrived at the same conclusion that we were, like, if you don't get the players to sign up, then it doesn't go ahead.

"As the state government, we've made clear to LIV that we're not going to be paying for an event that doesn't represent the calibre of what we've had in the past, and if the players aren't up for it, then it doesn't go ahead, and it looks like that's been the case with BC Capital Partners as well.

"The contractual arrangements between the state and LIV don't come into effect because we only pay them when we put on an event, so we don't pay for anything we don't get.

"In terms of other arrangements, we'll have to take advice on that in regard to others, but clearly the event as far as we can tell won't be going ahead at Kooyonga next year."

Former world number one Jon Rahm is among a wave of high-profile golfers who have left LIV Golf since it filed for bankruptcy protection.

LIV is expected to appear at a hearing on Thursday, local time, in US bankruptcy court in Trenton, New Jersey, to discuss various contracts, leases and assets. It is unclear whether LIV's ultimate fate may also be discussed.

In October, BC Partners made an initial investment in LIV Golf, providing up to $300 million in financing to help the league emerge from restructuring and strengthen its finances ahead of the 2027 season.

LIV Golf lured leading players from the PGA Tour, including Phil Mickelson, Bryson DeChambeau, Brooks Koepka and Dustin Johnson, with lucrative contracts.

DeChambeau, one of the biggest names on LIV's player roster, recently said the league's business model for the proposed 2.0 era "makes a lot of sense" and that he hoped that it would last "forever".

Others have been critical of LIV Golf, with DP ‌World Tour chief executive Guy Kinnings saying LIV sought to undermine the European circuit.

"They took players; they took sponsors; they turned professional golf into an arms race," Rory McIlroy told reporters earlier on Wednesday ahead of the Abu Dhabi Championship.

World.title: Live battleground tracker: The two races too close to call – and every seat the Democrats flipped
World.content:
The Democrats took firm control of the senate by flipping several key seats.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The Democrats have delivered a comprehensive blow to Donald Trump ahead of his final two years in the White House, sweeping control of the Senate and the House. Several key battleground races – particularly in the Senate – were at the heart of this emphatic Democratic Party win. Below, we track which seats were flipped, retained – and which remain in play. Follow our full live coverage of the 2026 US midterms here. STILL TO CALL Alaska Surging heating fuel, electricity and grocery prices are disproportionately whacking residents of this remote, traditionally red state. Democrat Mary Peltola, who says Alaskans endure the highest healthcare costs in the country, is facing off against Republican senator Dan Sullivan, and an unaffiliated retired teacher who goes by the same name – Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.



Mississippi Well, this is the race no one saw coming – which is why we’ve updated this list to include it. Trump won Mississippi by 23 points just two years ago, while incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith won her first term by double digits. But disaffection with Trump and the charisma of Democratic candidate Scott Colom has thrust this firmly into the too close to call category. SENATE – FLIPPED BY DEMOCRATS South Carolina: Annie Andrews This race found the spotlight for two reasons – it was a toss-up, and Republican candidate Darline Graham is the sister of the late senator Lindsey Graham. She has lost the seat to Annie Andrews - that’s a big upset in what’s typically a safe red state.



Ohio: Sherrod Brown Democratic candidate Sherrod Brown is a former senator who chaired the Senate banking committee from 2021 to 2024, when he was a vocal critic of crypto. Ad-tracking business AdImpact says the crypto sector spent $US68 million on defeating Brown. It didn’t work – he’s defeated Republican incumbent Jon Husted in a high-stakes Senate race. Texas: James Talarico Democrat James Talarico has become the first Democrat elected to the US Senate from the conservative state of Texas since 1988. He defeated Republican candidate Ken Paxton. Kansas: Adam Hamilton



A Democrat hasn’t been elected to the Senate in Kansas for 94 years – that’s something the popular pastor Adam Hamilton has just changed by taking down Republican Roger Marshall. Iowa: Josh Turek Maine: Troy Jackson In one of the last remaining moderate strongholds for Republicans, incumbent Susan Collins has historically outperformed bad polling numbers to win time and time again. But with a poor net approval rating, she was knocked out by Democrat Troy Jackson.



SENATE – HELD Michigan: Abdul El-Sayed In the swing state of Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed – a doctor, unionist and Muslim – and Republican Mike Rogers had a tight race for the Senate seat being vacated by Democrat Gary Peters. El-Sayed prevailed. Georgia: Jon Ossoff This race was cruisy for Jon Ossoff, who won re-election and has been linked with a run at the White House in 2028. He beat Republican Mike Collins.

World.title: LIV Golf thought it had a financial saviour. It’s just walked away
World.content:
SportGolfLIV Golf Series LIV Golf thought it had a financial saviour. It’s just walked away Reuters November 5, 2026 — 9:26am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

BC Partners is dropping its bid to relaunch LIV Golf due to an inability to secure enough player commitments, the Financial Times reported on Wednesday. The professional men’s golf league, a competitor to the PGA Tour, filed for bankruptcy protection in New Jersey in September as part of a restructuring after Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, which has ​invested more than $US5 ⁠billion ($7 billion) in LIV since its launch in 2022, announced it was ending its financial backing after the 2026 season. The sinking LIV Golf series has copped another financial blow. LIV has said it plans to continue operating while it reorganises. The private capital firm’s decision came as a deadline loomed to show there was enough player support to hold a tournament series in 2027, the FT said, citing people directly familiar with the matter.



Related Article World golf Former world No.1 quits LIV golf as Smith’s lawyers seek exit from old contract BC Partners – which provides financing to middle-market companies – and LIV Golf did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Former world No.1 Jon Rahm is among a wave of high-profile golfers who have left LIV Golf since it filed for bankruptcy protection. LIV is expected to appear at a Thursday hearing in US bankruptcy court in Trenton, New Jersey, to discuss various contracts, leases and assets. It is unclear whether LIV’s fate may also be discussed. In October, BC Partners made an initial investment in LIV Golf and planned to provide up to $US300 million ($428 million) in financing to help the league emerge from restructuring and strengthen its finances ahead of the 2027 season.



LIV Golf launched in 2022 with funding from Saudi Arabia and lured leading players from the PGA Tour including Phil Mickelson, Bryson DeChambeau, Brooks Koepka, Australian Cameron Smith and Dustin Johnson with lucrative contracts. DeChambeau, one of the biggest names on LIV’s player roster, said recently the business model for the league’s proposed 2.0 era “makes a lot of sense” and that he hoped that it would last “forever”. Australian Cameron Smith was one of the stars who jumped from the PGA Tour to LIV Golf. Getty Images Others have been critical of LIV Golf, with DP ‌World Tour chief executive Guy Kinnings saying that LIV had sought to undermine the European circuit. Kinnings is having to weigh up regaining some star power with unhappiness among some of his members that LIV players are just walking back onto the tour having caused so much disruption.



In an interview with The Scotsman newspaper, Kinnings accepted there was a balance to strike in integrating the returning players. “But we also have to protect the tour against an entity who spent, so we are told, over $7 billion, with one of their aims being to ‘destroy the DP World Tour,’” Kinnings said. “I have heard that from so many different people they talked to, who I have known for over 30 years within the game and who I trust implicitly. Rory McIlroy has been outspoken in his criticism of LIV Golf. Getty Images “Clearly when you are faced with statements like that, and then people then ask why we are doing what we are doing with our membership and invite policy for 2027, then I think the answer becomes pretty obvious. Myself and everyone at the DP World Tour have a duty to our members to protect our tour.” Six-time major champion Rory McIlroy, who has been outspoken against LIV Golf since its formation, backed up Kinnings’ comments.



Related Article LIV Golf Series ‘We need a few more answers’: Why Cameron Smith’s future on LIV tour is still uncertain Speaking Wednesday at the Abu Dhabi Championship, McIlroy said: “I agree with everything that Guy said. They took players, they took sponsors, they turned professional golf into an arms race. “They were going around Augusta saying they wanted to destroy the European tour.” McIlroy acknowledged that LIV’s investment had brought benefits, including the creation of the International Series on the Asian Tour, but said the latter had ultimately been left without the support it needed. “Where did that leave the Asian Tour? They left them high and dry,” he said, adding that the tour had since returned to the fold through partnerships with the PGA Tour and DP World Tour.



McIlroy said LIV’s financial model was always likely to face difficulties if investors failed to see a return or decided to redirect their money elsewhere, and that it was “ironic” that LIV Golf CEO Scott O’Neil’s motto is now “complete, not compete” – a reference to the breakaway league finding a place in golf’s ecosystem rather than trying to take over. McIlroy, 37, added the disruption caused by the breakaway league could ultimately leave men’s golf on a more sustainable footing. “For long-term sustainability for men’s professional golf, I think we are in a much better spot,” he said. World.title: Marooned in paradise: Albanese and the summit that could not have come at a worse time
World.content:
Analysis NationalPolitical leadership Marooned in paradise: Albanese and the summit that could not have come at a worse time David Crowe Updated November 5, 2026 — 9:20am ,first published 8:56am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

St John’s, Antigua and Barbuda: Nothing showed the utter isolation of Anthony Albanese and his fellow Commonwealth leaders quite like their retreat on the final day of their gathering in the Caribbean. The leaders stepped onto chartered boats to reach a private island where they could talk at a luxury resort secluded from everyone else at the Commonwealth meeting in Antigua and Barbuda. Anthony Albanese and Queen Camilla during an official dinner and reception at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in St John’s, Antigua and Barbuda on Tuesday. Getty Images Albanese did not choose the venue. As prime minister, he was right to join the other leaders at a forum Australia has supported for decades. He did not stay on the private island – his hotel was the same seaside resort as his British counterpart, Andy Burnham – and he headed for the airport to get home as soon as the retreat was over. But the gathering at Jumby Bay Island sent all the wrong signals about the Commonwealth leaders when so many of their citizens are suffering from declining living standards.



And that is a problem for Albanese when the Reserve Bank says its latest interest rate hike will feel like a recession to many households. What possessed the Commonwealth to do this? The leaders were on an island where Oprah Winfrey is rumoured to own a private chateau. A modern “cottage” at one of the hotels, with space for four people and a private pool, costs $US8200 per night (about $11,700) for those who want to book it for this Monday. You want to look out of touch to voters? Go to Jumby Bay. Jumby Bay Island, where Oprah is reported to have a holiday mansion, and cottages go for more than $8000 a night. allinclusiveoutlet.com The entire exercise highlighted the shocking waste of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, known as CHOGM, when so many people in its 56 member states live below the poverty line.



Yes, some Antiguans were glad to see the money flow into their small nation, but the gathering lifted their country’s population by about 5 per cent overnight. The talk about climate action would have ended quickly without the national desalination plant run from an electricity grid powered by diesel generators. If there is money to be spent in Antigua, it could be spent on the roads, the schools and the homes. While the beaches are every bit as beautiful as they look on Caribbean travel websites, the country is not wealthy. Who knows if the cash from hosting CHOGM will trickle down to those at the bottom? In any case, the country is hedging its bets on a search for supporters: the most impressive new housing in the capital, St John’s, is funded by China Aid. The Antigua meeting was an extravagance in hard times. It is no wonder the UK Foreign Office commissioned a study after the last CHOGM, in Samoa two years ago, to think seriously about scaling back these meetings. One top UK adviser involved in that review, Ben Judah, told Politico last week that the Commonwealth Secretariat was a “broken institution” and should take a new approach. Judah was an adviser to David Lammy, who was foreign secretary at the time of the Samoa summit.



Related Article Political leadership ‘Oh God, so it’s all my fault’: Albanese and King Charles joke over travel backlash One idea in the Foreign Office review was to hold the meetings every four or five years, perhaps aligning them with the Commonwealth Games. That looks like an idea Australia could support. The core Australian interest in the Pacific is already addressed at the annual Pacific Islands Forum. Sending prime ministers to CHOGMs in the Caribbean and Africa is not as important. Albanese was, on balance, right to go to this Commonwealth summit. Australia has played its part in the institution for decades. Albanese met Burnham as well as Canadian prime minister Mark Carney. As Carney said earlier this year, middle powers should work together at a time when America is an unpredictable ally and the old global order is splintering. Anthony Albanese met with Canadian Prime Minister mark Carney at CHOGM. Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press via AP “If we’re not at the table, we’re on the menu,” Carney said. That message could guide the Commonwealth to becoming more ambitious or useful. Even Carney, however, was prudent about how long he spent in Antigua: he flew in on Monday night and left on Tuesday night, skipping the retreat because he had to oversee a budget at home.



Albanese should have been equally cautious about spending too much time away. In a remark caught on camera, he told King Charles why he was there: because the King had asked him personally. There were other reasons, of course, including the ambition to secure votes around the world to put Australia on the United Nations Security Council. The trouble is that Albanese was in Antigua from Saturday night to Wednesday night. Who in Australia would be any worse off if he had arrived in Antigua a day later and skipped the private island retreat at the end? Nobody. When the Commonwealth leaders issued their statement at the end of the gathering, it looked inconsequential. There was some adjusted language on slavery and some fine words about climate. There was a slightly stronger message about “reparatory justice” for slavery, given Burnham said he was open to a discussion about an apology. But there was nothing substantial enough to justify the exorbitant use of time and money on so many days at so many resorts by so many leaders. Loading



Unfortunately for Albanese and the government, he cannot skip the next few summits. He has to attend the UN Climate Change Conference in Turkey, even if it would have been wiser to avoid co-hosting the event. Then he has to fly to the East Asia Summit in the Philippines on November 16-18 and go on to the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting in China on November 18-19. Then there’s the G20 with Donald Trump in Miami on December 14–15. All prime ministers face demands to spend more time on global problems, and most fall into the habit of travelling to more summits. But the political danger rises sharply when times are tough. Albanese, caught in a mid-term slump with low growth and high inflation, already faces a backlash over his travel. It will probably get worse. Spending too much time on the global stage will weaken Labor at home. If this means Albanese loses more of his personal standing in the polls, or struggles to be heard when he tries to convince voters he has an answer on the economy, then the cost to the prime minister and the government is simply too great. There is no time now to change the plans for 2026. There is still time to be ruthless with the diary for 2027. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: NAB profit falls to $6.1 billion, overdue home loan repayments tick up
World.content:
Breaking BusinessBanking & financeBig four NAB profit falls to $6.1 billion, overdue home loan repayments tick up Millie Muroi November 5, 2026 — 8:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. National Australia Bank has posted a $6.14 billion profit as overdue home loan repayments have ticked up. On Thursday, the bank announced its annual profit figure was 9 per cent lower than last year but that its net interest margin – a key measure of profitability – increased by 6 basis points to 1.8 per cent. NAB chief executive Andrew Irvine said many households and businesses are managing higher living and operating costs. Louise Kennerley The country’s biggest lender to businesses grew its market share in business loans with balances growing 9.8 per cent over the year. NAB chief executive Andrew Irvine said the economic outlook remained uncertain with global events weighing on confidence and many households and businesses managing higher living and operating costs.



“Household consumption growth is expected to slow, and the downturn in the housing market is likely to weigh on activity,” the bank said. “Cost pressures continue to post a material risk to the economy, while the correction in the housing market poses some additional downside risk to growth.” Related Article Big four Westpac expects 11 per cent house price fall, posts $6.8 billion profit The bank said household savings buffers remained strong with a low number of home loan borrowers in negative equity and an 11 per cent increase in offset balances over the year. However, NAB said arrears had deteriorated across the second half of the year, with loan repayments 30-days or more overdue climbing 11 basis points to 1.69 per cent between March and September this year. NAB’s credit impairment charge was $1.5 billion compared to $833 million last year reflecting “a more challenging economic outlook”, growth in the volume of loans, asset quality deterioration in business lending and the impact of house price declines on its Australian mortgage portfolio.



In October, NAB axed 2500 jobs in a move aimed at making the bank more efficient and responding to a tougher economy. The bank left dividends for the full-year unchanged at $1.70 a share. World.title: ASX set to soar as Wall Street rallies; Trump Media dives, Tesla, SpaceX fall; Oil prices tumble
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to soar as Wall Street rallies; Trump Media dives, Tesla, SpaceX fall; Oil prices tumble Stan Choe and David McHugh Updated November 5, 2026 — 8:37am ,first published 5:21am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

US stocks soared after President Donald Trump’s party lost its sole control of Washington in the midterm elections. Stocks generally do well in the months following any midterm US election, regardless of who wins, and the S&P 500 jumped 1.6 per cent for its best day in three months. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rallied 1,569 points, or 3 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 1.4 per cent. Wall Street soared higher. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to surge higher, with futures pointing to a rise of 181 points, or 2 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.6 per cent on Wednesday. Wall Street stocks of hospital owners and dollar stores serving low-income Americans helped lead the widespread rally following the nationwide losses for Republicans. Investors, meanwhile, see risks ahead for Trump’s social-media company, the artificial-intelligence industry and businesses owned by Elon Musk, who donated heavily to Republicans.



Related Article Opinion

US midterms We’ve seen peak Trump, but the next two years will be a rocky ride Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil also tumbled below $US95 and touched its lowest level in two months. Vice President JD Vance blamed Republicans’ midterm losses on the war with Iran, which caused a spike in oil prices. Strategists along Wall Street had been urging investors not to get swept up in the election because it may not matter much for the broad market in the long term. Prices for stocks depend more on where profits for companies and interest rates are heading than on who controls what in Washington. “Earnings trump elections,” according to Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management. Still, Wall Street may have gotten a preferred political scenario as Democrats are set to take control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives. Wall Street generally prefers split control of Washington because it lessens the risk of transformative changes to the economy.



Much remains impossible to predict, of course, and Trump retains executive authority over key areas such as defence, foreign policy and in some instances trade. A downbeat forecast could be that “Trump is not now a lame duck, but an angry duck” who might restart tensions over tariffs and NATO allies’ levels of military spending, said Carsten Brzeski, global chief of macro at ING Bank. Elon Musk’s companies are suffering heavy losses after the midterms. AP An optimistic view, Brzeski said, is that Trump becomes “a tame duck ... that he will slow down any disruptive efforts and that he will put more focus on trying to win the Nobel Peace Prize by ending the two big wars without big disruption, and on trade, nothing happens but a few words.” All told, the S&P 500 rose 119.70 points to 7,688.62. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rallied 1,569.40 to 53,356.12, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 364.50 to 25,736.51. Here’s a look at some of the moves that rippled through financial markets:



Trump’s social-media company, Trump Media & Technology Group, was one of the market’s bigger losers, down 24.5 per cent. Since briefly touching a peak of $US175 five years ago, it’s dropped to $US4.49. Its main business is Truth Social, which is most well known for Trump’s postings on the platform. Elon Musk’s businesses also struggled. Tesla fell 3.3 per cent, and SpaceX sank 3.8 per cent. Musk, a former top Trump adviser, is among the possible targets for investigations by a Democratic-controlled Congress. AI companies in general are under pressure Trump has been a big backer of the AI industry, and Democratic victories could mean more regulation or restrictions. Concerns have grown across political parties about AI in general.



Investors see Democratic wins in Texas in particular as possibly slowing the further build out of AI data centres. AI-related stocks came into Election Day already under pressure because of worries their prices had shot too high. Nvidia, the chip company that quickly became the poster child of the frenzy around AI-related stocks, sank 3.1 per cent and was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. CoreWeave, a company that rents out access to AI chips to customers over the cloud, dropped 9.9 per cent. Companies that have been spending heavily on AI chips held up better. Alphabet rose 3.2 per cent, for example. The parent company of Google had tumbled to its worst loss ever last Thursday on worries that it was spending too much on AI investments. A Democratic-led Congress could push Trump to pull back on the war with Iran. That hurt stocks of companies that make weapons and other equipment for the US military, including drops of 6.9 per cent for Lockheed Martin, 4.5 per cent for Northrop Grumman and 2.6 per cent for General Dynamics.



The possibility of pressure to pull back on the war sent the price for a barrel of Brent crude oil plunging 8.7 per cent to $94.62. That in turn hurt stocks of big oil companies, which had been rallying for much of the year. ExxonMobil fell 4.6 per cent, and ConocoPhillips dropped 5.2 per cent. Related Article US midterms ‘The reason is obvious’: Bloodletting begins over Republicans’ electoral wipeout Falling oil prices usually hurt stocks of renewable-energy companies because they can lessen the incentive to switch to other energy sources. But Democratic control of Congress could light the way for companies in the solar and wind industries. First Solar rose 4.6 per cent, and Enphase Energy climbed 3.7 per cent. A Democratic-led Congress could try to reverse some of the cuts to federal healthcare and food assistance that Republicans approved in their “One Big Beautiful Bill Act.”



That helped stocks climb across the healthcare industry, including a 10.3 per cent rise for HCA Healthcare, which runs hospitals and ambulatory sites. Retailers also benefited on hopes that Democrats may push policies to help Americans who are struggling to keep up with the fast-rising cost of living. Dollar Tree, which focuses in particular on lower-income Americans, rose 9.6 per cent. In the bond market, Treasury yields sank as oil prices dropped and took pressure off inflation. The move could also be a signal that investors see less risk of Washington piling more debt onto its already big mountain with the coming end to one-party control. Treasury yields had climbed through the summer and reached their highest levels in decades because of worries about the US government’s big debt, along with high inflation and other concerns. A Congress controlled by Democrats could provide a check against more spending and cuts to taxes that would widen Washington’s deficit. The yield on the 10-year Treasury dropped to 4.88 per cent from 4.95 per cent late Tuesday.



Indexes climbed across most of the world. Stocks leaped 2 per cent in Paris, 2.2 per cent in Shanghai and 1.8 per cent in London. Japan’s Nikkei 225 was an outlier and fell 1.4 per cent. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Kanga’s bold racing comeback bid: Controversial figure nominates for Flemington board
World.content:
Updated SportRacingVictorian racing Kanga’s bold racing comeback bid: Controversial figure nominates for Flemington board Danny Russell Updated November 5, 2026 — 7:59am ,first published 7:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.
