John Kanga has launched a bid to join the Victorian Racing Club board little more than 12 months after walking away from the racing industry amid a cloud of controversy. Kanga put to bed weeks of speculation and personal denials that he would run for a seat on the VRC committee by lodging his nomination on Wednesday night. Chairman John Kanga at Caulfield Racecourse last October. Getty Images Popular among racegoers, the colourful identity’s name adds extra spice to what is shaping as one of the most divisive and highly political VRC elections in the club’s history. Kanga alerted media outlets first thing on Thursday morning with a statement, saying “I am not interested in making promises I can’t deliver”. Nominations close on Thursday.



Related Article Racing integrity John Kanga’s resignation came after questions from The Age He has also declared his campaign would not be aligned to Melbourne Racing Club vice chairman and influential racing figure Jonathan Munz, who took Kanga’s vacant seat on the MRC board last year. “I am an independent candidate,” Kanga said. “I respect Jonathan and agree with most of his views on what is best for the industry, but he is not involved in my campaign and did not encourage me to run as a candidate.” There are four seats on the VRC board up for grabs. Chairman Neil Wilson is stepping away, leaving one vacancy, while three directors – chair-elect Vin Cox, treasurer Glen Carmody and Michael Saadie – are up for re-election.



More nominations for the board are expected by the close of Thursday. If more than two people are deemed suitable to run, it will mean all four seats will go to the VRC members’ vote at the end of this month. The Victoria Racing Club oversees the Melbourne Cup at Flemington. Getty Images Changes will be announced at the club’s December annual general meeting. Kanga resigned as Melbourne Racing Club chair on the eve of last year’s Caulfield Cup carnival after questions from The Age about loans and the use of his car in a 22-kilogram cocaine trafficking case in 2014.



Related Article Spring racing carnival Munz now wearing many hats in Victorian racing, but denies any conflicts Kanga said hehad resigned “to ensure the focus remains where it belongs – on racing, our members, staff, and delivering a world-class spring carnival”. The Age does not suggest Kanga was involved in any criminal activity, and he has never been accused of any crime. The Age reported last year that surveillance officers working on an investigation into “high-threat” money laundering, known as Taskforce Eligo, saw one of their targets, Assam “Sam” Lababidi, attending Kanga’s then-home and borrowing his car, according to an AFP report released under freedom of information. Lababidi was followed to a storage facility. It was later raided and 22.7 kilograms of cocaine and $118,500 in cash was uncovered.



Lababidi, who was sentenced to 12 years’ jail, said Kanga had “no involvement” in his criminal operation. Separately, financial records show Kanga had taken out loans in 2013 and 2016 with two people involved in the short-term, high-interest lending market. Kanga also had personal relationships with controversial figures in the racing industry. Loading During his time at Melbourne Racing Club, Kanga became popular among members after his board saved Sandown Racecourse from being sold for housing development, moved the mounting yard back in front of the Caulfield members’ stand and scrapped plans for a new $250 million grandstand. But he also cut through with rank-and-file racegoers by cutting beer and food prices at MRC racetracks.



In his media statement, Kanga said: “My focus is simple. Better service, better value for money and a better race-day experience for VRC members at Flemington. “I’ve never been one for sitting around the committee room when I could be out talking to members. You learn a lot more walking around the racecourse than you do sitting around a table. “When I was chairman of the Melbourne Racing Club, we delivered better value for money on food, drinks and membership, and importantly, we listened to our members. “Racing is also about the people who make it happen. Owners, trainers, jockeys, and other industry participants all have a stake in its future, and their voices need to be heard. “I bring strong commercial experience, a deep understanding of racing and wagering, and relationships across the industry here and internationally.





Related Article Oaks Day How a horse that ‘wobbled all over the place’ could take out the $1 million Oaks In theory, a 6-5 vote in favour of Cox is easily reversed with at least one director being replaced. Any change to the board also has ramifications for the VRC’s future. Wilson was staunchly opposed to the club losing its tradition or identity by merging with the MRC or Moonee Valley Racing Club. The Age reported last year that then MRC chairman Kanga met with Wilson at Munz’s Toorak mansion to discuss bringing Flemington and Caulfield racetracks under one administration. Ramsden also attended. But Wilson walked away not prepared to accept the proposal. Kanga was still open to the possibility of Melbourne’s metropolitan club’s merging this week.



“The government and RVL have encouraged club mergers and intuitively, there are big cost savings to be made,” he said. “I have heard $30 -$50 million reported. The club executive and board would need to do proper due diligence first and have the support from members. John Kanga was popular with racegoers at Caulfield, for reducing the cost of food and beverages. Getty Images “If it did happen, you would apply part of the savings towards immediate benefits to members, such as lower food and drink prices.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport are sent every Friday.

World.title: Live battleground tracker: The two races too close to call – and every seat the Democrats flipped
World.content:
The Democrats took firm control of the senate by flipping several key seats.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The Democrats have delivered a comprehensive blow to Donald Trump ahead of his final two years in the White House, sweeping control of the Senate and the House. Several key battleground races – particularly in the Senate – were at the heart of this emphatic Democratic Party win. Below, we track which seats were flipped, retained – and which remain in play. Follow our full live coverage of the 2026 US midterms here. STILL TO CALL Alaska Surging heating fuel, electricity and grocery prices are disproportionately whacking residents of this remote, traditionally red state. Democrat Mary Peltola, who says Alaskans endure the highest healthcare costs in the country, is facing off against Republican senator Dan Sullivan, and an unaffiliated retired teacher who goes by the same name – Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.



Mississippi Well, this is the race no one saw coming – which is why we’ve updated this list to include it. Trump won Mississippi by 23 points just two years ago, while incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith won her first term by double digits. But disaffection with Trump and the charisma of Democratic candidate Scott Colom has thrust this firmly into the too close to call category. SENATE – FLIPPED BY DEMOCRATS South Carolina: Annie Andrews This race found the spotlight for two reasons – it was a toss-up, and Republican candidate Darline Graham is the sister of the late senator Lindsey Graham. She has lost the seat to Annie Andrews - that’s a big upset in what’s typically a safe red state.



Ohio: Sherrod Brown Democratic candidate Sherrod Brown is a former senator who chaired the Senate banking committee from 2021 to 2024, when he was a vocal critic of crypto. Ad-tracking business AdImpact says the crypto sector spent $US68 million on defeating Brown. It didn’t work – he’s defeated Republican incumbent Jon Husted in a high-stakes Senate race. Texas: James Talarico Democrat James Talarico has become the first Democrat elected to the US Senate from the conservative state of Texas since 1988. He defeated Republican candidate Ken Paxton. Kansas: Adam Hamilton



A Democrat hasn’t been elected to the Senate in Kansas for 94 years – that’s something the popular pastor Adam Hamilton has just changed by taking down Republican Roger Marshall. Iowa: Josh Turek Maine: Troy Jackson In one of the last remaining moderate strongholds for Republicans, incumbent Susan Collins has historically outperformed bad polling numbers to win time and time again. But with a poor net approval rating, she was knocked out by Democrat Troy Jackson.



SENATE – HELD Michigan: Abdul El-Sayed In the swing state of Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed – a doctor, unionist and Muslim – and Republican Mike Rogers had a tight race for the Senate seat being vacated by Democrat Gary Peters. El-Sayed prevailed. Georgia: Jon Ossoff This race was cruisy for Jon Ossoff, who won re-election and has been linked with a run at the White House in 2028. He beat Republican Mike Collins.

World.title: 118 years of history: Inside Victoria’s newest over-50s community
World.content:
Sponsored LifestyleLife & relationshipsGemLife 118 years of history: Inside Victoria’s newest over-50s community Advertorial for GemLife Jaymie Hooper November 5, 2026 — 9:32am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. A 118-year-old homestead, century-old gardens and sweeping views of the Macedon Ranges are shaping the design of one of Victoria’s newest over-50s lifestyle communities, where heritage architecture and contemporary living are being brought together. At GemLife New Gisborne, the restoration of the historic Westport Homestead is central to an architectural approach that draws inspiration from the landscape, history and character of its surroundings. The historic Westport Homestead is to be at the heart of the GemLife New Gisborne community. “We look at the landscape, climate, history and local character, but importantly, also how people will live and connect there,” explains Phillip Nielsen, general manager of architecture and design at GemLife. With its beautifully restored heritage buildings and expansive green spaces, GemLife New Gisborne, which is currently under construction, provides a compelling example of this place-led approach to design.



“Our objective is for each community to feel as though it belongs to its setting,” Nielsen says. “At New Gisborne, the Westport Homestead, established gardens, mature trees and the Macedon Ranges provide a very strong sense of place, so those elements become the foundation of the design rather than simply a backdrop to it.” It’s a similar case at GemLife Kilcoy Greens, where the natural beauty of Queensland’s Somerset region is celebrated through floor-to-ceiling glazing, native-spotted gum timber, shaded verandahs and landscaped breezeways. “[Both locations] demonstrate how the same philosophy can lead to very different architectural outcomes,” Nielsen says. “The common thread isn’t a particular style it’s designing something that feels appropriate to its place and the people who will live there.” Respecting the past, designing for the future Set across 23 hectares in Victorian wine country, GemLife New Gisborne combines contemporary living with the character of its semi-rural setting. At the heart of the community is the Westport Homestead, a circa-1908 bungalow being restored by Melbourne-based architecture studio Taylor Knights.



“The Homestead was always going to be at the heart of the project,” says James Taylor, director and architect at Taylor Knights. “It has such a strong presence, with a level of craftsmanship and character that we wanted to celebrate rather than compete with.” Every space has been thoughtfully designed to facilitate community connection. The historic estate forms part of the luxurious Country Club precinct, which includes two additional buildings linked by a shared roofline. “The new buildings are deliberately separated from the homestead and are entirely single storey, sitting low within the landscape so the original building retains its prominence,” Taylor explains. While the homestead reflects the region’s history, the additional buildings sit comfortably beside it, taking cues from the natural environment.



“We were conscious that respecting heritage didn’t mean replicating it,” Taylor says. “Instead, we drew from the qualities that make the homestead so successful – its domestic scale, pitched roofs, deep verandahs, materiality and relationship with the garden – and reinterpreted them in a contemporary way.” A connected community The lounge and billiards room. Beyond its architectural significance, the Westport Homestead will also play an important role in the community’s social life, with a library, meeting room and traditional billiards room providing welcoming spaces for residents to gather. “These intimate heritage spaces sit alongside contemporary social, dining, recreation and wellness facilities, giving residents the best of both worlds,” Nielsen says.



Within the Country Club precinct, residents will enjoy access to a cafe, gym, sauna, indoor pool, creative arts studio, cinema, golf simulator and more. A central courtyard and sculptural fireplace help connect the spaces, while the wide verandah offers uninterrupted views of the century-old gardens. “We wanted to create more than a collection of facilities,” Taylor explains. “We thought carefully about how people move between these spaces, because the moments between destinations can be just as important as the destinations themselves. “You might be on your way to swim, see a neighbour, stop for a conversation and end up having a coffee together. Those small, incidental encounters are often how relationships begin, and we wanted the architecture to make room for them.” Where the landscape leads Located less than an hour from Melbourne, GemLife New Gisborne will feature 247 energy-efficient homes designed to complement their natural surroundings.



Landscape isn’t something added around the architecture – it’s fundamental to it. “At New Gisborne, landscape isn’t something added around the architecture – it’s fundamental to it,” Nielsen notes. “The established gardens, orchard and mature trees are being retained and rejuvenated, and the buildings have been conceived around their relationship with those landscapes and the wider Macedon Ranges.” Across the community, weatherboard, pitched metal roofs, chimneys and locally sourced stone and timber echo the region’s character, while garden pathways, pocket parks and walking trails connect homeowners with the surrounding landscape. “At times, the buildings frame the landscape. At others, they recede and allow the landscape to become the experience,” Taylor says. “The result is intentionally very specific to New Gisborne. It feels difficult to imagine these buildings belonging anywhere else.” GemLife creates vibrant lifestyle communities for Australians over 50 in sought-after tree change and sea change locations across Australia, including the newly launched GemLife New Gisborne in Victoria’s Macedon Ranges.

World.title: LIV Golf thought it had a financial saviour. It’s just walked away
World.content:
SportGolfLIV Golf Series LIV Golf thought it had a financial saviour. It’s just walked away Reuters November 5, 2026 — 9:26am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

BC Partners is dropping its bid to relaunch LIV Golf due to an inability to secure enough player commitments, the Financial Times reported on Wednesday. The professional men’s golf league, a competitor to the PGA Tour, filed for bankruptcy protection in New Jersey in September as part of a restructuring after Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, which has ​invested more than $US5 ⁠billion ($7 billion) in LIV since its launch in 2022, announced it was ending its financial backing after the 2026 season. The sinking LIV Golf series has copped another financial blow. LIV has said it plans to continue operating while it reorganises. The private capital firm’s decision came as a deadline loomed to show there was enough player support to hold a tournament series in 2027, the FT said, citing people directly familiar with the matter.



Related Article World golf Former world No.1 quits LIV golf as Smith’s lawyers seek exit from old contract BC Partners – which provides financing to middle-market companies – and LIV Golf did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Former world No.1 Jon Rahm is among a wave of high-profile golfers who have left LIV Golf since it filed for bankruptcy protection. LIV is expected to appear at a Thursday hearing in US bankruptcy court in Trenton, New Jersey, to discuss various contracts, leases and assets. It is unclear whether LIV’s fate may also be discussed. In October, BC Partners made an initial investment in LIV Golf and planned to provide up to $US300 million ($428 million) in financing to help the league emerge from restructuring and strengthen its finances ahead of the 2027 season.



LIV Golf launched in 2022 with funding from Saudi Arabia and lured leading players from the PGA Tour including Phil Mickelson, Bryson DeChambeau, Brooks Koepka, Australian Cameron Smith and Dustin Johnson with lucrative contracts. DeChambeau, one of the biggest names on LIV’s player roster, said recently the business model for the league’s proposed 2.0 era “makes a lot of sense” and that he hoped that it would last “forever”. Australian Cameron Smith was one of the stars who jumped from the PGA Tour to LIV Golf. Getty Images Others have been critical of LIV Golf, with DP ‌World Tour chief executive Guy Kinnings saying that LIV had sought to undermine the European circuit. Kinnings is having to weigh up regaining some star power with unhappiness among some of his members that LIV players are just walking back onto the tour having caused so much disruption.



In an interview with The Scotsman newspaper, Kinnings accepted there was a balance to strike in integrating the returning players. “But we also have to protect the tour against an entity who spent, so we are told, over $7 billion, with one of their aims being to ‘destroy the DP World Tour,’” Kinnings said. “I have heard that from so many different people they talked to, who I have known for over 30 years within the game and who I trust implicitly. Rory McIlroy has been outspoken in his criticism of LIV Golf. Getty Images “Clearly when you are faced with statements like that, and then people then ask why we are doing what we are doing with our membership and invite policy for 2027, then I think the answer becomes pretty obvious. Myself and everyone at the DP World Tour have a duty to our members to protect our tour.” Six-time major champion Rory McIlroy, who has been outspoken against LIV Golf since its formation, backed up Kinnings’ comments.



Related Article LIV Golf Series ‘We need a few more answers’: Why Cameron Smith’s future on LIV tour is still uncertain Speaking Wednesday at the Abu Dhabi Championship, McIlroy said: “I agree with everything that Guy said. They took players, they took sponsors, they turned professional golf into an arms race. “They were going around Augusta saying they wanted to destroy the European tour.” McIlroy acknowledged that LIV’s investment had brought benefits, including the creation of the International Series on the Asian Tour, but said the latter had ultimately been left without the support it needed. “Where did that leave the Asian Tour? They left them high and dry,” he said, adding that the tour had since returned to the fold through partnerships with the PGA Tour and DP World Tour.



McIlroy said LIV’s financial model was always likely to face difficulties if investors failed to see a return or decided to redirect their money elsewhere, and that it was “ironic” that LIV Golf CEO Scott O’Neil’s motto is now “complete, not compete” – a reference to the breakaway league finding a place in golf’s ecosystem rather than trying to take over. McIlroy, 37, added the disruption caused by the breakaway league could ultimately leave men’s golf on a more sustainable footing. “For long-term sustainability for men’s professional golf, I think we are in a much better spot,” he said. World.title: Marooned in paradise: Albanese and the summit that could not have come at a worse time
World.content:
Analysis NationalPolitical leadership Marooned in paradise: Albanese and the summit that could not have come at a worse time David Crowe Updated November 5, 2026 — 9:20am ,first published 8:56am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

St John’s, Antigua and Barbuda: Nothing showed the utter isolation of Anthony Albanese and his fellow Commonwealth leaders quite like their retreat on the final day of their gathering in the Caribbean. The leaders stepped onto chartered boats to reach a private island where they could talk at a luxury resort secluded from everyone else at the Commonwealth meeting in Antigua and Barbuda. Anthony Albanese and Queen Camilla during an official dinner and reception at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in St John’s, Antigua and Barbuda on Tuesday. Getty Images Albanese did not choose the venue. As prime minister, he was right to join the other leaders at a forum Australia has supported for decades. He did not stay on the private island – his hotel was the same seaside resort as his British counterpart, Andy Burnham – and he headed for the airport to get home as soon as the retreat was over. But the gathering at Jumby Bay Island sent all the wrong signals about the Commonwealth leaders when so many of their citizens are suffering from declining living standards.



And that is a problem for Albanese when the Reserve Bank says its latest interest rate hike will feel like a recession to many households. What possessed the Commonwealth to do this? The leaders were on an island where Oprah Winfrey is rumoured to own a private chateau. A modern “cottage” at one of the hotels, with space for four people and a private pool, costs $US8200 per night (about $11,700) for those who want to book it for this Monday. You want to look out of touch to voters? Go to Jumby Bay. Jumby Bay Island, where Oprah is reported to have a holiday mansion, and cottages go for more than $8000 a night. allinclusiveoutlet.com The entire exercise highlighted the shocking waste of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, known as CHOGM, when so many people in its 56 member states live below the poverty line.



Yes, some Antiguans were glad to see the money flow into their small nation, but the gathering lifted their country’s population by about 5 per cent overnight. The talk about climate action would have ended quickly without the national desalination plant run from an electricity grid powered by diesel generators. If there is money to be spent in Antigua, it could be spent on the roads, the schools and the homes. While the beaches are every bit as beautiful as they look on Caribbean travel websites, the country is not wealthy. Who knows if the cash from hosting CHOGM will trickle down to those at the bottom? In any case, the country is hedging its bets on a search for supporters: the most impressive new housing in the capital, St John’s, is funded by China Aid. The Antigua meeting was an extravagance in hard times. It is no wonder the UK Foreign Office commissioned a study after the last CHOGM, in Samoa two years ago, to think seriously about scaling back these meetings. One top UK adviser involved in that review, Ben Judah, told Politico last week that the Commonwealth Secretariat was a “broken institution” and should take a new approach. Judah was an adviser to David Lammy, who was foreign secretary at the time of the Samoa summit.



Related Article Political leadership ‘Oh God, so it’s all my fault’: Albanese and King Charles joke over travel backlash One idea in the Foreign Office review was to hold the meetings every four or five years, perhaps aligning them with the Commonwealth Games. That looks like an idea Australia could support. The core Australian interest in the Pacific is already addressed at the annual Pacific Islands Forum. Sending prime ministers to CHOGMs in the Caribbean and Africa is not as important. Albanese was, on balance, right to go to this Commonwealth summit. Australia has played its part in the institution for decades. Albanese met Burnham as well as Canadian prime minister Mark Carney. As Carney said earlier this year, middle powers should work together at a time when America is an unpredictable ally and the old global order is splintering. Anthony Albanese met with Canadian Prime Minister mark Carney at CHOGM. Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press via AP “If we’re not at the table, we’re on the menu,” Carney said. That message could guide the Commonwealth to becoming more ambitious or useful. Even Carney, however, was prudent about how long he spent in Antigua: he flew in on Monday night and left on Tuesday night, skipping the retreat because he had to oversee a budget at home.



Albanese should have been equally cautious about spending too much time away. In a remark caught on camera, he told King Charles why he was there: because the King had asked him personally. There were other reasons, of course, including the ambition to secure votes around the world to put Australia on the United Nations Security Council. The trouble is that Albanese was in Antigua from Saturday night to Wednesday night. Who in Australia would be any worse off if he had arrived in Antigua a day later and skipped the private island retreat at the end? Nobody. When the Commonwealth leaders issued their statement at the end of the gathering, it looked inconsequential. There was some adjusted language on slavery and some fine words about climate. There was a slightly stronger message about “reparatory justice” for slavery, given Burnham said he was open to a discussion about an apology. But there was nothing substantial enough to justify the exorbitant use of time and money on so many days at so many resorts by so many leaders. Loading



Unfortunately for Albanese and the government, he cannot skip the next few summits. He has to attend the UN Climate Change Conference in Turkey, even if it would have been wiser to avoid co-hosting the event. Then he has to fly to the East Asia Summit in the Philippines on November 16-18 and go on to the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting in China on November 18-19. Then there’s the G20 with Donald Trump in Miami on December 14–15. All prime ministers face demands to spend more time on global problems, and most fall into the habit of travelling to more summits. But the political danger rises sharply when times are tough. Albanese, caught in a mid-term slump with low growth and high inflation, already faces a backlash over his travel. It will probably get worse. Spending too much time on the global stage will weaken Labor at home. If this means Albanese loses more of his personal standing in the polls, or struggles to be heard when he tries to convince voters he has an answer on the economy, then the cost to the prime minister and the government is simply too great. There is no time now to change the plans for 2026. There is still time to be ruthless with the diary for 2027. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: NAB profit falls to $6.1 billion, overdue home loan repayments tick up
World.content:
Breaking BusinessBanking & financeBig four NAB profit falls to $6.1 billion, overdue home loan repayments tick up Millie Muroi November 5, 2026 — 8:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. National Australia Bank has posted a $6.14 billion profit as overdue home loan repayments have ticked up. On Thursday, the bank announced its annual profit figure was 9 per cent lower than last year but that its net interest margin – a key measure of profitability – increased by 6 basis points to 1.8 per cent. NAB chief executive Andrew Irvine said many households and businesses are managing higher living and operating costs. Louise Kennerley The country’s biggest lender to businesses grew its market share in business loans with balances growing 9.8 per cent over the year. NAB chief executive Andrew Irvine said the economic outlook remained uncertain with global events weighing on confidence and many households and businesses managing higher living and operating costs.



“Household consumption growth is expected to slow, and the downturn in the housing market is likely to weigh on activity,” the bank said. “Cost pressures continue to post a material risk to the economy, while the correction in the housing market poses some additional downside risk to growth.” Related Article Big four Westpac expects 11 per cent house price fall, posts $6.8 billion profit The bank said household savings buffers remained strong with a low number of home loan borrowers in negative equity and an 11 per cent increase in offset balances over the year. However, NAB said arrears had deteriorated across the second half of the year, with loan repayments 30-days or more overdue climbing 11 basis points to 1.69 per cent between March and September this year. NAB’s credit impairment charge was $1.5 billion compared to $833 million last year reflecting “a more challenging economic outlook”, growth in the volume of loans, asset quality deterioration in business lending and the impact of house price declines on its Australian mortgage portfolio.



In October, NAB axed 2500 jobs in a move aimed at making the bank more efficient and responding to a tougher economy. The bank left dividends for the full-year unchanged at $1.70 a share. World.title: ASX set to soar as Wall Street rallies; Trump Media dives, Tesla, SpaceX fall; Oil prices tumble
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to soar as Wall Street rallies; Trump Media dives, Tesla, SpaceX fall; Oil prices tumble Stan Choe and David McHugh Updated November 5, 2026 — 8:37am ,first published 5:21am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. US stocks soared after President Donald Trump’s party lost its sole control of Washington in the midterm elections. Stocks generally do well in the months following any midterm US election, regardless of who wins, and the S&P 500 jumped 1.6 per cent for its best day in three months. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rallied 1,569 points, or 3 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 1.4 per cent. Wall Street soared higher. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to surge higher, with futures pointing to a rise of 181 points, or 2 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.6 per cent on Wednesday. Wall Street stocks of hospital owners and dollar stores serving low-income Americans helped lead the widespread rally following the nationwide losses for Republicans. Investors, meanwhile, see risks ahead for Trump’s social-media company, the artificial-intelligence industry and businesses owned by Elon Musk, who donated heavily to Republicans.



Related Article Opinion

US midterms We’ve seen peak Trump, but the next two years will be a rocky ride Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil also tumbled below $US95 and touched its lowest level in two months. Vice President JD Vance blamed Republicans’ midterm losses on the war with Iran, which caused a spike in oil prices. Strategists along Wall Street had been urging investors not to get swept up in the election because it may not matter much for the broad market in the long term. Prices for stocks depend more on where profits for companies and interest rates are heading than on who controls what in Washington. “Earnings trump elections,” according to Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management. Still, Wall Street may have gotten a preferred political scenario as Democrats are set to take control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives. Wall Street generally prefers split control of Washington because it lessens the risk of transformative changes to the economy.



Much remains impossible to predict, of course, and Trump retains executive authority over key areas such as defence, foreign policy and in some instances trade. A downbeat forecast could be that “Trump is not now a lame duck, but an angry duck” who might restart tensions over tariffs and NATO allies’ levels of military spending, said Carsten Brzeski, global chief of macro at ING Bank. Elon Musk’s companies are suffering heavy losses after the midterms. AP An optimistic view, Brzeski said, is that Trump becomes “a tame duck ... that he will slow down any disruptive efforts and that he will put more focus on trying to win the Nobel Peace Prize by ending the two big wars without big disruption, and on trade, nothing happens but a few words.” All told, the S&P 500 rose 119.70 points to 7,688.62. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rallied 1,569.40 to 53,356.12, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 364.50 to 25,736.51. Here’s a look at some of the moves that rippled through financial markets:



Trump’s social-media company, Trump Media & Technology Group, was one of the market’s bigger losers, down 24.5 per cent. Since briefly touching a peak of $US175 five years ago, it’s dropped to $US4.49. Its main business is Truth Social, which is most well known for Trump’s postings on the platform. Elon Musk’s businesses also struggled. Tesla fell 3.3 per cent, and SpaceX sank 3.8 per cent. Musk, a former top Trump adviser, is among the possible targets for investigations by a Democratic-controlled Congress. AI companies in general are under pressure Trump has been a big backer of the AI industry, and Democratic victories could mean more regulation or restrictions. Concerns have grown across political parties about AI in general.



Investors see Democratic wins in Texas in particular as possibly slowing the further build out of AI data centres. AI-related stocks came into Election Day already under pressure because of worries their prices had shot too high. Nvidia, the chip company that quickly became the poster child of the frenzy around AI-related stocks, sank 3.1 per cent and was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. CoreWeave, a company that rents out access to AI chips to customers over the cloud, dropped 9.9 per cent. Companies that have been spending heavily on AI chips held up better. Alphabet rose 3.2 per cent, for example. The parent company of Google had tumbled to its worst loss ever last Thursday on worries that it was spending too much on AI investments. A Democratic-led Congress could push Trump to pull back on the war with Iran. That hurt stocks of companies that make weapons and other equipment for the US military, including drops of 6.9 per cent for Lockheed Martin, 4.5 per cent for Northrop Grumman and 2.6 per cent for General Dynamics.



The possibility of pressure to pull back on the war sent the price for a barrel of Brent crude oil plunging 8.7 per cent to $94.62. That in turn hurt stocks of big oil companies, which had been rallying for much of the year. ExxonMobil fell 4.6 per cent, and ConocoPhillips dropped 5.2 per cent. Related Article US midterms ‘The reason is obvious’: Bloodletting begins over Republicans’ electoral wipeout Falling oil prices usually hurt stocks of renewable-energy companies because they can lessen the incentive to switch to other energy sources. But Democratic control of Congress could light the way for companies in the solar and wind industries. First Solar rose 4.6 per cent, and Enphase Energy climbed 3.7 per cent. A Democratic-led Congress could try to reverse some of the cuts to federal healthcare and food assistance that Republicans approved in their “One Big Beautiful Bill Act.”



That helped stocks climb across the healthcare industry, including a 10.3 per cent rise for HCA Healthcare, which runs hospitals and ambulatory sites. Retailers also benefited on hopes that Democrats may push policies to help Americans who are struggling to keep up with the fast-rising cost of living. Dollar Tree, which focuses in particular on lower-income Americans, rose 9.6 per cent. In the bond market, Treasury yields sank as oil prices dropped and took pressure off inflation. The move could also be a signal that investors see less risk of Washington piling more debt onto its already big mountain with the coming end to one-party control. Treasury yields had climbed through the summer and reached their highest levels in decades because of worries about the US government’s big debt, along with high inflation and other concerns. A Congress controlled by Democrats could provide a check against more spending and cuts to taxes that would widen Washington’s deficit. The yield on the 10-year Treasury dropped to 4.88 per cent from 4.95 per cent late Tuesday.



Indexes climbed across most of the world. Stocks leaped 2 per cent in Paris, 2.2 per cent in Shanghai and 1.8 per cent in London. Japan’s Nikkei 225 was an outlier and fell 1.4 per cent. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Full year profit dips to $1.1 billion at BNZ
World.content:
Strong competition and cost increases have put a dent in BNZ's full-year net profit.

The company has posted a statutory net profit of $1.157 billion for the year to the end of September, down 22.8 percent on the previous year.

A large chunk of the decline was due to a one-off reduction in BNZ's capitalised software assets that was announced in April.

However, even excluding the one-off charges, BNZ said its net profit was down almost 6 percent to $1.41b.

Its net interest margin - which is a measure of what it charges borrowers and pays depositors - was 2.30 percent, down 10 basis points in what it said was a highly competitive market for both lending and deposits.

Revenue was up 1.5 percent to $3.536b, while operating expenses, excluding the one-off adjustment, grew 4.2 percent to $1.437b, driven by investment in technology, more frontline staff and inflationary pressures.

BNZ's chief executive Dan Huggins noted that while the Middle East conflict has had a disruptive impact on the New Zealand economic recovery, businesses were resilient.

"Confidence, while fragile, has strengthened, with strong conditions in the agriculture, tourism and infrastructure sectors."

However, he said conditions remained challenging for some households due to the cost of living.

"Against this backdrop, we have continued to support our customers, helping businesses to invest and grow and New Zealanders to buy their first or next home."

Huggins said the bank expected the economy to strengthen next year.

"Barring any external shocks, we expect economic growth to strengthen through 2027."

Backing business as confidence returns

When it comes to lending to firms, BNZ's total business lending increased by $2.6b, or 5.5 percent, to $49.5b.

Home lending, meanwhile, was up $4.9b, or 7.7 percent, on the prior year to $68.8b.

World.title: Kohli in the runs as India thrash New Zealand in first ODI
World.content:
Virat Kohli smashed his 80th half-century in one-day internationals and took a screamer of a catch to help India thrash New Zealand by five wickets in the rain-hit series opener in Auckland on Wednesday.

A day before his 38th birthday, Kohli underlined his enduring class with a knock of 74 in 51 balls at Eden Park as India chased down 143 on the Duckworth-Lewis-Stern method after repeated rain showers interrupted their reply.

Talisman Kohli eventually holed out to deep square leg off the bowling of Jacob Duffy and exited waving his bat for the Indian fans who dominated the crowd.

Only five days after piling up 259 for seven in the fourth T20 match, New Zealand were bundled out for a paltry 185 in 40.2 overs after losing the toss to India captain Shubman Gill.

"I think we were very good with the bowling," said Gill. "Overall a very good team performance."

Pace duo Arshdeep Singh (4-70) and Gurnoor Brar (3-44) took seven wickets between them, rattling through New Zealand's top order as the home batters repeatedly succumbed to short-pitched bowling.

Fast-bowling all-rounder Anshul Kamboj was impressive in his second ODI, taking two wickets and conceding a miserly 22 runs from his 10 overs to be man of the match.

"The way both of them bowled tonight was really magnificent to watch," Gill said of Kamboj and Brar.

Kohli delivered Kamboj his first wicket with a brilliant, diving slips catch, plucking a one-hander above the grass to remove all-rounder Nathan Smith for one.

Tim Seifert opened the batting for New Zealand, replacing the concussed Devon Conway, and top-scored for the hosts with 38 in his first ODI in over 18 months.

The five-match series moves to Wellington on Saturday. - Reuters

World.title: The attack ad election: Inside the parties' Facebook campaigns
World.content:
Negative campaigning has surged since 2020, with National and Labour each devoting more than half their Facebook posts to attacks, new research shows.

An analysis of 2222 posts made by political parties and their leaders between 5 October and 1 November deemed National to be the most negative campaigner.

National published 371 negative posts, about 66 percent of its total, followed by Labour with 214, or about 51 percent of its total.

Victoria University of Wellington political scientist Dr Mona Krewel said that was a "massive increase" since 2020, when about 13 percent of the posts analysed were negative.

New Zealand First, ACT, the Greens, Opportunity and Te Pāti Māori were all below 40 percent this election, with Te Pāti Māori the lowest at 16 percent.

The research, by the university's Internet, Social Media and Politics Research Lab, also revealed differences in who the two major parties were attacking.

Labour's criticism was almost "exclusively focused" on Christopher Luxon and National, with less than 4 percent of posts dedicated to the minor coalition partners, ACT and NZ First.

National's main target was the Labour Party, but it directed 100 negative posts at Greens' co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick, compared with 87 aimed at Labour leader Chris Hipkins.

'They have made her the bogeyman of the election' - Krewel

Krewel said National's intense focus on Swarbrick was unusual for a governing party.

"Chlöe Swarbrick should not be their go-to target."

She said incumbent governments usually ran more positive campaigns and focused their attacks on their main political rival.

Instead, National had repeatedly warned Swarbrick could become finance minister under a Labour-led government, despite Hipkins insisting Barbara Edmonds would get the job.

Krewel described the attacks as largely "fearmongering", more reminiscent of American political rhetoric - though not to the same degree.

"They have made her the boogeyman of the election."

She queried whether the strategy was working given posts targeting the Greens' co-leader attracted, on average, more angry emoji reactions than posts targeting Hipkins.

National finance spokesperson Nicola Willis is defending the targeting of Chlöe Swarbrick. RNZ/Nick Monro

Swarbrick accused National on Monday of effectively cyber-bullying her, but National finance spokesperson Nicola Willis defended the party's approach.

In a post on social media, Willis said the Greens' polling strength would give them "huge leverage" in coalition negotiations with Labour.

"In other words, Labour cannot form a government without giving the Greens what they want," Willis wrote.

Long-time National campaigner and volunteer Brigitte Morten agreed the historically low combined support for Labour and National had changed the dynamic between major and minor parties.

Morten, managing director of Franks Ogilvie, said Hipkins would therefore find it harder to reject the Greens' more "radical" demands in coalition talks.

She said negative campaigning attracted more attention: "No campaign can avoid putting out those negative messages."

But former National government press secretary and political commentator Ben Thomas was sceptical whether the attacks were helping the party.

He described the intense focus on Swarbrick as "bewildering" in the final stretch of the campaign.

"There is a sense that National are kind of throwing things at the wall."

World.title: US midterm election results could boost local NZ economy - Auckland Business Chamber
World.content:
Audio player for " Simon Bridges on state of Auckland business sector " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/business/2355589%2Fus-midterm-election-results-could-boost-local-nz-economy-auckland-business-chamber

Simon Bridges on state of Auckland business sector Nine To Noon Download MP3 14m

The head of Auckland's Business Chamber says last night's midterm results in the US could boost the local economy.

The Democrats rode a wave of support to take control of both chambers of the Congress.

Auckland Business Chamber chief executive Simon Bridges said New Zealand's economy had pockets of growth but international conditions had held it back.

He said the economy had been struggling to recover since Covid.

"We thought we were having a recovery in [20]25, but then we had Liberation Day that sucked the sentiment out of a lot of places, including New Zealand.

"This year it's been the Iran war."

He said the US midterm elections could spell the end of the war in Iran and bring down the price of oil - a major driver of inflation.

"I think being a Trump soothsayer is a difficult proposition to be in. [But] I mean, the markets are up."

He said there had been growth in some areas like tech, but to get more of it, more investment was needed.

"The truth is the big four banks and their big KiwiSaver providers are very conservative."

He said a small government push to help New Zealand funds could "make an enormous difference".

He said there were lessons to learn from SME growth banks and funds overseas.

"So there are options. I kind of think we've just got to seize them."

Bridges also argued for lower corporate tax rates to be competitive internationally.

He said they would lure bigger businesses to the country - as they had done in Ireland - to employ more people and offer higher wages.

"But I also think in terms of New Zealand and New Zealand Inc, if you're that SME and you know that your tax rate's gone from 28 percent to let's say 22 percent, I do think at a level that is a spur to do more, to take more risk, to invest more.

"And that's exactly what New Zealand needs right now."

He said having mandatory KiwiSaver contribution lower than 12 percent would also free up capital for small businesses.

Finally, Bridges wanted energy reform: he wanted long-term planning and to break up the gentailers.

He said currently gentailers had no incentive to produce more supply.

"But what the settings mean is they are rewarded when there's just enough or maybe not quite enough supply."

World.title: Timor-Leste musicians bring stories of survival and identity to life
World.content:
Audio player for " Timor-Leste's history brought to life through new music " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/pacific/2355556%2Ftimor-leste-musicians-bring-stories-of-survival-and-identity-to-life

Timor-Leste's history brought to life through new music Pacific Waves Download MP3 4m

Artists from Timor-Leste have have brought stories of survival and identity to live in three new albums and a single released through the Wantok Musik Foundation.

The new music is a celebration of Timorese culture, language and identity; and also explores darker elements of conflict and surviving Indonesian occupation.

For the creatives behind these releases, the songs are more than pretty melodies.

Wantok Musik Foundation co-artistic director David Bridie said the project grew from a desire to preserve traditional songs and stories that were at risk of being lost.

"We got funding to do a project to go and work with younger artists who got together with their uncles and their aunties and their nannies and koros (choir) and recorded some of these old songs that they thought were in danger of being lost."

But the albums also carry heavier elements. They capture the stories of a people whose history have been marred by conflict, and marked by tales of resilience and their fight for independence.

"We worked with 16 young women songwriters, storytellers and filmmakers who engaged with women survivors from the war.

"They sat down with these older women and heard their stories and listened to them and spent time with them and then went away and wrote a whole lot of songs based on honouring their story of survival and the sacrifice that women had made during the war."

Screenshot from the making of 'Feto Nia Lian, Feto Nia Istoria'. Supplied / Wantok Musik Foundation

The three albums are IzuPi, Lolobremu, Feto Nia Lian - Feto Nia Istoria, and a single Pirilampu Nia Lalatak.

They explore the country's history, cultural identity, and the experiences of its people who lived through Indonesian occupation from 1975-1999.

Bridie saw immense value in capturing this history through music.

"During that 25 years of the occupation, cultural practice and ceremonies stopped because it wasn't safe to go anywhere.

"Timor Leste lost one in three people during that time, which was an incredible statistic. So for this record, for these younger artists who were so keen to get their the older ones to to record and tell them these stories meant even more."

Screenshot from the making of 'Feto Nia Lian, Feto Nia Istoria'. Supplied / Wantok Musik Foundation

One of the artists is IzuPi, who believes the music will play an important role in educating younger generations about their country's past.

"We can sing all the songs about love, about nature, things like that. But I think the important one to bring it up; education for the new generation will come.

It's more than music, it's still about Timor, still about the people, it's for Timoresian people to know about the history, to respect the history itself."

IzuPi hopes listeners will take the time to understand the history behind the songs, and find connections to their own lived experiences.

"The world need to know about music from Timor to share with other people.

"I think that not only in Timor that faces this struggle like this, but also other people from the other country, also face the same, like what we face in our country."

Timor-Leste artist IzuPi. Supplied / Joe Tham Studio

Bridie said it was imperative that the stories were told by the community itself.

The project not only supports musicians developing their career, it also helps communities retain control over how their history is portrayed.

"Every artist and all and the in the case of when there's you know the songs are recorded by the younger artists, but the songs were written by the older artists, for they own all of their copyright and they and their stories retold and written down," he said.

The music will be further celebrated through the Ita Nia Lian, Ita Nia Istoria - Our Voices Our Stories concert series in Australia, which will bring together Timorese arrtists with Australian First Nations and other regional performers.

The concerts are scheduled for Melbourne on 20 November and Sydney on 21 November.

Screenshot from the making of 'Feto Nia Lian, Feto Nia Istoria'. Supplied / Wantok Musik Foundation

Screenshot from the making of 'Feto Nia Lian, Feto Nia Istoria'. Supplied / Wantok Musik Foundation

World.title: Chris Hipkins puts job on the line over no new taxes beyond CGT
World.content:
Audio player for " Labour leader Chris Hipkins " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2354786%2Fchris-hipkins-puts-job-on-the-line-over-no-new-taxes-beyond-cgt

The polls are indicating a tight race between the left and right groups, meaning National or Labour would need to negotiate with multiple partners in order to form a government.

In an extended interview with Nine to Noon, Labour leader Chris Hipkins said his party has heard the message from voters who rejected the government he was leading in its final months before the last election.

"The cost of living was the number one issue in 2023 and we didn't have answers that the voters were convinced by."

Watch Chris Hipkins' full interview:

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407925225112

In contrast, it has been front and centre of this year's campaign, he said.

With unemployment at an 11-year high, it was critical to ensure small businesses were a priority so they could flourish and start hiring again.

Government contracts would help ease the woes in the construction sector and more apprenticeships would be a part of that.

No increases in fuel taxes, three free GP visits and public transport fare caps would all help ease cost of living pressures, Hipkins said.

"Pay equity will be huge for the New Zealand economy. When you give tens of thousands of care and support workers a pay increase you lift kids out of poverty and you put more money into the local economy."

No room for a wealth tax

Labour's priority would be to balance the budget and not add new taxes which meant the Greens' desire for a wealth tax would not be accommodated.

"It [a wealth tax] hasn't worked anywhere else in the world and there's a reason why countries that have them are taking them away because ultimately they don't work."

While the Greens, Te Pāti Māori and Opportunity had plans for major tax reforms, "there isn't a public appetite for tax reform that is that radical," Hipkins said.

"We will not support new taxes that we do not have a public mandate for."

Hipkins said he would put his job on the line over not introducing new taxes, apart from a capital gains tax.

A capital gains tax was supported by the public and was "long overdue".

He cited its success in Australia where it had increased revenue for the government over time.

Chris Hipkins on the campaign trail in Palmerston North. Zach Cornelisen / RNZ

Inflation blame

Hipkins was asked if the last Labour government borrowed and spent too much during the pandemic, causing inflationary pressure that was still persisting. He disagreed.

New Zealand's peak rate in the post-pandemic period was 7.4 percent while other countries, such as the United Kingdom, reached double figures.

"We were hit by a global wave of inflation."

Inflation was at 4.6 percent when Labour left office and had risen when the coalition government took office, Hipkins said.

Ryan said Labour's fiscal plan was similar to National's despite Labour accusing the coalition government of producing an austerity Budget last year and people were confused as to how these things added up.

Hipkins responded it was important to balance the Budget and pointed to the Clark government in the 1990s which had demonstrated that if the Budget was balanced, big legacy items such as interest free student loans, free early childhood education, KiwiSaver, and Working for Families were options that could be brought to fruition.

Ryan pointed out that they also came from bigger Budget surpluses than even Treasury had estimated and asked how Labour could pay for bringing back the pay equity scheme if it wanted to be fiscally responsible.

By doing away with the current government's Investment Boost which largely benefited major businesses, millions of dollars would be saved. Instead, some funding would be directed at small businesses, Hipkins said.

"That will save us some money and we are going to put that money into pay equity, amongst other things. So we have set out different choices and different piorities but we will be responsible with the way we manage the government's finances."

The new capital gains tax would provide billions of dollars for the health system.

Labour had released a specific policy on easing the emergency care crisis in public hospitals, Hipkins said.

Those with winter ailments should be treated elsewhere, he said.

"So making primary care free will be the biggest change to the health system since the first Labour government made hospital care free. That will keep people out of hospital."

The other major pressure on hospitals was the increase in elderly patients when care in the community would be much more preferable and was part of Labour's policy.

It would take a "significant investment", he said.

Education changes

The literacy standards introduced by the current government was based on work the previous Labour government had done and would be retained, he said.

The NCEA changes would need to be slowed down because "ramming through big changes to the school qualification system" wasn't something politicians should do.

The system needed to be changed because it was resulting in children being overassessed and "a grab-bag of credits for kids".

Hipkins was confident he could lead a multi-party government despite his time as prime minister being when Labour was the sole party in government.

He would set clear standards of what was expected.

"Everybody does need to work together to make government work. You can't have a situation where Winston Peters, Shane Jones, David Seymour, whoever is going out go out and pretend ing to be a separate government."

He ruled out sharing the role of Finance Minister which would be filled by Barbara Edmonds and there would be no Treasurer.

World.title: St John will delay shut down of specialist paramedic team who help police and firefighters
World.content:
St John ambulance says it is delaying the shut down of three specialist emergency response teams that back police and firefighters during armed confrontations.

RNZ revealed earlier on Thursday, the ambulance service told police and Fire and Emergency as late as Tuesday it was shutting down the paramedic teams from December 20.

The teams have backed up police in armed confrontations including at the mosque attacks in 2019, and firefighters in cliff, tunnel and gas emergencies. St John said they primarily supported police at tactical operations.

The teams have no dedicated funding, St John said, and it had to focus on core services.

Health New Zealand confirmed to RNZ it turned down a funding request.

St John now said it was delaying its decision to shut them down for several weeks.

It "had advised its people and partners of an operational decision to stop operating its Specialist Emergency Response Team (SERT) in December 2026," deputy chief executive Dan Ohs said in a statement on Thursday morning.

Deputy chief executive Dan Ohs. (File photo) RNZ / Nate McKinnon

"This reflected a change in the way services have been delivered, and would not result in a reduction in frontline roles.

"As part of other operating discussions since then, St John has decided to delay its decision to stop SERT operations while additional detail is worked through."

Ohs expected this to take several weeks and would confirm the future of SERT as soon as feasible.

A union, the NZ Ambulance Association said St John had asked police to help fund SERT. St John has not confirmed this.

The Emergency Management Minister and Police Minister Mark Mitchell's office referred RNZ's query to the associate health minister.

"This activity is provided on a 'best endeavours' basis and is not something St John is contracted to provide by Health New Zealand or ACC," Ohs said.

On Thursday morning the government announced $258m extra funding for St John for over 220 additional ambulance officers, call handlers, dispatchers and clinicians.

The first 22 paramedics and technicians would be ready by mid 2027 under a new four-year contract that had been agreed in principle.

"This investment means more crews on the road, more people answering calls, and better equipment for the people who respond," Associate Health Minister Casey Costello said in a statement.

About $220m of funding would go towards helping recruit volunteers, boosting crew safety and buying clinical equipment and digital and data systems among other things.

Day-to-day operating costs would be fully funded through Health NZ, ACC and patient part charges by mid-2028.

Another $22m from Budget 2026 and $15m from ACC would go on two new ambulance hubs and one smaller station in Auckland, among other things.

World.title: 'Nothing to do': Young people hit hard by job shortage - youth worker
World.content:
Audio player for " Alex Le Long on youth unemployment rising to 15.2 percent " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/business/2355246%2Fnothing-to-do-young-people-hit-hard-by-job-shortage-youth-worker

Alex Le Long on youth unemployment rising to 15.2 percent Morning Report Download MP3 5m

Young jobless people are left feeling bored and apathetic as they struggle to find jobs or training opportunities, a youth worker says.

Unemployment among those aged between 15 and 24 is sitting at almost three times the rate of the general population.

The latest unemployment figures which were released on Wednesday were higher than expected, at 5.7 percent, the highest they have been in 11 years.

That means 174,000 people are now out of work, 3000 more than in the June 2026 quarter.

Unemployment among people aged 15 to 24 increased to 15.2 percent, almost three times the general population rate.

The number of 15 to 24 year olds who are not in employment, education or training (NEET) is up from 13.8 percent to 14.1 percent.

The numbers are much higher in the regions.

Alex Le Long, who runs Te Araroa Evolutions Charitable Trust in Ōpōtiki where almost half of young people are not in employment, education or training, said she was seeing more people struggling with finding employment or education.

"Walking around very late at night, sometimes up to 11 o'clock, they've got nothing to do.

"They're very bored, apathetic. They're sitting in homes, sitting in places at the playground. There's nothing for them to do.

"We've just had two very important programmes closed down here, and that has reinforced the need to wrap around our young people even more."

She said the first programme to close was the Youth to Employment programme that specifically supported young people into programmes to develop their confidence and help them get into employment.

That was followed by the closure of Te Ara Tau, which helped full-time parents get back into work.

"They need confidence, understanding, someone who can actually hear them, listen, create a safe space for them to be able to figure out what their passions are. And we don't really have many safe places like that in Ōpōtiki outside of school and those programmes."

Le Long said a lot of the jobs in the region were seasonal, with local larger businesses such as Mitre 10 and New World doing what they could to take on younger people.

She said places like Ōpōtiki would benefit from career and jobs expos to showcase what jobs were actually available. A recent job opening received 47 applications.

"We have some incredible organisations in our town that already do mahi with our young people. One of them is Charlie Hayes Engineering. They do incredible work with all of our young kids that are interested in welding.

"It's about developing confidence in our young people. So I'm incredibly optimistic, but we also have to be realistic because our young people don't feel comfortable when they come back from university, some kids have still not found jobs after going to university.

World.title: Rarely used rule sees Renegades claim final ball win in WBBL thriller
World.content:
One of cricket's rarely needed rules has cost the Hobart Hurricanes in a four-wicket WBBL loss to the Melbourne Renegades.

With one ball remaining in the Renegades' run chase, scores were locked at 154 runs apiece in a Wednesday night thriller in Hobart.

Renegades batter Deandra Dottin missed the final delivery, which was taken by wicketkeeper Lizelle Lee standing up to the stumps.

But as players readied for a super over finish, replays showed Lee had taken the ball just in front of the stumps, leading to a no-ball — and a Renegades victory.

The Hurricanes, with captain Nicola Carey top-scoring with 62 from 43 balls, posted 7-154 despite Renegades skipper Sophie Molineux capturing 4-22.

The Renegades, powered by opener Hayley Matthews (59 from 44 balls), were cruising at 1-101 in the 13th over.

But the visitors stumbled, losing 5-37 to set up a bizarre finish that also featured a fielding restriction penalty against Hobart.

The Hurricanes remain winless on the bottom of the ladder after three games amid injury concern over West Indian ace Chinelle Henry.

Henry smacked 36 from 18 balls in Hobart's innings but, after bowling just one over costing 14 runs, hobbled from the field with a suspected hip injury.

Henry's departure came as her compatriot Matthews dominated Hobart's bowlers with a classy knock laced with eight boundaries.

Matthews and Courtney Webb (29 from 25) advanced the Renegades to 1-101 before late twists.

Webb's dismissal was rapidly followed by Molineux (six) falling to a spectacular caught-and-bowled by Molly Strano, who leapt high to complete a one-hander.

In the next over, the dangerous Matthews was bowled by Graham as the visitors slipped from 1-101 in the 13th over to a precarious 4-108 in a 12-ball span.

With 33 runs required from the last four overs, the Renegades took the power surge and soon whittled down their target to five runs from three balls.

Then, a fielding restriction penalty was imposed on the Hurricanes for not bowling their 20 overs in the specified time: they were only allowed two fielders outside the circle.

After a dot ball, Dottin edged the penultimate ball to the deep third man boundary, where a fielder likely would have been stationed.

With scores tied, Dottin couldn't make contact with the last ball and players converged, expecting a super over.

As they huddled, replays showed the gloves of Hurricanes keeper Lee taking the ball in front of the stumps and the umpires called a no ball, giving the Renegades the winning run and their first win of the tournament.

AAP

World.title: Keeper breaks silence after collision that led to Spanish player's death
World.content:
Warning: the video in this article may cause distress for some readers

Jesus Owono says he is going through the most difficult days of his life following the death of Tenerife forward Jesus De Miguel.

Owono and De Miguel were involved in a collision during a match between Andorra and Tenerife on Monday, after which the striker was taken into intensive care. De Miguel died on Tuesday morning.

"These are the most difficult days of my life," Owono said in a statement released by his club FC Andorra on Wednesday, local time.

Footballer dies after on-field collision Tenerife forward Jesús de Miguel dies after a horrific clash with an opposition goalkeeper that has sparked an investigation by Spanish police.

"I struggle to find the words, and I find it very hard to process what has happened. I know there will be many questions to address, and I will face whatever comes with the utmost respect.

"But right now, honestly, I cannot think about anything other than Jesus and the pain we are experiencing. Rest in peace, Jesus."

Owono deactivated his Instagram account on Tuesday after receiving abuse online, with some users commenting 'murderer' on his posts. Andorra said that they were offering psychological support to anyone at the club who needed it following De Miguel's death.

Andorra centre back Lautaro Spatz defended his teammate Owono on Tuesday evening.

"I also want to say a few words about my teammate, goalkeeper and friend, who is deeply affected by what has happened," Spatz said on social media.

"Those of us who know him know the kind of person he is, how much he is suffering at this moment, and that he would never intentionally hurt anyone."

"In football, unfortunate incidents can happen, but no one could imagine that one of them might end with such tragic consequences," continued Spatz, also sending his condolences to De Miguel's family and Tenerife.

The Equatoguinean Football Federation expressed support for Owono in a statement on Tuesday, adding that the 25-year-old was going through profound sorrow and grief.

Owono has made 47 international appearances for Equatorial Guinea.

Can Vidalet goalkeeper Michel Owono said on social media that he was receiving racist abuse, with people confusing him with the Andorra player.

Spanish national police have opened a routine investigation into De Miguel's death.

Reuters

World.title: Opetaia moves up to heavyweight to fight former world champ Wilder
World.content:
Jai Opetaia has been handed the fight of his life as he gambles on moving up to heavyweight to take on thunder-hitting former world champion Deontay Wilder.

Australia's unbeaten cruiserweight maestro, a contender for the sport's best pound-for-pound fighter, will venture into uncharted waters by tackling the explosive American veteran on the undercard of the blockbuster Tyson Fury-Anthony Joshua show at Principality Stadium in Cardiff on December 11.

Wilder is now 41 and perhaps not the destructive force of old, but taking on one of the biggest hitters the sport has witnessed still represents a daring gamble for Opetaia, who is 10 years his junior, as the world-beating Gold Coast-based southpaw and The Ring Magazine champion protects his perfect 31-fight record.

It is the first major fight above the 200-pound division for Opetaia, with his promoter Dana White admitting: "It's a very dangerous fight for him considering where he sits in his division right now.

"But he's a fighter; he'll fight anybody, even at heavyweight with a guy who hits as hard as Wilder does."

It looks poised to be a one-off, with Opetaia likely returning to cruiserweight afterwards to chase a showdown with American David Benavidez, the division's other major unbeaten force.

Last time out in Nevada in September, Opetaia stopped Noel Mikaelian in the ninth round and called out ringside observer Benavidez, whose heritage has earned him the nickname the "Mexican Monster", with the request: "Respectfully, let's get it on.

"That's the fight Jai really wants, so we've got to figure that one out," White said.

"He wants to stay active, he wants to fight, and he doesn't care if it's at heavyweight or wherever. He's ready to go."

Wilder, though, is by far the biggest name Opetaia will have faced, a champion who held the WBC belt for five years between 2015 and 2020 and who had an epic trilogy of fights with Briton Fury, coming off worse twice after an extraordinary draw in their first bout.

But he has lost four of his last seven contests and, in his last outing, had to battle to earn a scruffy points win over British contender Derek Chisora in London in April, leaving his career record at 45 wins, four losses and a draw.

The all-British bill-topper between Fury ​and Joshua is being sold as the biggest night of boxing ever witnessed in the UK, with tickets in Cardiff going within an hour of going on sale and the bill being screened globally on Netflix.

AAP

World.title: Aussie stuns Djokovic to end tennis legend's ATP Finals chances
World.content:
Australian Rinky Hijikata has pulled off a stunning upset over 24-time grand slam champion Novak Djokovic, eliminating him from the Paris Masters and ending his hopes of qualifying for the end-of-year ATP Finals.

Hijikata played the match of his life as he cracked 37 winners, including 29 forehand bullets, that earned him a 2-6, 6-3, 6-3 comeback triumph in the second round.

Djokovic had a chance to make the Finals if he could reach the Paris semifinals, but he found an inspired opponent in Hijikata.

Loading Instagram content

"I wasn't even close to his level in that set. I couldn't touch his serve either, he was acing me for fun," beamed Hijikata in an interview with Sky Sports.

"I knew I just had to really hang tough, and take it to him and play aggressive, impose myself, and I guess in the end I was glad I could maintain my level for as long as I did and trust myself in the big moments."

Meanwhile, Australia's number one ranked player Alex de Minaur had his hopes of making the ATP Finals for a third consecutive year dashed with an upset loss to world number 31 Tomas Martin Etcheverry.

De Minaur was nowhere near his best as Etcheverry earned his first ever victory over a top-10 player 7-6 (7-2), 6-3 at Paris's Plenitude Arena.

But with an inconsistent display that mirrored his uneven season, de Minaur really missed his chance when Etcheverry, who quite out-served the Aussie, had a lapse when serving at 5-6 down in the opening stanza to cough up a couple of set points.

Tomas Martin Etcheverry (left) knocked Australian Alex De Minaur (right) out of the Paris Masters. (Getty Images: Shi Tang)

But the Argentine rallied to take the set into a tiebreak and then proved the more patient in its long, drawn-out rallies as he took the last five points in row.

At 2-3 down in the second set, de Minaur served a crucial double fault to give Etcheverry the key break that he never looked like surrendering.

The dispiriting reverse left de Minaur stranded in ninth place in the live Race to Turin standings, one spot behind young Spanish sensation Rafael Jodar, with no chance of picking up any more points as Paris is the last qualifying event.

His only hope now of getting into the Turin field is if one of the current top-eight pull out. Flavio Cobolli, who's already qualified, isn't competing in Paris because of his leg injury but he's expected to be fit for the Italian event.

And de Minaur could, in any case, yet be overtaken by others before the week in Paris is out.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Swans star returns positive drug test during roadside stop
World.content:
Sydney Swans star Tom Papley has returned a positive preliminary drug test after being pulled over by NSW Police, who allege he was driving with a suspended licence.

NSW Police confirmed a 30-year-old-man was stopped around 10.30am on Monday, November 2, for random testing.

Police said the man allegedly returned a positive result for methylamphetamine.

In their own statement, the Sydney Swans said Papley was pulled over by police on Monday for a roadside licence check.

Papley was issued with a court attendance notice for driving with a suspended licence, due to an unpaid parking fine.

Papley then completed a random drug test that returned a positive preliminary indication. A second sample was taken for analysis.

The results of that second sample will not be received for at least four weeks.

The Swans said Papley informed the club of the matter "immediately". The AFL has also been informed.

Papley has played 216 games for Sydney and is one of the Swans' best players. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Papley, who has played 216 games for the Swans, is one of the club's best players and widely regarded as one of the AFL's best small forwards.

It has been a controversial few months for the Sydney Swans, headlined by the scandal at the Pullman Hotel in Melbourne in August.

Vice-captain Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice were stood down from round 24 and the club's two finals for what the Swans termed a "serious breach of expected club behaviour and standards".

Those AFL-endorsed club bans were separate from the ongoing police investigation into an alleged sexual assault at the Pullman Hotel. No charges have been laid, and there is no suggestion of wrongdoing on the part of the suspended players.

World.title: Staggs says he means no harm by refusing to sing Australian anthem
World.content:
Kotoni Staggs says his decision not to sing the national anthem comes from a place of respect, as he and his Kangaroos teammates find themselves at the centre of a culture war.

Staggs and several fellow Australia team members, who will face Samoa in Sunday's World Cup semifinal at the Sydney Football Stadium, have been criticised throughout the tournament because of their refusal to sing the pre-game anthem.

The Brisbane centre received the backing of Broncos teammate Pat Carrigan for his stance, hoping the decision would open up a wider discussion about Australia's history.

Kangaroos pile on the points in World Cup thrashing of Cook Islands The Kangaroos go undefeated through the group stage of the Rugby League World Cup as they close out the Pool A action with a 66-6 win over Cook Islands in Townsville.

Staggs, who has won nine caps for the Kangaroos since his debut in 2023, said: "I'm a proud Wirajudri boy and I'm proud of who I am and where I come from, and me not singing an anthem doesn't mean that I'm not grateful.

"I still love wearing that jersey. When the anthem is getting played you look around and get emotional.

"But me not singing, it's a whole different meaning to that and that's just me."

Staggs said his position on singing Advance Australia Fair came from wanting to honour his ancestors.

"Obviously in the past and what happened back in the day I've just learned from that," Staggs said.

"You also talk to your elders from back home and grandparents and stuff and [understand] what they had to go through. It's more of a respect for my elders and my family.

Kotoni Staggs says his refusal to sing the national anthem does not take away from his love of representing Australia. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

"I'm a proud Australian as well but at the end of the day it's just something that I've lived by, and I've got no harm in it. It doesn't take anything away from the jersey I wear."

Criticism of Staggs and other Indigenous Kangaroos stars, including Latrell Mitchell, is nothing new.

Jillaroos coach Jess Skinner, a proud Barkindji and Māori woman, has also stressed the importance of walking out alongside the Australian, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Island flags during the World Cup.
